After the gate allows a call it applies the tool's own path containment: `read`, `find`, `inspect`, `repo_map` and `analyze` refuse a path outside the project root in every mode but `yolo`, and `write` and `edit` refuse one in every mode, reported as `DENY` decided by `<tool> tool path containment`. The `decision model:` line says `consulted`, `not needed: a rule, a setting or the mode settled this call`, or `not consulted: <why> The verdict is the one the gate gives without a decision model.` (none set, `No Decision Model`, or the set model failing). A remembered-rules file that cannot be read is named on the `rules:` line (the running app refuses every call until it loads). It does not use the workspace trust of the directory. Treat `ASK` as "this reaches an owner prompt". It exits `0`; with no subject it prints usage and exits `2`. With `--json` the fields include `mode`, `savedMode`, `modeReason`, `decisionModel`, `decisionModelConsulted`, `containment` and `verdict`.

## The decision model

The decision model answers judgment calls at the gate and many other decisions (reading a natural-language schedule, triaging mail, reading a channel message for card details, grading a merchant). Every decision has a stated fallback.

### Decision model policy

`judgment.policy` takes three values. It is independent of `permissions.mode`.

| Value | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `Hybrid` (default) | Uses the set decision model. When it fails (unreachable, too slow, a refused or missing key, a malformed answer), work continues without it: each decision takes its fallback, and you are told once, naming the model, what failed and the next step. You are told again when it answers. |
| `Decision Model Only` | Uses the set decision model. When it fails, work that needs it stops and reports the model, what failed and the next step. At the gate, the call fails with the model's error instead of asking you. |
| `No Decision Model` | Makes no decision-model requests. |

With no decision model set, every policy runs without one: nothing is asked, nothing waits, and no error is shown.

All `judgment.*` settings are kept in the daemon's settings file (`~/.goodvibes/daemon/settings.json`): one value, shared by the terminal app, the Agent and the daemon. Changing `judgment.policy` from any app changes it for all of them until it is changed back; there is no per-session decision model policy.

Only a failure of the set model downgrades `Hybrid`. An answer, an abstention, a privacy refusal, a limit or a cancellation does not. A setting value outside the three is reported by name with the valid values, and the product runs on `Hybrid`.

```text
/settings set judgment.policy No Decision Model
/settings set judgment.policy Hybrid
```

### Setting up the hosted decision model (Jev)

Prerequisite: a TypeSafe API key for the hosted endpoint.

1. Put the key in the environment variable `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` for the process (or the daemon service), or store it in the secret store and point the settings at it:

   ```text
   /secrets set TYPESAFE_API_KEY <your-api-key> --scope user
   /settings set judgment.keySource secret
   /settings set judgment.keyName TYPESAFE_API_KEY
   ```

2. Leave `judgment.endpoint` and `judgment.model` empty to use `https://api.typesafe.ai` and `jev-latest`.
3. Check: `goodvibes status` prints under `Decision model:` either `A decision model is in use (Hybrid (default)).` or `No decision model is in use: none is set, so decisions take their fallbacks. To use one, choose a Decision model in /settings open.`

`judgment.keySource` takes `env` (read the environment variable named by `judgment.keyName`), `secret` (read the secret-store entry named by `judgment.keyName`) or `none` (no authentication, for a local deployment). `judgment.keyName` is a name, never a key value.

### Setting up another decision model

| Setting | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `judgment.endpoint` | The decision endpoint's base URL (`http` or `https`). Empty uses `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL`, then the hosted endpoint `https://api.typesafe.ai`. A loopback address (`localhost`, `127.x.x.x`, `::1`) marks a local model. Embedded credentials, query strings and fragments are refused. While `judgment.keySource` is not `none`, the endpoint is changed or reset only in the same update as `judgment.keySource` or `judgment.keyName` (keep it by sending its current value, or clear it with `none`); alone it is refused with `CREDENTIAL_DESTINATION_UNBOUND` and nothing is saved, so a key is never sent to an address nobody chose it for. The settings screens do this for you: the terminal's decision-model picker asks for the credential with the endpoint, and the web UI's edit and Reset set authentication to none. |
| `judgment.model` | The model name sent in each request. Empty uses `TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL`, then `jev-latest`. |
| `judgment.keySource` | `env`, `secret` or `none`. |
| `judgment.keyName` | The environment variable (`env`) or secret-store entry (`secret`) holding the key. It must be a non-empty name (letters, digits, `_ . / : -`); with `keySource` `none` it is ignored, so leave it as it is. |
| `judgment.backend` | Optional `{ "adapter", "maxInputBytes", "maxQuestions", "responseModels" }` for the primary target. |
| `judgment.fallbacks` | Ordered backup targets, each `{ "endpoint", "model", "keySource", "keyName" }` plus optional `"backend"`. In a fallback, `keySource` may be `env`, `secret` or `none`, and `none` requires `"keyName": ""`. The default is `[]` (no backups). |
| `judgment.timeoutMs` | Timeout per target, default `30000`; `0` means the default. |
| `judgment.decisionDeadlineMs` | How long a decision that a person or a tool call waits on may take, default `1500`, range 1 to 120000, permission decisions at the gate included (one deadline for the whole decision). Past it the decision takes its stated fallback (see "Timeouts and the decision deadline"). A target that misses the deadline three times in a row is skipped for a minute. |

#### The wire protocol ("System One")

Every adapter except `cloudflare-workers-ai` speaks the System One protocol of `@typesafe-ai/sdk`:

- `POST <endpoint>/v1/systemone` with headers `Content-Type: application/json`, `Accept: application/json`, and `Authorization: Bearer <key>` unless `keySource` is `none`. Redirects are refused.
- Request body: `{ "model": "<judgment.model>", "state": <text, JSON object or array, or null>, "questions": { "<name>": <question>, ... } }`. A question is one of:
  - `{ "type": "noul", "instructions": ..., "criteria": { "true": ..., "false": ... } }` (yes or no);
  - `{ "type": "choice", "instructions": ..., "criteria": { "<label>": <description>, ... } }`;
  - `{ "type": "score", "instructions": ..., "criteria": [<description for 0>, <for 1>, ...] }`.
- Response body (HTTP 200): `{ "model": "<model that answered>", "answers": { "<name>": <answer>, ... }, "usage": { "input_tokens": <n>, "output_tokens": <n> } }`, with one answer per question name:
  - `{ "type": "noul", "noul": <probability of yes, 0 to 1> }`;
  - `{ "type": "choice", "choice": "<label>", "confidence": <0 to 1>, "probabilities": { "<label>": <p>, ... } }`;
  - `{ "type": "score", "score": <expected score>, "confidence": <0 to 1>, "legend": {...}, "probabilities": { "0": <p>, ... } }`.
- `usage` is required. A response that reports cut-off input (`truncated: true`, `usage.truncated` true or above 0, `usage.state_tokens_dropped` above 0, a non-empty `usage.truncated_questions`, or `usage.state_tokens_used` below `usage.state_tokens`) is refused as incomplete evidence.
- The answering `model` must equal the requested one. For a request of `jev-latest` or `jev-preview`, a pinned `jev-<x>.<y>.<z>` answer is accepted; any other alias the server answers with must be listed in `backend.responseModels`.
- An HTTP 400 with `detail.error_type` `max_tokens_exceeded` means the input is too long. Other HTTP errors: 408, 429 and 5xx count as the model being unavailable (retried once, then the next target); any other status as a refusal.
- `GET <endpoint>/v1/models` lists models (`{ "data": [{ "id": ... }] }` or `{ "models": [{ "name": ... }] }`); it is used only by model pickers.

The adapters:

| `backend.adapter` | Protocol | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `system-one` (default) | As above. | TypeSafe's hosted Jev and every local server on the same protocol. |
| `cloudflare-workers-ai` | `POST` to the endpoint URL itself (a Workers AI run URL, `https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/<account-id>/ai/run/@cf/cloudflare/clef` or `.../clef-flash`) with the same body; the answer comes wrapped as `{ "success": true, "result": { ...the response above... } }`. | Chosen automatically for such a URL. The model must be `clef` or `clef-flash` and match the URL's last segment. At most 64 questions with names of letters, digits, `_ . -`, and a bounded input size. The key is a Cloudflare API token (for example `keyName` `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`). |
| `laya` | `POST /v1/systemone`. | The server must keep truncation and Jev confidence metadata (`x_jev_confidence`; do not run it with `LAYA_JEV_STRICT`). An answer marked `abstain`, `unbound` or routed to review stops the decision. |

The named models (starting configurations, not a closed list):

| Name | `judgment.model` | Adapter | Where it comes from |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Jev | `jev-latest` | `system-one` | TypeSafe, hosted at `https://api.typesafe.ai` (docs.typesafe.ai/api). |
| Clef | `clef` | `cloudflare-workers-ai` | Cloudflare Workers AI. |
| Clef-flash | `clef-flash` | `cloudflare-workers-ai` | Cloudflare Workers AI. |
| DiffusionGemma Jev | `dgemma` | `system-one` | Self-hosted; github.com/mmastrac/djev. |
| Kev-9B | `kev-latest` | `system-one` | Self-hosted; github.com/jaredpalmer/kev. |
| Laya | `english` (answers as `laya-rl-agent`; put that in `backend.responseModels`) | `laya` | Self-hosted; github.com/NandhaKishorM/laya. |

#### A self-hosted decision model that stops the product when it is down

Prerequisite: a server speaking the protocol above, for example Kev-9B listening on `http://127.0.0.1:8080`.

```text
/settings set judgment.keySource none
/settings set judgment.endpoint http://127.0.0.1:8080
/settings set judgment.model kev-latest
/settings set judgment.backend {"adapter":"system-one"}
/settings set judgment.fallbacks []
/settings set judgment.policy Decision Model Only
/settings set permissions.mode jev-decides
```

- `judgment.fallbacks []` makes sure no hosted model answers in its place.
- `judgment.keySource none` comes first: while a credential is configured, `judgment.endpoint` changes only together with it (see below).
- `Decision Model Only` makes an outage stop work instead of falling back: a call that needs the model fails with the model's error (`System One could not be reached`, `System One answered HTTP <status>`), and the gate does not ask you instead. With `Hybrid` an outage would fall back silently after one notice.
- `permissions.mode jev-decides` is set explicitly: the unchosen default would behave as `ask-me` on a model the shipped calibration did not measure.
- With an authenticated server: `/secrets set KEV_API_KEY <your-api-key> --scope user`, `/settings set judgment.keySource secret`, `/settings set judgment.keyName KEV_API_KEY`.
- Check with `goodvibes status`. While the model answers, the `Decision model:` block reads `A decision model is in use (judgment.policy Decision Model Only).` After it has failed, the block and the one notice in the conversation read `The decision model <model> is unavailable (<what failed>); work that needs it stops (judgment.policy is Decision Model Only; Hybrid would continue without it). Next: <step>`. Under `Hybrid` the same line ends `continuing without it. Next: <step>`. Then ask for a change in the conversation: with the server stopped, the call fails with the error above.
- What stops and what does not: facts (reads and recoverable edits inside the project, matching rules, owner-only asks) never ask the model and keep working; only judgment calls and other work that needs the model fail.

#### Timeouts and the decision deadline

Two limits apply, to different requests:

- A permission decision (the reading of a judgment call, the boundary readings and Jev's decision in `jev-decides` and `just-vibes`) has one deadline for the whole decision: `judgment.decisionDeadlineMs` (default 1500). Each request it makes gets what is left of it, across retries and `judgment.fallbacks` targets (each attempt is still bounded by `judgment.timeoutMs`). When the model has not answered in time, the request fails as a missed deadline and the decision takes its fallback, as every other decision does: under `Hybrid` the gate's no-model rule decides (asks you, or holds the call in `just-vibes`) and the conversation gets the one failure notice; under `Decision Model Only` the tool call stops with `The decision model did not answer within <n> ms.` and nothing is asked. The missed deadline also starts a failure episode (see "When a decision model counts as working"). A target that misses the deadline three times in a row is skipped for a minute, so the next decisions take their fallback at once.
- `judgment.decisionDeadlineMs` (default 1500) bounds the other decisions a person or a tool call waits on (for example reading an inbound channel message). When one is not answered in time, it takes its own stated fallback in every policy, `Decision Model Only` included; the deadline is not a model failure and does not stop work. A target that misses the deadline three times in a row is skipped for a minute, and while every target is skipped those decisions take their fallback at once.
- Where the keys live: `judgment.*` is kept in the daemon's settings file (`~/.goodvibes/daemon/settings.json`), so one write from any app (or `goodvibes-daemon config set judgment.policy "Decision Model Only"`) sets it for every program and the daemon. `permissions.mode` is kept per program: the daemon has its own, so for daemon-run work (routines, triggers, channel turns) set it there too: `goodvibes-daemon config set permissions.mode jev-decides`.

### How you can tell no decision model is in use

- The conversation says so once when none is set or `No Decision Model` is chosen, once when a set model starts failing, and once when it answers again. A failure is not repeated every turn.
- `goodvibes status` and `goodvibes-agent status` print the policy and a `Decision model` line.
- A headless run prints the line on stderr and adds `diagnostics.decisionModel` to its JSON result without changing the exit code.
- The web UI's header chip names the permission mode in force: `Jev decides · asking you for now` while `jev-decides` is chosen and no decision model works (on a phone `Asking you for now`), otherwise the chosen mode (`Ask me`, `Just vibes`, `YOLO`). Opening it shows why in one sentence (for example `You chose Jev decides, but decision models are switched off, so GoodVibes asks you instead for now.`) and `Change`, which opens Settings, Permissions.
- Results that no decision model checked say so instead of claiming model verification.

Without a decision model, conversation, tools, editing, commands, tests and session recovery work as usual. Work that needs one says so when none is in use: autonomous contract execution, independent semantic knowledge verification, merchant and checkout interpretation, and semantic recommendations or grading.

### Call-volume alerts

`judgment.volumeMonitor` raises local alerts when decision traffic passes a budget. Alerts go to the runtime log; they never call a model or stop work.

```text
/settings set judgment.volumeMonitor {"enabled":true,"budgets":[{"name":"All decisions","maxLogicalDecisions":1000,"maxWireAttempts":2000}]}
```

Enabled monitoring needs 1 to 100 budgets. Optional per budget: `battery` or `site` to restrict it. Optional: `windowMs` (default one hour, 1 second to 30 days), `intervalMs` (default one minute, 1 second to 1 day), `limit` (default 10000 log entries, 1 to 100000). The environment variable `GOODVIBES_JUDGMENT_MONITOR` names a budget file that applies even when the setting is disabled.

### Exporting gate decisions

`telemetry.decisionOtlpEnabled`, `telemetry.decisionOtlpEndpoint` and `telemetry.decisionOtlpSignal` (`span`, `log` or `both`) export each permission decision to an OTLP/HTTP JSON collector: spans to `<endpoint>/v1/traces`, logs to `<endpoint>/v1/logs`. Off by default.

## Managed policy bundles

A managed policy is a versioned bundle of rules the gate reads before the owner's remembered rules. It is used only when `permissions.engine` is `policy-engine` (restart to apply) and `policy.registryEnabled` is `true`.

```text
/security policy-screen                   open the policy screen (terminal app)
/security policy                          the bundle in force, the candidate, the history
/security load-policy <bundle-file>       load a candidate bundle from a JSON file
/security simulate-policy                 rule diff and the recorded calls the candidate decides differently
/security compare-policy                  rule diff, current against candidate
/security lint-policy                     lint the active and candidate bundles
/security preflight                       review proactive policy and MCP risk state
/security enforce-policy                  enforce the candidate simulate-policy showed (asks first; only you; a candidate loaded or changed since is refused: simulate it first)
/security restore-policy                  restore the previous active bundle (asks first; only you)
```

### Bundle file format

A bundle is one JSON object:

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bundleId` | yes | A non-empty string naming this bundle version. |
| `issuedAt` | no | ISO 8601 time the bundle was issued. Part of the signed content. |
| `issuer` | no | Who issued it, shown in `/security policy`. Part of the signed content. |
| `payload` | yes | `{ "version": <number>, "rules": [ ... ], "description": "<text>" }`. `rules` must be an array. |
| `signature` | no | Hex HMAC-SHA256 of the canonical JSON of `{ bundleId, issuedAt, issuer, payload }` (keys sorted at every level, undefined fields left out). |

Every rule has `id` (string), `type`, `effect` (`allow` or `deny` only; `ask` is refused in a bundle), an optional `description`, and an optional `origin`, which may only be `managed` (the loader marks every bundle rule managed). The types:

| `type` | Fields | Matches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `prefix` | `toolPattern`; optional `commandPrefixes` (list), `exactCommands` (list) | Calls of the tools whose command starts with a prefix, or equals an exact command. With neither list, every call of the tools. |
| `arg-shape` | `toolPattern`, `argMatchers` (a non-empty object) | Calls whose arguments hold every listed key with that value; a value starting with `/` is a regular expression. |
| `path-scope` | `toolPattern`, `pathPatterns` (non-empty list) | Calls whose path arguments fall under a pattern. Relative patterns are read from the project root. A pattern with no wildcard covers that path and everything below it; `*` matches within one segment, `**` across segments, `?` one character; `dir/**` covers `dir` too. Braces and negation are not supported. |
| `network-scope` | `toolPattern`, `hostPatterns` (non-empty list of host globs); optional `ports` (0 to 65535; `0` means any) | Calls to those hosts. |
| `mode-constraint` | `toolPattern`, `activeModes` (non-empty list of `default`, `plan`, `allow-all`); optional `classifications` (`read`, `write`, `escalation`) | Calls made in those modes. `default` is `ask-me`, `jev-decides` and `just-vibes`; `allow-all` is `yolo`. |

`toolPattern` is a tool name, `"*"` for any tool, or a list of names. A bundle with a malformed rule is refused whole, naming the rule, for example `Not a policy bundle: rule 2 (path-scope) needs pathPatterns: a non-empty list of path globs.`

Example (`/home/me/policy/team.json`):

```json
{
  "bundleId": "team-2026-11",
  "issuedAt": "2026-11-18T09:00:00Z",
  "issuer": "platform team",
  "payload": {
    "version": 1,
    "description": "No force pushes, no writes outside src, fetch only from our hosts",
    "rules": [
      { "id": "no-force-push", "type": "prefix", "effect": "deny", "toolPattern": "exec", "commandPrefixes": ["git push --force", "git push -f"] },
      { "id": "src-only-writes", "type": "path-scope", "effect": "allow", "toolPattern": ["write", "edit"], "pathPatterns": ["src/**"] },
      { "id": "our-hosts", "type": "network-scope", "effect": "allow", "toolPattern": "fetch", "hostPatterns": ["*.example.com"] }
    ]
  }
}
```

Loading and promoting it:

```text
/settings set permissions.engine policy-engine
/settings set policy.registryEnabled true
(restart the app)
/security load-policy /home/me/policy/team.json
/security simulate-policy
/security enforce-policy
```

The managed evaluator's default for a call no rule matches is deny; that deny is reported as managed policy only when a rule decided it, so an unmatched call continues through the ordinary order. `/security load-policy` reports `[policy] Candidate loaded` and suggests `/security simulate-policy`; a refused bundle prints `[policy] Load failed: <reason>` and leaves the current and candidate bundles unchanged. A promoted bundle is recorded in `policy-activation.json` beside `permission-rules.json` and is enforced again at the next start while it is unchanged.

`policy.bundleSource` `file` with `policy.bundlePath` (absolute, or relative to the working directory) loads a bundle as a candidate at start; a bundle that cannot be read or is refused is logged and named in `/security policy`. `policy.requireSignedBundles` refuses every bundle without a valid signature made with the hex key in `GOODVIBES_POLICY_SIGNING_KEY` (at least 16 bytes, 32 hex characters; restart to apply). A bundle whose signature is present but does not verify is refused whatever this setting says. `permissions.simulation` (default on) runs the other evaluator beside the active one and records where they disagree, without changing what is enforced; `permissions.divergenceDashboard`, `permissions.divergenceThreshold` and `permissions.maxDivergenceRecords` control that record. The policy actions of `/security` work in both terminal programs; the policy screen is the terminal app's.

## Workspace trust

Every workspace (working directory) has a trust level: `trusted`, `restricted`, or undecided.

| Level | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `trusted` | All tools may run, subject to the permission mode and rules. |
| `restricted` | Only reads run. Every write, command and delegation is refused, in every mode including `yolo`. |
| undecided | Reads run. Calls settled without asking run. The first call that would ask you raises the trust question instead: "New workspace: choose a trust level", with "Trust this workspace" and "Keep restricted (read-only)". Choosing trust forwards the original ask to you. |

```text
/security folder                     show the level, whether it is decided, and the registration
/security trust-folder               trust this folder (loosens a protection: asks first, only you)
/security restrict-folder            restrict this folder
/security trust                      what is trusted: permission mode, secrets, services, plugins, MCP servers
/security save-trust <file> [--replace]
/security read-trust <file>
```

- Decisions are kept in `~/.goodvibes/shared/workspace-registrations.json`, one row per directory by its real path, shared by every product. A `trust.json` inside a project is not honoured; `/security folder` says so when it finds one.
- When a decision cannot be saved, it applies to this session only and the app says it will ask again next time.
- With nobody to answer (a headless run without `--answer-permissions`), a call that needs the trust answer is refused: `Workspace trust for <dir> is undecided and the trust question was not answered here, so the workspace stays undecided.` Fix: run `/security trust-folder`, or answer the workspace-trust prompt of a run started with `--answer-permissions`.
- An unreadable trust record is treated as restricted for autonomous work until a level is chosen.
- `goodvibes status` shows `Workspace: trust: <level>` and the registration.

### Path containment

Two separate checks:

- The gate classes paths lexically against the working directory: a read or recoverable edit runs without asking only inside it (step 8). A path outside it makes the call a judgment call in every mode but `yolo`.
- The tools resolve symbolic links and refuse a path that lands outside the project root with `Path '<p>' is outside the project root`. The `write` and `edit` tools refuse it in every mode, `yolo` included (they also refuse the verification journal under `.goodvibes/verification` and any directory that contains it). The `analyze` tool refuses it in every mode. The `read`, `find` and `inspect` tools refuse it in every mode except `yolo`, where they read outside. That `yolo` exception follows the mode in the app's settings (saved, `--yolo`, `-c permissions.mode=yolo`, Shift+Tab, or a saved `behavior.autoApprove`), not a hosted session's own `yolo` set through `sessions.permissionMode.set`. Whatever the gate or the owner answered, these tools never write outside the project, and read outside it only in `yolo`; a shell command run through `exec` (for example `cat` or `cp`) is not stopped by this check, only by the gate and the exec sandbox.

## The exec sandbox

On Linux with bubblewrap (`bwrap`) installed, each shell command the `exec` tool runs is contained:

- the workspace is writable, and so are the paths in `sandbox.workspaceWritable`;
- the rest of the file system is read-only, `/tmp` is private, `$HOME` is masked;
- credential-bearing environment variables are removed;
- the network is off. It is opened only when both hold: the decision model reads the command as needing the network, and every command in the line is listed in `sandbox.egressAllowlist`. The allowlist alone never opens it: a listed command the model reads as not needing the network gets none, and with no decision model in use no command gets the network, listed or not (the command is put to you instead: `Without a decision model, this did not assess command host-access needs; owner approval is required inside the sandbox`, and approving runs it inside the boundary, still offline). A command read as needing the network and fully listed is put to you as `wants network (on egress allowlist, granted inside the boundary once approved)`; approving grants it for that run. Who answers that ask follows the mode: in `ask-me`, and in `jev-decides` without a working decision model, it is put to you on the approval card (annotated per `sandbox.judgment`); otherwise the call's own recorded admission (Jev's decision) answers it. One read as needing the network but not fully listed is told `denied inside the boundary and approval does not change that; add it to sandbox.egressAllowlist`.

Where bubblewrap is missing, on macOS, and on native Windows, the exec path runs on the host and the sandbox reports itself unavailable. On Windows, run GoodVibes in WSL 2 with bubblewrap installed to get the boundary.

| Setting | Default | Applies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sandbox.enabled` | `true` | Turning it on takes effect at the next start (the host is probed then). Turning it off applies from the next command. |
| `sandbox.workspaceWritable` | `[]` | Absolute paths only; a relative path is refused. From the next command. |
| `sandbox.egressAllowlist` | `[]` | Command names, for example `["git","npm"]`; `["*"]` counts every command as listed (the decision model must still read a need). From the next command. |
| `sandbox.judgment` | `annotate` | `off`: plain asks. `annotate`: a model verdict with reasons annotates a sandbox escalation ask; you still decide. `auto-approve`: also approves looks-safe verdicts. Never auto-denies. |
| `sandbox.mcpIsolation` | `disabled` | `disabled`: stdio MCP servers run as host processes. `contained`: each runs in its own bubblewrap boundary (workspace writable, system files and its own install read-only, `$HOME` and `/tmp` private, host network shared). Applies when a server next connects (`/mcp reload`). On a host without bubblewrap a contained server does not start. |

How the sandbox affects asks: in `ask-me`, a call asked about only because of where it could reach (for example a command that might send secrets out) runs without asking when it runs inside the sandbox; the decision records that the sandbox settled it, not you. A call asked for any other reason (owner-only, irreversible, security-weakening, obfuscated) is asked whether contained or not. An `exec` call carrying `file_ops`, a malformed `cmd_base64`, or a working directory other than the session's is always shown to you.

The `repl` tool is registered only where the sandbox is available; each evaluation runs as one sandboxed command.

```text
/security sandbox-screen                         open the sandbox screen (terminal app)
/security sandbox                                the current boundary
/security sandbox-advice                         what to set, and why
/security sandbox-profiles
/security sandbox-presets                        each preset, what it sets and its notes
/security sandbox-probe
/security contain-mcp                            MCP servers start inside their own boundary
/security host-mcp                               MCP servers start as host processes (loosens a protection: asks first, only you)
/health check sandbox                            the boundary on this host, checked
/security sandbox-sessions
/security start-sandbox <command|mcp-server> [--host] [name]
/security sandbox-session <session>
/security run-in-sandbox <session> <command line>
/security stop-sandbox <session>
/security save-sandbox <session> <file>
/security read-sandbox <file>
```

A sandbox session is contained or not started. On a host without bubblewrap, or for the `command` profile (network off) on a host whose bubblewrap cannot take the network away, `/security start-sandbox` refuses and names why, with the next step (install bubblewrap). `--host` starts a host session on purpose: no boundary and the host network, whatever the profile says; the session's backend is `host` and its detail line reads `asked for with --host`.

The sandbox actions of `/security` work in both terminal programs; sandbox sessions and the sandbox screen are the terminal app's. In the Agent, change `sandbox.enabled` and `sandbox.judgment` with `/settings set <key> <value>`, and the two list settings in the settings workspace (`/settings sandbox`). `goodvibes status` prints an `Exec sandbox:` block: `active`, `configEnabled`, `backend` (`bubblewrap`), `available`, `network: isolation confirmed`. The QEMU backend is retired. Old settings `sandbox.qemu*`, `sandbox.vmBackend`, `sandbox.replIsolation` and `sandbox.windowsMode` are removed from a settings file on load, and a VM `sandbox.mcpIsolation` value becomes `contained`.

`permissions.commandParser` (`ast` default, or `flat`) decides whether an `exec` command is parsed into segments first; `ast` refuses a command with a segment that runs nothing.

## Secrets

### Stores and read order

A secret is looked up in this order; the first that has it wins:

1. the process environment;
2. the daemon's store, `~/.goodvibes/daemon/secrets.enc` (moved by `GOODVIBES_DAEMON_HOME`);
3. your own store for the app, `~/.goodvibes/<surface>/secrets.enc`, then its plaintext file;
4. the store of the project you opened, `<project>/.goodvibes/<surface>/secrets.enc`.

`<surface>` is `tui` for the terminal app. Directories above the project are never read. The encrypted stores use AES-256-GCM under a random 32-byte key file `~/.goodvibes/secrets.key` (mode 0600). `GOODVIBES_HOME` moves the whole tree.

A key in a project's store is part of the checkout, so it is used only after you stored it there yourself or confirmed it once with `/secrets trust <KEY>`. Until then `/secrets list` marks it `not used until confirmed: /secrets trust <KEY>`. A confirmation lasts until the value changes.

`storage.secretPolicy`: `preferred_secure` (default: encrypted when available), `require_secure` (refuse to store unencrypted), or `plaintext_allowed`.

### Command line

```sh
goodvibes secrets list
goodvibes secrets providers
goodvibes secrets test goodvibes://secrets/env/OPENAI_API_KEY
goodvibes secrets set OPENAI_API_KEY <your-api-key> --user
printf '%s' '<your-api-key>' | goodvibes secrets set OPENAI_API_KEY --stdin --user
goodvibes secrets link OPENAI_API_KEY goodvibes://secrets/env/OPENAI_API_KEY --user
goodvibes secrets delete OPENAI_API_KEY --user
```

`goodvibes-agent secrets` takes the same forms.

- Without `--user`, `set` and `link` write to the project store. Use `--user` for your own store. The Agent files a credential the daemon reads (channel tokens, mail passwords and other daemon-owned keys) in the daemon store whatever scope you ask for, and says so.
- `--plaintext` stores the value unencrypted; `--secure` (default) encrypts it.
- `--stdin` reads the value from standard input without its trailing newline; use it for a value that starts with `--`.
- The value is exactly one argument. Several value words are refused: `Not stored: 2 values were given for <KEY>.`
- `delete` without a scope flag removes the key from every store that has it and lists where it was removed from. A key not stored exits non-zero: `No stored secret named <KEY>. Nothing was deleted.`
- `test` exits `0` when the reference resolves and `1` when it does not. It prints `resolved <redacted>` or `missing`, never the value.
- An unknown verb prints usage and exits non-zero.

Example:

```text
$ goodvibes secrets list
GoodVibes secrets
  policy: preferred_secure
  secure available: yes
  stored keys: 0
```

### Slash commands

```text
/secrets                           the list of actions, "See your secrets" first
/secrets list
/secrets providers
/secrets storage                   how secrets are kept and where each store is
/secrets set <KEY> <value> [--scope project|user] [--storage secure|plaintext]
/secrets set <KEY>                 type the value on a hidden line
/secrets link <KEY> <secret-ref> [--scope project|user] [--storage secure|plaintext]
/secrets get <KEY>                 confirms it is stored; never prints it
/secrets test <secret-ref>
/secrets trust <KEY>               use a key in this project's store (asks once; never from a model)
/secrets delete <KEY> [--scope project|user] [--storage secure|plaintext]   (asks once)
/secrets use <NAME>                type a value on a hidden line; kept as an environment variable for this session only
```

`project` and `secure` are the defaults; `--storage plaintext` loosens a protection, so it asks first and a model cannot choose it.

A value with spaces goes inside quotes. A value that starts with `--` goes after a bare `--`.

### Secret references

A reference names where a secret is, never the value: `goodvibes://secrets/<source>/<id-or-path>?key=value`.

| Source | Example |
| --- | --- |
| `env` | `goodvibes://secrets/env/OPENAI_API_KEY` |
| `goodvibes` | `goodvibes://secrets/goodvibes/SLACK_BOT_TOKEN` (a key in your store) |
| `file` | `goodvibes://secrets/file/%2Fhome%2Fme%2F.token` |
| `exec` | runs a command and uses its standard output |
| `1password` | `goodvibes://secrets/1password?vault=Private&item=OpenAI&field=password`, or `op://Private/OpenAI/password` |
| `bitwarden` | `goodvibes://secrets/bitwarden?item=GoodVibes%20Slack&field=password`, or `bw://<item>/<field>` |
| `vaultwarden` | `goodvibes://secrets/vaultwarden?item=GoodVibes%20Slack&field=password&server=https%3A%2F%2Fvault.example.test` |
| `bitwarden-secrets-manager` (alias `bws`) | `goodvibes://secrets/bws/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000?field=value`, or `bws://<id>/<field>` |

Which program runs a password-manager reference, and which token variables it gets, are this machine's settings (`storage.secretProviders.*`), never part of a reference. A project settings file may carry only `goodvibes://secrets/goodvibes/<KEY>` references; any other reference in it is skipped with a notice. The old `secret://` scheme is not supported.

### Credential settings

A setting that holds a credential (channel tokens, `surfaces.email.password`, `cluster.secret`, webhook URLs and the rest of the declared list) takes only a `goodvibes://secrets/` reference. `/settings set <credential-key> <value>` and the settings workspace store the value in the secret store and write the reference for you:

```text
/settings set surfaces.slack.botToken <your-bot-token>
Set surfaces.slack.botToken: stored in the daemon secret tier as GOODVIBES_SURFACES_SLACK_BOT_TOKEN (value hidden).
```

A plain value in a settings file for such a key is refused with the command that stores it. Card numbers and card security codes are never settings: they go to the daemon's card store through `/payments add-card` or the web UI.

## Headless runs and permissions

In `goodvibes run` and `goodvibes-agent run`, a call that needs the owner is refused unless the run uses `--output stream-json --answer-permissions`; then each such call writes a `PERMISSION_PROMPT` frame and waits for a `{"type":"PERMISSION_ANSWER","callId":"<id>","approved":true}` line on standard input. An unanswered call is refused, never approved. `--just-vibes` and `--yolo` work in `run` as in the interactive apps. The frame formats are under "Headless runs" in "The terminal app (`goodvibes`)".

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Every command asks even in `jev-decides`. | No working decision model, or the default `jev-decides` on an endpoint or model the calibration did not measure. | Check `goodvibes status`. Set `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`, or choose `jev-decides` explicitly: `/settings set permissions.mode jev-decides`. |
| A tool never runs, in any mode except `yolo`: "refused by the setting permissions.tools.<x> = deny". | A per-tool deny. | `/settings set permissions.tools.<x> prompt`. |
| "refused by the saved rule ..." | A remembered deny rule. | `/permissions rules`, then revoke it. |
| "plan mode is on and <tool> would change something". | Plan mode. | `/plan off` or Shift+Tab. |
| Writes refused in a new directory with "Workspace trust ... is undecided". | Trust question unanswered. | `/security trust-folder`. |
| Writes refused: "Explicit restricted workspace forbids this operation". | Workspace set to restricted. | `/security trust-folder`. |
| A request from Slack never runs in `yolo`. | A channel request always needs the owner's answer. | Answer it in the terminal app, the web UI or the conversation; or ask from the terminal. |
| A request from email, a webhook or ntfy is refused. | Those surfaces cannot direct changes. | Ask from the terminal, Telegram or another owned surface. |
| `just-vibes` finished without doing some steps. | They were held. | `/held`, `/held approve <id>`, then ask to carry on. |
| "Decision model ... failing" once, then work continues. | `Hybrid` fell back. | Fix the endpoint or key named in the notice; the app says when it answers again. |
| Work stops with a decision-model error. | `Decision Model Only` and the model failed. | Fix the model, or `/settings set judgment.policy Hybrid`. |
| Commands have no network. | The exec sandbox turns it off. | Add every command of the line to `sandbox.egressAllowlist`, and have a working decision model: without one the sandbox never opens the network. |
| A contained MCP server does not start. | `sandbox.mcpIsolation` is `contained` and bubblewrap is missing. | Install bubblewrap, or `/security host-mcp`. |

Full entries (files, project rule, environment variable): "Settings" in the part "Reference", under "behavior".

| Key | Type | Default | Allowed | Stored in | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `judgment.backend` | object | `{}` | data object with optional adapter, positive maxInputBytes/maxQuestions and explicit responseModels | daemon file | Optional adapter (system-one, cloudflare-workers-ai or laya), maxInputBytes, maxQuestions and responseModels for the primary deployment. Limits apply to the complete request; evidence is never silently shortened. Cloudflare run URLs select their adapter automatically. |
| `judgment.decisionDeadlineMs` | number | `1500` | integer in [1, 120000] | daemon file | How long a decision that a person or a tool call waits on may take, in milliseconds, before it takes its fallback (for example asking you, or the safe default). A decision target that misses this deadline three times in a row is skipped for a minute, so the next decisions take their fallback at once. |
| `judgment.endpoint` | string | `""` | empty, or an http(s) URL without embedded credentials, query or fragment | daemon file | Address of the decision model server the engine asks for judgments (a server that answers the decision API, POST /v1/systemone, as the hosted Jev does); empty uses TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, then the hosted endpoint. A loopback address selects a local model. While judgment.keySource is not none, change or reset it only together with judgment.keySource or judgment.keyName in one update (keep or clear the credential), or it is refused; embedded credentials, query strings and fragments are refused. |
| `judgment.fallbacks` | array | `[]` | array of { endpoint, model, keySource: "env" \| "secret" \| "none", keyName } (keyName empty for "none"); no credentials in URLs or inline keys | daemon file | Ordered decision targets with endpoint, model, keySource, keyName and optional backend capabilities. Each target may use a different decision model or adapter. keySource is env, secret or none; none requires an empty keyName. Credentials are privately resolved from references, never inline values. An empty array disables inherited fallbacks. Each target is attempted with a finite timeout; when the chain is exhausted, a decision that has a fallback takes it and any other decision stops. |
| `judgment.keyName` | string | `"TYPESAFE_API_KEY"` | a credential reference name | daemon file | Primary decision credential reference, such as TYPESAFE_API_KEY or CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN; never an inline key value. Ignored when keySource is none. |
| `judgment.keySource` | enum | `"env"` | `env`, `secret`, `none` | daemon file | Where the decision model's key comes from: env reads an environment variable, secret reads the secret store, and none sends no key. This setting stores only one of those three words, never a credential or a credential reference. |
| `judgment.model` | string | `""` |  | daemon file | Judgment model or alias; empty uses TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL, then jev-latest. |
| `judgment.policy` | enum | `"Hybrid"` | `Hybrid`, `Decision Model Only`, `No Decision Model` | daemon file | Hybrid (default) uses the set decision model and, when none is set or it fails, continues without it: decisions take their fallbacks and a failure is shown once with the model, what failed and the next step. Decision Model Only stops the operation and reports when the set decision model fails. No Decision Model makes no decision-model calls. With no decision model set, every policy continues without one. |
| `judgment.timeoutMs` | number | `30000` | integer in [0, 2147483647] | daemon file | Finite timeout per judgment target in milliseconds; legacy 0 uses the default 30000 ms. Cancellation may stop the operation sooner. |
| `judgment.volumeMonitor` | object | `{"budgets":[],"intervalMs":60000,"windowMs":3600000,"limit":10000,"enabled":false}` | object with enabled and up to 100 budgets; enabled monitoring needs at least one budget | daemon file | Local decision call-volume alerts. Set enabled:true and budgets:[{name:"All decisions",maxLogicalDecisions:1000,maxWireAttempts:2000}]. Optional battery/site restrict each budget; windowMs defaults to one hour, intervalMs to one minute, limit to 10000 log entries. Alerts report usage without calling models or stopping work. Disabled settings retain the optional GOODVIBES_JUDGMENT_MONITOR file override. |

Full entries (files, project rule, environment variable): "Settings" in the part "Reference", under "judgment".

| Key | Type | Default | Allowed | Stored in | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `policy.bundlePath` | string | `""` |  | each program | Filesystem path to the policy bundle JSON loaded at startup when policy.bundleSource is "file" and policy.registryEnabled is true. Empty disables file loading. The loaded bundle enters the registry as a candidate (subject to the divergence gate before promotion); once promoted, the same unchanged bundle is enforced again at every start. |
| `policy.bundleSource` | enum | `"none"` | `none`, `file` | each program | Where the policy bundle registry loads its initial bundle from at startup: none (no bundle loaded; bundles supplied programmatically or via commands), or file (load policy.bundlePath). Only consulted when policy.registryEnabled is true. |
| `policy.registryEnabled` | boolean | `false` |  | each program | Enable the versioned policy bundle registry with promote/rollback semantics and the /security load-policy, simulate-policy, compare-policy, enforce-policy and restore-policy actions. Enforcement requires passing divergence-gate evidence first; default off until that evidence exists. |
| `policy.requireSignedBundles` | boolean | `false` |  | each program | Require a valid HMAC-SHA256 signature on every policy bundle: a bundle that is unsigned, altered or signed with another key is refused, and so is every bundle when no signing key is set. The key is read from the GOODVIBES_POLICY_SIGNING_KEY environment variable (hex, at least 16 bytes). Restart to apply. Default off until divergence evidence clears the governance gate. |

# Automation and services

This part covers work that runs without a conversation (scheduled routines, supervised triggers, watchers, check-ins), notifications, and the services the platform connects to: mail, calendar, Google, chat channels, voice, the browser, purchases, CI watch, occasions and plans. It ends with the list-valued settings and the settings reference for each area.

## Before you start: who owns these services

- The daemon (`goodvibes-daemon`) owns every service in this part. Mail, calendar, channels, purchases, CI watches, occasions and daemon-kept routines run in the daemon, so they keep working with every terminal closed. The terminal apps and the web UI are clients of it.
- The daemon is on when `daemon.enabled` is `true` (the default). `goodvibes status` shows the service state under `Service:`.
- Settings under `surfaces.`, `payments.`, `occasions.` and the other daemon-owned prefixes are written to the daemon's settings file, `~/.goodvibes/daemon/settings.json`, whichever app writes them.
- How to change a setting:
  - Terminal app: `/settings <key>` opens the settings workspace at that key, and `/settings set <key> <value>` writes it directly. The value is read as JSON when it parses (`true`, `5`, `["a","b"]`, `{"k":1}`, `"quoted text"`); otherwise it is taken as text.
  - Agent: `/settings <key>` opens the workspace, and `/settings set <key> <value>` writes text, numbers, `true`/`false` and enum words. The Agent's `/settings set` takes no JSON list or object: set those in the settings screen (`/settings open <key>`).
  - Daemon command line: `goodvibes-daemon config set <key> <value>` (JSON or text, as the terminal app).

  The examples in this part use `/settings set`, the same line in both programs.
- A credential setting (a token, a password, a webhook URL) is never written into a settings file. `/settings set <key> <value>` stores the value in the secret store and writes a `goodvibes://secrets/...` reference into the key. A daemon-owned credential lands in the daemon's store, `~/.goodvibes/daemon/secrets.enc`. Example:

  ```text
  /settings set surfaces.telegram.botToken <your-bot-token>
  Set surfaces.telegram.botToken: stored in the daemon secret tier as GOODVIBES_SURFACES_TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN (value hidden).
    surfaces.telegram.botToken now holds the reference goodvibes://secrets/goodvibes/GOODVIBES_SURFACES_TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN; the value itself is never written to a config file.
    The daemon reads that tier, so this keeps working with this client closed.
  ```

  The secret key name is `GOODVIBES_` followed by the setting key in upper case with dots and camel-case boundaries turned into `_`. The same value can be stored directly with `/secrets set GOODVIBES_SURFACES_TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN <value>`.
- Everything a service sends as the owner passes the permission gate described in "Permissions, decisions and safety": a new recipient is the owner's to allow, and a change asked for on a channel is the owner's to approve.

## Scheduled routines

A routine is a prompt that runs on a schedule. Each time it fires it produces a run. The daemon keeps routines as automation jobs, so a routine runs once whether or not a terminal is open, and the list is the same in the web UI, channels and agents.

### Schedule kinds

| Kind | Value | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cron` | A five-field cron expression, optional `--tz <IANA zone>` and `--stagger <ms>` | `"*/30 * * * *"` |
| `every` | An interval such as `15m`, `2h`, `1d` | `15m` |
| `at` | One date and time, ISO form; read in this machine's zone when it has no zone | `2026-12-01T09:00` |
| `when` | Natural language, read by the decision model into one of the three above | `"every weekday at 9am"` |

### `/schedule`, in both programs

`/schedule` alone opens its list of actions (in a script or for a model it prints the schedules, as "See your schedules" does). Both programs take the same lines; the terminal app keeps a schedule with the daemon (or runs it itself while the daemon is off), the Agent keeps it on its connected host. A line with something missing opens the step that asks for it.

| Action | Line | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| See your schedules | `/schedule list` | |
| Schedule something to run | `/schedule add (--when <words> \| --at <date> \| --every <interval> \| --cron <pattern>) [options] <what it does...>` | |
| Run a schedule now | `/schedule run <schedule>` | |
| Pause a schedule | `/schedule pause <schedule>` (picked from the ones that run) | |
| Resume a schedule | `/schedule resume <schedule>` (picked from the paused ones) | |
| Change a schedule | `/schedule change <schedule> [--when ... \| --at ... \| --every ... \| --cron ...] [--tz <zone>] [--stagger <duration>] [--name <name>] [--task <task> --success-criteria <result>] [<what it does...>]` | |
| Remove a schedule | `/schedule remove <schedule>` | cannot be undone |

```text
/schedule add --when "every weekday at 9am" post the standup summary
/schedule add --cron "0 9 * * 1-5" --tz America/Chicago summarize open pull requests
/schedule add --every 15m check the build status
/schedule add --at 2026-12-01T09:00 send the release reminder
/schedule pause weekly-report
```

A schedule is named by its id, its name or the start of its id (one that names more than one is refused with the candidates). Options of `add` ("Anything else?" in the guided form; each blank keeps the usual setting):

| Option | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--name <name>` | Its name; default is the first 40 characters of what it does. |
| `--model <model>`, `--provider <provider>` | The model to run it with. |
| `--fallback <a,b>` | Fallback models. |
| `--reasoning <level>`, `--thinking <mode>` | Reasoning effort and thinking mode. |
| `--target isolated\|main\|background\|pinned` | Where it runs: a fresh conversation each time (the usual), the main conversation, a background session, or the pinned one. |
| `--wake now\|next-heartbeat` | Run at once when due, or with the next heartbeat. |
| `--template <tmpl>` | A prompt template. |
| `--tool <name>` | Allow only these tools (repeat the option). A run limited this way does not get the mail and calendar tool unless `--tool google` is given. |
| `--deliver <channel>` | Where each run's answer goes: a channel written as in settings, `telegram`, `slack:C123` and so on (`telegram` alone uses `surfaces.telegram.defaultChatId`). Without it the answer goes to the owner inbox. |
| `--external-source <kind>` | Marks where outside content comes from. |
| `--allow-unsafe-external-content` | May act on content from outside sources ("Yes" loosens a protection: it asks first, and a model's line is refused). |
| `--paused` | Kept, but runs only once resumed. |
| `--light-context` | Run with a small context. |
| `--tz <zone>`, `--stagger <duration>` | For a pattern or a description: its time zone, and a spread of the start (such as `5m`). |

In the web UI the same actions are the Schedules screen and its sheets (see "Slash command actions in the web UI" in the daemon part). There a time described in words is read by the daemon (`automation.schedules.preview`, in the browser's time zone when `--tz` is blank) and shown as `Read as: ...` with the next run before the button keeps it; nothing is kept by the reading.

Successful `add` output (the id is generated):

```text
Scheduled.
"check the build status": every 15m; next run 2026-11-18 10:15 America/Chicago (runs once, with or without a terminal open).
The answer goes to your owner inbox. Id job-3f9c2a1b7d.
```

With `daemon.enabled` off, the terminal that holds the routine lock keeps and runs the routines while it is open (`kept and run by this terminal (daemon off)`); another terminal can list them but not change them. When the daemon is turned on later, routines kept by a terminal are moved to the daemon and the move is reported.

Failures:

| Message | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `Schedules are kept and run by the GoodVibes daemon ... it cannot be reached: <reason> Nothing was scheduled or changed.` | Start the daemon; check `goodvibes status`. |
| `Not kept: "<value>" is not a date and time. ...` | Use an ISO timestamp. |
| `Not kept: <time> has already passed.` | Pick a future time. |
| `Not kept: the timing is <reason>; give it as a date (--at), an interval (--every) or a pattern (--cron) instead.` | The decision model could not read the words, or none is set. Use `--at`, `--every` or `--cron`. |
| `/schedule add has no option --x.` | Use one of the listed options. |

### The Agent: `/routines promote`, and a schedule's runs

An Agent routine becomes a schedule on the connected host with `/routines promote <routine> --how <cron|every|at> --when <pattern, interval or time> [--timezone <tz>] [--name <name>] [--delivery-channel <channel[:route]>]... [--delivery-route <route>]... [--delivery-webhook <url>]... [--delivery-link <name>]... [--provider <id>] [--model <id>] [--disabled]` (or the guided form, "Run a routine on a schedule"); `/routines receipts`, `/routines receipt <receipt>` and `/routines reconcile` read what promotion recorded. From the shell: `goodvibes-agent routines promote <routine-id> --cron "0 9 * * *" --timezone America/Chicago --yes`.

A schedule's runs, in both programs, are `/schedule` actions: `run <schedule>`, `pause <schedule>`, `resume <schedule>`, `stop-run <run>` (asks first) and `retry-run <run>`.

### The model's `schedule` tool

The model can list and create schedules with the `schedule` tool (its inputs are in the tool reference). A routine the model creates passes the permission gate like any change.

### How runs behave

- A run uses the permission mode and sandbox of the owner who created its job; a job has no permission setting of its own. A run in a mode that would ask gets its asks through the owner inbox and the attached surfaces.
- A run ends at the job's own timeout, or `automation.defaultTimeoutMs` (two hours; `0` means no limit). Past it the run fails with `Timed out after <duration>`.
- A run in flight when the daemon stopped is failed when it starts again ("Agent state lost before completion").
- An occurrence that comes due while an earlier run of the same job is still running is skipped.
- A one-time job whose time passed while the daemon was down for longer than `automation.catchUpWindowMinutes` is recorded as missed and disabled.
- After a failure, the job waits `automation.failureCooldownMs` before it may run again.
- A cancelled run stays cancelled and is not retried. Cancelling a check-in that is still deciding stops it before its judgment and its delivery.
- A run still starting when the daemon stops starts no agent and saves no record afterwards; the next start reconciles what was recorded.
- At most `automation.maxConcurrentRuns` runs execute at once; `automation.runHistoryLimit` runs per job are kept.
- `automation.enabled` `false` stops the whole subsystem.
- In a group of machines (`cluster`), a routine made on any machine is listed on every machine and runs once in the group, on the machine holding the `automation` role; disabling or removing it on any machine applies on all of them, and when the role moves the new holder carries on from the last occurrence started. A run still starting on the machine that lost the role starts no agent and saves nothing more. See "What a cluster does and does not do" under "Clusters" in "The daemon, the web UI and networking". The scheduled check-in is the exception: it follows the `checkin` role.

### Where a routine's result goes, and what a routine can use

- Each run's answer goes to the surface named on the routine. `/schedule add` takes `--deliver <channel>` in both programs; `/routines promote` and the Agent model's schedule tools take `--delivery-channel <surface>` (for example `telegram`), `--delivery-channel <surface>:<route id>`, `--delivery-route <route id>`, `--delivery-webhook <url>` or `--delivery-link <name>`. In the Agent's flags the part after `:` is a route binding id, not a chat id. A Telegram delivery with no route or address goes to `surfaces.telegram.defaultChatId`; with neither, that send fails with `Missing Telegram chat id`.
- A routine that names no surface, or whose every named surface failed, leaves its answer in the owner inbox as a report titled `Scheduled run: <name>` (the answer, cut at about 3,800 characters; when a send failed, the reason first). It stays open until you answer it `read` (`/questions`, the web UI's Work view, or a channel). A failed or missed run of such a routine leaves `Scheduled run failed: <name>` (or `missed`) there too. Every run is also kept in the run history (the web UI and the `automation.runs.*` methods). The routine itself keeps how its last run ended for the person as `lastOutcome`: `delivered` (a named surface took it), `not-delivered` (every named surface failed; it went to the inbox instead), `inbox` (it names no surface) or `failed` (the run failed); It is on the routine's record (`automation.jobs.list`) and on its fleet node (`schedule.lastOutcome`).
- A routine the terminal app keeps itself (with `daemon.enabled` off) has no owner inbox to fall back to: an answer with no surface is kept only in its run history.
- A run's answer is owed from the moment the run ends (saved with the run's end) until its delivery is recorded. A daemon that stops in between delivers it at its next start, under the same identity, so a surface that drops repeats drops a second copy. A one-shot routine is removed only once its run's answer was delivered.
- The model's `schedule` tool with `action:"remind"` does not send its text as is: at each run a model turn is started with the text framed as a reminder ("GoodVibes Agent scheduled reminder. Reminder: <text> ... Keep the reminder concise and state any next action"), and its answer is delivered. `/schedule add` sends what it does as written.
- A scheduled run is an agent the daemon starts with the platform's tool set (files, shell, fetch, web search, MCP, channel tools, and the like). Once you have connected mail or a calendar (a Google account with `/google connect`, or a CalDAV server in `surfaces.calendar.caldavUrl` and `surfaces.calendar.caldavUser`), it also gets the `google` tool: `mail.list` and `mail.read` on the connected Gmail, and `calendar.list` on the daemon's calendar (the CalDAV server when one is set, otherwise the Google calendar). Its calls pass the same permission gate as any turn. A send or a calendar event it makes may not carry what it read from mail or a calendar, and `calendar.create` is refused in a scheduled run (nobody asked for that event at that moment). A routine limited with `--tool` gets the tool only when `google` is listed.

### A daily 8 am summary of mail and calendar delivered to Telegram

1. Connect the mail and calendar to the daemon: in the Agent, `/google connect` (Gmail and Google Calendar over OAuth, Path B in "Google" below: the model's `google` tool reads mail only through it, in a conversation as in a scheduled run), or set a CalDAV server for the calendar. `/google status` shows the connection.
2. Set up Telegram as in "Telegram" (owner claim accepted) and give it a delivery chat: `/settings set surfaces.telegram.defaultChatId <your-numeric-id>`.
3. Create the schedule (either program):

   ```text
   /schedule add --cron "0 8 * * *" --tz America/Chicago --deliver telegram Summarize my unread mail from the last 24 hours and today's calendar events. Group the mail by sender and give the events in time order.
   ```

   ```text
   Scheduled.
   "Summarize my unread mail from the last": 0 8 * * * [America/Chicago]; next run 2026-11-20 08:00 America/Chicago (runs once, with or without a terminal open).
   The answer goes to telegram. Id job-3f9c2a1b7d.
   ```

4. Try it at once: `/schedule run job-3f9c2a1b7d`. The run reads the mail and the calendar with the `google` tool and its answer arrives in your Telegram chat. If the send fails (the bot cannot reach the chat), the answer is in the owner inbox instead, with the reason.

In the Agent the same line keeps the schedule on the connected host; its run has the same tools.

## Supervised triggers

A trigger watches something and starts an agent turn when it happens, without holding a turn open. There are three kinds:

| Kind | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `on-exit` | Runs a command and fires once when it ends, with its exit status and the tail of its output. |
| `stream` | Runs a long-lived command and fires on output lines that match a pattern, in batches. |
| `condition` | Checks a URL, file, command or platform tool on an interval and fires when a rule holds. |

### Turning triggers on

Triggers are off by default. Nothing runs and nothing is written until they are on and a trigger exists.

```text
/settings set watchers.triggers.enabled true
```

Stored triggers start being supervised at once. Triggers are saved in `triggers.db` inside the project tree of the process that supervises them: `<working directory>/.goodvibes/<surface>/triggers.db` (for the daemon, its own working directory and `tui`). `/triggers` reads and changes the triggers of the daemon the terminal app is connected to. A trigger's agent turn is started by that process's agent manager, so it runs in the daemon under the daemon's own settings. One process supervises a store at a time; another window can list them and reports `another process supervises them`; a change from that window is refused and names the process to use.

### `/triggers`

`/triggers` alone opens its list of actions (in a script or for a model it prints the supervisor's state and the triggers, as "See your triggers" does). A line with something missing opens the step that asks for it.

| Action | Line | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| See your triggers | `/triggers list` (who supervises them, then each trigger) | |
| Watch for something | `/triggers watch <name> [-- <command>...] [--match <pattern>] [--url <address>] [--file <path>] [--definition <json>] [--every <interval>] [--say <text>] [--deliver <channel>] [--run <approved command>]` | |
| See what a trigger did | `/triggers history <trigger> [--count <1-200>]` | |
| Stop a trigger | `/triggers stop <trigger>` | cannot be undone |
| Start a trigger that gave up | `/triggers restart <trigger>` | |
| See commands triggers may run | `/triggers commands` | |
| Let triggers run a command | `/triggers allow-command <name> -- <command>...` | loosens a protection |

"Watch for something" asks what to watch: a command finishing (the command after `--`; an `on-exit` trigger), a line a command prints (`--match`; a `stream` trigger), a web address changing (`--url`, looked at `--every`, default 5m; a `condition` with an `http` probe and a `change` rule), a file changing (`--file`, likewise with a `file` probe), or something else written out (`--definition`, the `{ "spec": ..., "action": ... }` JSON below, for any probe, rule or action). Its id is made from the name. Then it asks what happens: the agent looks at it (`--say` adds your instructions; `--deliver` names the channel its answer goes to, else the owner inbox), or a command you let triggers run (`--run`).

The model creates, lists, cancels and resets triggers with the `trigger` tool. Only the owner lets triggers run a command: `/triggers allow-command` from a model is refused before anything is asked.

The web UI's Triggers screen has the same actions; its "Watch for something" sheet asks the same blanks, and the daemon reads them into the definition (`watchers.triggers.preview`, the same reading as the terminal apps') and shows what it will watch before `Watch` makes it.

### Definition JSON

```json
{
  "id": "build",
  "label": "Build finished",
  "spec": { "kind": "on-exit", "command": "npm", "args": ["run", "build"] }
}
```

The definition also takes an optional `description` (the trigger's purpose). `action` is optional; the default is `{"kind":"agent-turn"}`. An agent-turn action starts one agent turn, in the process that supervises the trigger, with this message:

```text
A GoodVibes trigger fired.

Trigger: <label>
Purpose: <description>            (only when a description is set)
Why it fired: <reason>

Act on what this actually indicates. Verify before assuming anything the trigger did not directly observe.
```

`{"kind":"agent-turn","prompt":"<text>"}` puts `<text>`, a blank line, then that message. `{"kind":"agent-turn","model":"<provider:model>"}` runs the turn on that model; without it the supervising process's default model is used. A `sessionId` in an agent-turn action is refused on a new trigger. When the turn ends its answer is delivered: to the channel `deliverTo` names (`{"kind":"agent-turn","deliverTo":"telegram"}`, or `"slack:C123"`; written as in settings), else to the owner inbox as a report titled `Trigger <label>`. A send that fails puts the answer in the owner inbox with the reason. A `deliverTo` that names no delivery surface is refused when the trigger is created. The firing is also recorded in the trigger's runs (`/triggers history <trigger>`, with the action's result, `agent:<id>`) and the turn appears with the supervising process's agents (the web UI Work view for the daemon). The turn gets the same tools as a scheduled run, the `google` mail and calendar tool included once mail or a calendar is connected. `{"kind":"action-grant","grantId":"<id>","digest":"<digest>"}` runs a command the owner let triggers run with `/triggers allow-command`; `/triggers commands` shows each one's digest.

Spec fields:

| Kind | Fields |
| --- | --- |
| `on-exit` | `command`, `args`, `cwd`, `env`, `maxDurationMs` (default `watchers.triggers.onExitMaxDurationMs`, six hours), `stdin` (`none` or `empty`), `outputTailBytes` |
| `stream` | `command`, `args`, `cwd`, `match` (a regex extract, required), `exclude`, `batchLines`, `batchIntervalMs`, `queueLimit`, `dedupTtlMs`, `restart` (default `true`) |
| `condition` | `probe`, `extract`, `rule`, `intervalMs` (up to 24 hours; default `watchers.triggers.defaultCheckIntervalMs`) |

Probes (`condition`):

| Probe | Fields |
| --- | --- |
| `{"kind":"http"}` | `url`, `method` (`GET`, `HEAD`, `POST`), `headers`, `body`, `timeoutMs`, `capture` (`body`, `status`, `envelope`) |
| `{"kind":"file"}` | `path`, `capture` (`content`, `stat`), `maxBytes` |
| `{"kind":"command"}` | `command`, `args`, `cwd`, `timeoutMs`, `capture` (`stdout`, `stderr`, `exit-code`, `envelope`) |
| `{"kind":"platform-tool"}` | `tool`, `input`, `timeoutMs` |

Extracts: `{"kind":"jsonpath","path":"$.status"}`, `{"kind":"regex","pattern":"...","flags":"i","group":1}`, `{"kind":"jq-subset","expression":".status"}`, `{"kind":"raw"}`. A pattern may be at most 512 characters.

Rules:

| Rule | Fires when |
| --- | --- |
| `{"kind":"change","fireOnFirst":false}` | The value differs from the previous check. |
| `{"kind":"value","operator":"eq","operand":"down","level":false}` | The value satisfies the comparison (on the entering edge, or every check with `level`). Operators: `eq`, `ne`, `lt`, `lte`, `gt`, `gte`, `contains`, `not-contains`, `matches`. |
| `{"kind":"transition","from":"running","to":"done"}` | One specific previous-to-current change. |
| `{"kind":"threshold","direction":"above","enter":90,"exit":80}` | Crossing `enter`; re-arms after crossing back past `exit`. |
| `{"kind":"debounce-n","count":3,"inner":{...}}` | The inner rule matched that many checks in a row. |
| `{"kind":"dedup-ttl","ttlMs":600000,"inner":{...}}` | The inner rule, at most once per fingerprint in the window. |
| `{"kind":"rate-of-change","windowMs":60000,"operator":"gt","operand":5,"per":"second"}` | The change rate in the window satisfies the comparison. |
| `{"kind":"windowed-aggregate","windowMs":300000,"aggregate":"mean","operator":"gt","operand":2,"minSamples":3}` | An aggregate (`min`, `max`, `mean`, `sum`, `count`, `stddev`) satisfies the comparison. |
| `{"kind":"correlation","triggerIds":["a","b"],"withinMs":60000,"require":"all"}` | The named triggers fired inside the window (`all`, `any` or `sequence`). |

Example: fire when a health endpoint stops answering `ok` three checks in a row.

```text
/triggers watch "API health" --definition '{"spec":{"kind":"condition","probe":{"kind":"http","url":"https://api.example.com/health","capture":"body"},"extract":{"kind":"raw"},"rule":{"kind":"debounce-n","count":3,"inner":{"kind":"value","operator":"ne","operand":"ok"}},"intervalMs":60000}}'
```

### Trigger states and failures

- Only an `on-exit` trigger finishes when it fires (state `fired`, final). A `condition` or `stream` trigger records each firing (`firedCount`, a `fired` entry in its runs) and keeps watching. A cancelled trigger is finished. Cancelling a running `on-exit` trigger stops its process and records the run's termination as `cancel-requested` (not observed) until the supervisor sees the process end, then as what it saw (`signalled` or `exited`, reason `cancelled`); a process started before a daemon restart is not ours to stop, so its cancel records no termination and says the process was not stopped. "Start a trigger that gave up" (`/triggers restart`) applies only to `idle`, `backoff`, `circuit-open` and `failed` triggers; another is refused with what to do instead.
- A failing check backs off along `watchers.triggers.backoffLadderMs`; after `watchers.triggers.breakerStrikes` failures in a row the breaker opens (`circuit-open`) until reset.
- An action that fails to deliver is kept owed and delivered again when due, once at a time: an action slower than the supervision tick is not started a second time, and a batch leaves the owed list only when the attempt that delivered it ends. A stream keeps at most eight undelivered batches; a dropped one is recorded in the trigger's runs.
- A save that fails sets `lastError` to `not saved: <cause> (<path>)` and is retried on the next tick; the trigger keeps running.
- `/triggers` answers `<what> was not done: <reason>` when the daemon refuses (for example `Stopping it was not done: ...`).

## Watchers

A watcher is a daemon-managed poller over an external source: a URL requested every interval, a file whose size and modification time are checked, or a manual watcher that runs only when started by hand. Each run records a checkpoint (what it observed) and emits runtime events on the `watchers` domain: `WATCHER_STARTED`, `WATCHER_HEARTBEAT`, `WATCHER_CHECKPOINT_ADVANCED` (the observation changed), `WATCHER_FAILED` and `WATCHER_STOPPED`. A watcher does not start an agent or send a message by itself; an operator client or the event stream reads its events. To have the assistant act when something changes, use a supervised trigger (above).

Where watchers are managed:

| Surface | Create | List | Start, stop, run now | Change | Remove |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Operator API | `watchers.create` (`POST /api/watchers`) | `watchers.list` (`GET /api/watchers`) | `watchers.start`, `watchers.stop`, `watchers.run` (`POST /api/watchers/<id>/start`, `/stop`, `/run`) | `watchers.update` (`PATCH /api/watchers/<id>`) | `watchers.delete` (`DELETE /api/watchers/<id>`) |
| The Agent (model) | the `agent_operator_method` tool with `methodId:"watchers.create"`, after the owner confirms | same tool, `watchers.list` | same tool | same tool | same tool |
| Web UI | no | Work, Processes (a watcher is one row of the fleet) | Stop only | no | no |
| Terminal app | no | no | no | no | no |

Creating needs the `write:watchers` scope (an admin operator token); listing needs any signed-in client. Each operator method can also be called as `POST /api/control-plane/methods/<method-id>/invoke` with the input as `{"body": { ... }}`. Tokens and their scopes are described under "Credentials and pairing" in "The daemon, the web UI and networking".

`watchers.create` input:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `label` | Required. A name. |
| `id` | Optional id; generated when absent. |
| `kind` | `polling` (default), `webhook`, `filesystem` or `manual`. `socket` and `integration` are refused with `WATCHER_NOTHING_TO_RUN`: those are registered by the component that owns them. |
| `url` | Required for `polling` and `webhook`: the URL requested each run. Its response is what the watcher observes; a non-2xx answer fails the run. A URL on your own network is refused with `WATCHER_TARGET_NOT_ALLOWED` unless its host is approved in `network.privateDeliveryHosts`. |
| `endpoint` | `polling` only: an alternative to `url`. |
| `method` | HTTP method, default `GET`. |
| `headers` | Request headers. A header that carries a credential must be a `goodvibes://secrets/<KEY>` reference; the daemon reads the secret at request time and, when it cannot, fails the run without sending the request. |
| `path` | Required for `filesystem`. |
| `intervalMs` | How often it runs; default `watchers.pollIntervalMs`. |
| `sourceId`, `sourceKind`, `metadata` | Optional labels. |

Example:

```sh
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3421/api/control-plane/methods/watchers.create/invoke \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <operator-token>" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"body":{"label":"status page","kind":"polling","url":"https://status.example.com/api.json","intervalMs":300000,"headers":{"Authorization":"goodvibes://secrets/goodvibes/STATUS_PAGE_TOKEN"}}}'
```

The answer is the watcher record: `id`, `label`, `kind`, `state`, `source`, `lastCheckpoint`, `lastError`. Remove it with `watchers.delete` and `{"body":{"watcherId":"<id>"}}`.

- After a restart, a watcher owned by a component reads `awaiting its owner since <time>` until that component registers it again; start or run is refused with `WATCHER_AWAITING_OWNER`.
- Updating, stopping or deleting a watcher while it runs stops that run (its request is aborted) and its outcome is not written: the record shows the new definition's runs only.
- The daemon itself runs one watcher, `daemon-heartbeat`, while `watchers.enabled` is on.
- When the watcher store cannot be saved, a change still applies and its answer carries `persisted: false`.
- Settings: `watchers.enabled`, `watchers.pollIntervalMs`, `watchers.heartbeatIntervalMs`, `watchers.recoveryWindowMinutes`, and `watchers.ciPollIntervalMs` for CI watches (never below 15 seconds).

## Proactive check-ins

On a cadence, the daemon assembles a briefing and the decision model judges whether anything needs the owner now; only then is a message delivered. The briefing holds: approvals and questions waiting in the owner inbox (and for how long), contracts waiting for the owner's decision (with their question), automation runs that failed since the last check-in, and messages a session has not picked up yet. It does not read mail, calendar or channels. With no decision model in use (none set, `No Decision Model`, or `Hybrid` after the set model failed), the check-in takes its fallback without a model request for the decision: when something waits for the owner (an approval, question or report in the owner inbox, a contract waiting for his decision, a failed run) it contacts him with the note the conversation model writes, sent as written and marked `(Not independently checked: no decision model is in use.)`, and its receipt's reason reads `Decided from the current state (no decision model is in use): <n> items are waiting for you; the note was not independently checked`; when nothing waits it records `quiet` (`Nothing needs the owner: ...`) and sends nothing. With none set or `No Decision Model` chosen this is silent; under `Hybrid` with a set model failing, the same fallback runs and the model's failure is reported as everywhere else. The outcome `skipped-decision-models-disabled` ("Decision models are unavailable; automatic check-in contact and note verification were not completed.") is recorded only when a decision the check-in needs has no fallback and fails with decision models off. Inside quiet hours it is recorded as `skipped-quiet-hours`. A note too long for one message on its channel goes out as several; when only some of them arrive, the receipt is `partial` with `partsSent` and `partsTotal` and says how many did not arrive (the run reports `partly delivered`; it is not sent again, since the owner already has the start). Each receipt's summary states how many items wait for the owner (the same count the decision reads), then only the counts that are not zero: sessions running, sessions with messages not yet picked up, channel messages not yet picked up, runs finished recently (`11 items waiting for you.`).

```text
/settings set checkin.enabled true
/settings set checkin.cadence "0 */4 * * *"
/settings set checkin.deliveryChannel telegram
/settings set checkin.quietHours 22:00-07:00
/checkin            view the settings and recent receipts
/checkin run        run one now
```

`checkin.deliveryChannel` is `surfaceKind` or `surfaceKind:address` (for example `slack:C0123456`); empty uses the owner profile's `contactMe.channel`. `checkin.quietHours` is `HH:MM-HH:MM` local time; empty uses the owner profile's `contactMe.quietHours`.

## Notifications

Agent and workstream outcomes, approvals waiting and budget alerts are announced to the notification transports: Slack, Discord and webhook URLs.

```text
/notify add https://ntfy.sh/<your-topic>
/notify list            each address shown by its site; --show reveals them (asks first, the owner's only)
/notify remove 1
/notify clear           asks first
/notify test            asks first
/notify send <message>  asks first
/notify failed          notifications this app could not deliver
/notify resend <id|all> [--to-current]
/notifications          open the notification history view
```
