| See repeat purchases you have allowed | `/payments repeats` | |
| Stop a repeat purchase | `/payments stop-repeat <repeat purchase>` (picked from the ones you allowed) | |
| Add a card | `/payments add-card` (asks each field, hidden) | |
| Remove a card | `/payments remove-card <card>` (picked from the daemon's cards) | cannot be undone |
| Set your billing or shipping address | `/payments address <billing\|shipping> [--name ...] [--line1 ...] [--line2 ...] [--city ...] [--region ...] [--postal-code ...] [--country ...]` (blank keeps what is set) | |

Every action is the owner's own: a line a model runs is refused, naming the action. Each needs a paired owner credential with the `read:payments` and `write:payments` scopes. An action marked "spends money" or "cannot be undone" asks first, with the sentence that says what it does. `/payments address` in the terminal app writes this machine's settings; in the Agent it writes the connected host's settings.

`/payments approve <shop> --most <amount> <item...>`: the shop's domain, the most it may cost (in `payments.currency`), and the item in your words. The approval is used once, for a purchase matching all three that begins within five minutes; such a purchase needs no further answer up to that amount. Approving the same shop, item and amount again while the first approval is unused returns that approval rather than making a second. When recording an approval cannot be confirmed, the answer is `OUTCOME_UNKNOWN` ("The approval may have been recorded ..."), and the web UI says it may have been approved instead of "Nothing was approved". The approval is for that amount in the currency `payments.currency` named when it was given (the reply names it): a begin after `payments.currency` changed is a different purchase, does not spend it, and with `payments.confirmEveryPurchase` on is refused saying the merchant, item, amount or currency differs.

```text
/payments approve shop.example --most 25.00 USB-C cable
Approved ahead of time: "USB-C cable" from shop.example, at most 25.00.
It ends 11/18/2026, 10:20:00 AM; the amount is in USD.
```

"Allow a repeat purchase" lets a scheduled routine or trigger buy one thing without asking, within limits. Its blanks:

| Blank | Option | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shop | `--shop` (again for each further shop) | 1 to 8 shop domains, each with a dot; picked from the shops you have bought from, or typed. |
| What may be bought | `--item` | Your words, 1 to 200 characters. |
| Most per purchase | `--each` | Above zero. |
| Most in any period | `--per-period` | At least the per-purchase amount. |
| Period | `--days` | 7, 30 (the usual), 90 or 365 days; typed, any whole number 1 to 366. |
| Last day | `--until` | Optional, `YYYY-MM-DD`. Without it the authorisation lasts until you stop it. |

At most 32 repeat purchases are kept.

```text
/payments repeat --shop shop.example --shop pets.example --item "dog food" --each 60.00 --per-period 120.00 --days 30 --until 2027-06-30
Allowed: "dog food" from shop.example, pets.example. Stop it any time: Stop a repeat purchase.
/payments repeats
/payments stop-repeat standing-1a2b3c4d
```

In the web UI the Repeat purchases screen lists the same allowances, each with Stop, under `Allow a repeat purchase…`, a sheet with the same six blanks and sentence; both are sent as the owner's own request.

The example lets a scheduled run buy "dog food" from either shop, at most 60.00 a purchase and 120.00 every 30 days, until 30 June 2027. A routine's purchase names the authorisation as `standingId` when it calls `payments.checkout.begin`. Every budget, ceiling and purchase window still applies to each purchase under it. A refusal names the field and ends with `Nothing was added.`, for example `maxPerPeriod must be one amount in USD, at least the per-purchase maximum.`

How a purchase is started: there is no owner command that buys. You ask the Agent in conversation ("buy one USB-C cable from shop.example, at most 25 dollars"). The Agent's model opens the shop's checkout page with its `browser` tool, then calls its `agent_operator_method` tool with `methodId` `payments.checkout.begin` and the open page (`sessionId`, `pageId`), `requestId`, `merchantDomain`, `checkoutUrl`, `item`, the requested and quoted lines, the shipping options, the stated total, the currency and optionally `cardId` (else `payments.defaultCardId`) and `requestedMax`. The daemon then reads the page itself, applies the decision below and runs the window. "Accepted" in the answer does not mean bought: `payments.purchase.status` with the `requestId`, `/payments pending` and the web UI Purchases panel show where it stands. The terminal app's model has neither tool, so purchases are started from the Agent (or from a daemon-hosted Agent session, or by an operator client calling `POST /api/payments/checkout/begin` with the `write:payments` scope). A routine or trigger purchase must name a standing authorisation as `standingId`.

How that call is checked, in order:

1. The permission gate decides the `agent_operator_method` call like any other tool call. `payments.checkout.begin` and `payments.purchase.cancel` are not owner-only methods, so the call is a judgment call: with a working decision model Jev decides it in `jev-decides` and `just-vibes` (held instead of refused in `just-vibes`), `ask-me` runs it unless the reading is critical, irreversible or security-weakening; without a decision model it is asked (held in `just-vibes`); `yolo` runs it; `plan` refuses it. The owner-only methods (answering a window, typing a card code, approving in advance, adding a standing authorisation) are refused to the model in every mode.
2. The tool screens the request: it is held if it would carry text the model may not send on (the judgment-input boundary) or card material. It does not run the outward-content check other operator calls get: a purchase's taint is judged by the daemon against the purchase itself.
3. A begin without `standingId` is sent as the owner's own request (the explicit-user-request context); a begin naming `standingId` claims no owner request and is bound to that entry's shops, item and maximums.
4. The daemon then applies every payment gate below (purchases enabled, the owner asked directly, taint of item, maximum, merchant and link, this daemon runs payments for its group, a card, a shipping address), then the budget decision and the window. These apply in every permission mode, `yolo` included.

The model may start a purchase (`payments.checkout.begin`) and cancel one, and read status and the purchase list. Everything else (answering a window, typing a security code, approving in advance, adding a standing authorisation) is the owner's act and is refused to the model.

### How a purchase is decided

1. Gates, each a refusal with no approval path: purchases enabled; the purchase was asked for by the owner directly, not by content he read; this daemon runs payments (alone it always does; in a cluster exactly one machine holds the group's payments role, chosen by the election, and every other machine refers the owner to it: `Refused: in this group of machines purchases run on one machine at a time, and that is <name>. Ask there (its terminal app, web UI or channels); it buys with its own card, address and daily budget.`); a usable card; a shipping address; item and maximum not taken from untrusted content; a checkout link that passes full link validation.
2. The merchant is graded on the domain that takes the card. Established recourse makes the later window a veto window; anything else makes it an approval window. Grading needs a decision model: with none in use (or under `Hybrid` after the set model failed) the merchant is "not judged, because no decision model is in use", which is not established recourse, so every purchase opens an approval window (60 minutes, silence denies), even within every budget. An eBay auction or Best Offer listing is refused. `payments.majorRetailersAdditional` and `payments.majorRetailersExcluded` adjust the grade; `payments.ebayMinSellerFeedbackCount` (100) and `payments.ebayMinSellerPositivePercent` (98) set the eBay seller bar.
3. The page's prices are parsed into numbers, the cart must hold only what was asked for, and a subscription or recurring charge is refused. Without a decision model, a cart line whose label is not exactly a requested item is never passed over because the requested quantities are met: it is listed in the approval window for the owner to see.
4. Budget: the item price against what is left of `budget.dailyItem` (over it, the purchase needs approval: "This item costs USD 40.00 and only USD 25.00 is left in today's item budget, USD 15.00 short."; it is not refused for that); tax, mandatory fees and delivery against `budget.dailyOverage`, stepping delivery down from `payments.shipping.preferredTier` (`normal`, `fast`, `fastest`) one tier at a time until it fits; then the overage tolerance pool if `budget.overageToleranceEnabled`; otherwise refused. The full total is checked against the card's declared issuer cap (over it is refused), the per-purchase ceiling (over it needs approval) and the maximum the owner asked for (over it needs approval). A checkout in another currency is refused.
5. The pools are reserved before the owner is asked.
6. One notification goes out with what was chosen and what it will cost:
   - Veto window (within budget, recourse established): silence for `payments.windows.vetoMinutes` (10) proceeds; an objection cancels. An answer that could not be read (an unreadable owner inbox) is not silence: nothing is bought, and the purchase is refused `answer-unreadable`. An objection or denial given through `payments.purchase.deny` or `payments.purchase.cancel` (the web UI's buttons) is written to the purchase's record before it is reported accepted, so a daemon that stops right after never resumes that window and never buys on its silence.
   - Approval window (over budget, over the requested maximum, or no recourse): silence for `payments.windows.approvalMinutes` (60) denies; only an explicit approve proceeds. When the notice cannot be delivered, a within-budget purchase proceeds and an over-budget one is refused.
   - `payments.confirmEveryPurchase` `true` makes every purchase need the owner's approval.
7. The card is filled and the order submitted. Without a decision model, code checks the live page first: the approved total must be the amount on the order summary's total line (a "Total", "Order total" or "Grand total" line, never a subtotal), and when the page offers delivery choices the quoted one must be the one shown as selected; otherwise nothing is submitted and the purchase stops for the owner to start again. A card security code, 3-D Secure or CAPTCHA pauses for the owner (`/payments pending`). With `payments.cvvHandling` `prompt`, the security code is not stored and is asked every time.
8. The purchase is recorded as `purchased` only when the page the submit landed on, on the merchant's own domain, shows an order number, or shows a confirmation together with this submit's own total. Confirmation wording alone ("Thank you for your order") records `submitted-unverified`: the money is counted as spent, and the owner confirms or denies the order (`payments.purchase.reconcile`, the Purchases panel) or the shop's confirmation mail settles it.
9. The owner's report of a recorded purchase is saved with the purchase record and marked sent once a channel took it; a report the daemon did not get out before it stopped is sent at its next start.

While the daily item budget or the per-purchase ceiling is `0`, every purchase that gets past the overage check asks; the first time, the owner inbox offers once to set that limit. The overage check comes first: with `payments.budget.dailyOverage` at `0`, a checkout with tax, fees or a paid delivery is refused before any question: `Refused: tax, fees and even the lowest delivery option I could choose come to <amount> and only USD 0.00 is left in today's overage budget, <amount> short. ... The daily overage budget is not set (0). Set payments.budget.dailyOverage ...`.

### Two purchases worked through

Settings: `payments.budget.dailyItem 50`, `payments.budget.perPurchaseCeiling 30` (ceiling on, the default), `payments.budget.dailyOverage 10`, overage tolerance off, `payments.shipping.preferredTier normal`, a card with no declared cap, currency USD. "Price" below is the item price on the checkout page; tax, fees and delivery come on top.

Purchase A, item price 25.00, tax 2.00, standard delivery 8.00 (nothing faster offered):

1. Item 25.00 against today's item pool 50.00: fits.
2. Tax plus delivery 10.00 against today's overage pool 10.00: fits (a draw equal to what is left fits).
3. Full total 35.00 against the ceiling 30.00: over by 5.00, so it needs approval: "This purchase comes to USD 35.00 and is over the per-purchase ceiling of USD 30.00 by USD 5.00."
4. The pools are reserved (item 25.00, overage 10.00) and an approval window opens: silence for 60 minutes denies; `approve` buys.

If delivery were 9.00 instead (tax plus delivery 11.00 over the 10.00 pool, and no cheaper tier offered), purchase A is refused at step 2 with `overage-pool-exhausted`, before the ceiling is looked at.

Purchase B, the same day after A was bought, item price 40.00, tax 3.00, delivery 5.00:

1. Item 40.00 against what is left of the item pool, 25.00: over by 15.00. On its own this would only need approval ("only USD 25.00 is left in today's item budget, USD 15.00 short").
2. Tax plus delivery 8.00 against what is left of the overage pool, 0.00: does not fit at any tier, and tolerance is off, so it is refused (`overage-pool-exhausted`).

Purchase B on a fresh day: item 40.00 fits the pool of 50.00; tax plus delivery 8.00 fits 10.00; total 48.00 is over the ceiling 30.00 by 18.00: an approval window ("over the per-purchase ceiling of USD 30.00 by USD 18.00").

A purchase within every limit (for example item 15.00, tax 1.00, delivery 4.00, total 20.00) at a merchant with established recourse opens a veto window: silence for 10 minutes buys it. At a merchant without established recourse, or with no decision model in use, it opens an approval window even within budget.

### Where payment data lives

| Data | Location |
| --- | --- |
| Settings | `~/.goodvibes/daemon/settings.json` |
| Card numbers, expiry, security code, name | Daemon secret store `~/.goodvibes/daemon/secrets.enc`, keys `GOODVIBES_PAYMENTS_CARD_<ID>_<FIELD>`; never returned by any method |
| Card list (id, label, brand, last 4, kind, expiry, issuer cap) | `~/.goodvibes/tui/control-plane/payments-cards.json` |
| Purchase ledger, budget pools, approvals, checkout journal | `~/.goodvibes/tui/control-plane/payments-*.json` |

Not supported: a checkout quoted in another currency, a subscription or recurring charge, and crediting a pool for money that comes back (a refund does not restore the budget).

## CI watch

CI watch reports a GitHub repository's CI status job by job and can watch a branch or pull request until its verdict is in.

Prerequisites: the `gh` CLI installed and signed in (`gh auth login`) on the daemon's machine.

```text
/ci status my-org/my-repo
/ci status my-org/my-repo#42            a pull request
/ci status my-org/my-repo@main          a branch, tag or commit
/ci watch my-org/my-repo#42 telegram
/ci watch my-org/my-repo@main slack:C0123456 --fix-session
/ci watches
/ci run <watch>
/ci unwatch <watch>                    asks first
```

```sh
goodvibes-agent ci status my-org/my-repo --ref main
goodvibes-agent ci status my-org/my-repo --pr 42
goodvibes-agent ci watches list
goodvibes-agent ci watches create my-org/my-repo --ref main --delivery-channel slack:C0123456 --trigger-fix-session --yes
goodvibes-agent ci watches run <watchId>
goodvibes-agent ci watches delete <watchId> --yes
```

- Every job and its conclusion is listed; the overall verdict comes from the jobs, never a rollup. A job configured `continue-on-error` cannot be detected through `gh` and is not flagged.
- The delivery channel is `surfaceKind` or `surfaceKind:address`.
- `--fix-session` (`--trigger-fix-session` in the Agent) starts a fix session on a red verdict, seeded with the tails of up to five failing jobs' logs.
- A standing watch is polled every `watchers.ciPollIntervalMs` (never faster than 15 seconds), sends its verdict once, then retires. A watch whose branch is gone, or that gets no verdict in time, ends with a "no verdict" notice.
- A `git push` or `gh pr create` run through the `exec` tool creates a watch for the pushed branch by itself, delivered to the web UI.

## Occasions and plans

The daemon keeps dated facts about the owner's life and raises them ahead of time.

- An occasion (a birthday, an anniversary) is dated, usually annual, and needs an action. It is raised `occasions.leadDays` (10) days ahead, and the owner's answer is remembered until the next occurrence.
- A plan (a trip with dates and a place) is ambient: nothing is asked, but nudges are moved out of the time the owner is away (`occasions.awayAdjust`).

Both are written in the owner profile, `~/.goodvibes/daemon/owner-profile.md` (another location with `profile.path`), under `## Important dates` and `## Plans`, one line each:

```markdown
## Important dates
- Sarah's birthday · 03-14 · annual · gift-giving · for Sarah · lead 21
- Dad · 11-02 · annual · remember-only
- Our anniversary · 2015-09-12 · annual · gift-giving · for Jane

## Plans
- Lisbon · 2026-09-12..2026-09-19 · away · in Lisbon
```

Segments after the title may be in any order; `|` may be used instead of `·`. A date `MM-DD` is annual and `YYYY-MM-DD` is a one-off unless `annual` or `once` says otherwise; `once` needs a year, so a `MM-DD` line marked `once` is reported as unreadable. The kind is `gift-giving` (offers a gift conversation), `remember-only` (no gift) or `neither`, and is always the owner's choice; nothing infers it. `for <name>` says who it is about; `for me` marks the owner's own date (a `remember-only` date of his own is listed but never pushed at him). `lead <n>` overrides the lead time for one occasion. A line that cannot be read is reported with a reason and never rewritten; you may also edit the file by hand.

### Where occasions are managed

- The Agent: the model's `occasions` tool, used in ordinary conversation ("remember that Sarah's birthday is 14 March"). The terminal app has no occasions command or tool and never receives nudges.
- The web UI: Personal, Occasions tab: open items, upcoming occasions and plans; "Add occasion" and "Add plan" (preview, then confirm), Edit, answering, resolving a conflict, continuing a gift interview, gift history, and the sweep.
- The operator methods `occasions.*` (scope `read:occasions` or `write:occasions`).

### The `occasions` tool (Agent)

Each call names an `action`:

| Action | What it does | Main inputs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `list` | Every occasion with its next occurrence, days away, window and recorded answer; unreadable lines with reasons; conflicts. The only read that returns real dates. | |
| `pending` | Everything outstanding: nudges (naming the occasion with a word such as approaching, soon or imminent, never the date), open interviews, conflicts. | |
| `state` | What the machine-owned store holds: counts and reasons. | |
| `gifts` | What the owner landed on in earlier years. | `occasionId` |
| `plans` | Plans, and whether one has the owner away today. | |
| `propose` | Draft an occasion and return the one-line confirmation to read back plus a `proposal` token. Writes nothing. | `title`, `date`, `kind`, `person`, `recurrence`, `leadDays`, `self` |
| `confirm` | Write exactly the proposed line to the profile. Refused without a kind. | `proposal`, `kind` |
| `plan_propose` / `plan_confirm` | The same two steps for a plan. | `title`, `from`, `to`, `away`, `destination`, `details` (list); then `proposal` |
| `answer` | The owner's answer to a nudge: `yes`, `no`, `later` or `acknowledged`. | `occasionId`, `answer`, `occurrence` |
| `interview` | Resume a gift interview at its unanswered question. | `interviewId` |
| `interview_answer` | Record one answer and return the next question. | `interviewId`, `stepId`, `text` |
| `interview_record` | Close the interview with what the owner settled on; written to gift history. | `interviewId`, `landedOn` |
| `remove` | Remove an occasion's line (named in the answer as `removedLine`) and every record against it, after asking the owner once. When other lines still declare the same occasion, only the first line goes and its records stay. | `occasionId`, `confirmed: true` |
| `resolve_conflict` | Two lines for one thing: with `keep`, keep the first line with that date and remove the others; without it, return the recorded dates to ask about (lines that agree on the date need no `keep`). | `occasionId`, `keep` |
| `sweep` | Run one pass now. | |

A date heard in conversation is confirmed with the owner once, at the time ("Noted your anniversary as 12 September, right?"), then written.

### Answers and the gift interview

- `yes` on a gift-giving occasion opens a short gift interview: up to `occasions.interviewQuestions` (3, range 1 to 8) questions that open from what the profile already knows about the person and from what the owner chose last time ("Last time you went with <gift>. Something in the same vein, or somewhere different this year?"). The agent does not recommend a gift. Each answer is recorded with `interview_answer`; the interview ends with `interview_record` and what the owner landed on, which is kept in gift history for `occasions.giftHistoryYears` years. An interview the owner walks away from is not finished: it resumes at the unanswered question, the next day.
- `no` ends the question for this occurrence; next year asks again with no memory of the refusal. For a one-off, it is final.
- `later` is not a no: it comes back roughly halfway to the date.
- `acknowledged` means "I have it in hand": the item stays open and listed, and stops being pushed. It never replaces a yes or no already given.

### When nudges are sent

- An occasion is pushed at most twice: once when it enters its lead window (`occasions.leadDays`, default 10 days before), and once on the day. Between those it stays open and quiet, and `pending` always lists it.
- Pushes go to `occasions.nudgeChannel` (default `telegram`; a comma list of `surface` or `surface:address`, for example `telegram:12345,agent`; empty makes it pull-only). `agent` means the Agent reads outstanding items at the end of each turn and when the daemon says one is waiting.
- Nothing is pushed outside `occasions.activeHours` (default `08:00-22:00`, in `daemon.timezone`); it waits.
- A plan with `away` moves a nudge due during the trip to the day before departure (`occasions.awayAdjust`).
- Two lines for one thing (different dates, or the same date written twice) are raised at once and again every `occasions.cadenceDays` (3) days until resolved.
- `occasions.calendarMirror` copies occasions into the calendar; `occasions.suppressMirroredNudges` then avoids a second reminder.
- The daemon checks every `occasions.sweepIntervalMinutes` (60); a sweep runs soon after start when the last one is older than that.

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `occasions.enabled` | `true` | Master switch. |
| `occasions.leadDays` | `10` | Days ahead an occasion is first raised. |
| `occasions.nudgeChannel` | `telegram` | Where nudges go. Never the terminal app. |
| `occasions.activeHours` | `08:00-22:00` | When nudges may be sent. |
| `occasions.cadenceDays` | `3` | How often an unresolved date conflict is raised again (1 to 60). It does not repeat birthday reminders. |
| `occasions.awayAdjust` | `true` | Move nudges out of away plans. |
| `occasions.calendarMirror` | `false` | Mirror occasions into the calendar. |
| `occasions.suppressMirroredNudges` | `true` | No push for a mirrored occasion. |
| `occasions.interviewQuestions` | `3` | Questions in a gift interview (1 to 8). |
| `occasions.giftHistoryYears` | `10` | How long gift history is kept. |
| `occasions.sweepIntervalMinutes` | `60` | How often the daemon checks. |

Answers, interviews, gift history and calendar-mirror records are kept apart from the profile, in the daemon's `occasions-state.json`.

Operator methods: `occasions.list`, `occasions.pending`, `occasions.state`, `occasions.sweep`, `occasions.propose`, `occasions.confirm`, `occasions.update`, `occasions.remove`, `occasions.answer`, `occasions.acknowledge`, `occasions.interview.get`, `occasions.interview.answer`, `occasions.interview.record`, `occasions.gifts`, `occasions.conflict.resolve`, `occasions.plans.list`, `occasions.plans.propose`, `occasions.plans.confirm`, `occasions.plans.update`, `occasions.plans.remove`. The methods that write the profile (`confirm`, `update`, `remove` and the plan equivalents) take a required `authority`; `update` without `confirmed` returns the line to put to the owner and writes nothing.

## List-valued settings

Some settings hold a whole list. Each is read and written as one JSON value; a malformed list is refused whole.

| Setting | What it is for | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `notifications.webhookUrls` | Webhook URLs that receive this machine's notifications (turn ends, approvals waiting, budget alerts). Each member is a `goodvibes://secrets/` reference to a URL kept in the secret store; a literal URL is refused. Applies at the next start. Managed by `/notify add`. | `["goodvibes://secrets/goodvibes/GOODVIBES_NOTIFY_WEBHOOK_1A2B3C4D5E6F"]` |
| `sandbox.egressAllowlist` | Command names the exec sandbox lets reach the network. From the next command. | `["git","npm"]` |
| `sandbox.workspaceWritable` | Extra absolute paths sandboxed commands may write. From the next command. | `["/home/me/.cache/build"]` |
| `surfaces.email.imap.authservIds` | Authserv-ids your mailbox's receiving server writes in `Authentication-Results`, for a provider that is not built in. An entry starting with `.` matches the hosts under that domain. | `["mx.example.com"]` |
| `provider.fallbackModels` | Your fallback order: the provider-qualified models a turn moves to, in every program (terminal app, `run`, the Agent, hosted sessions, the daemon's agents), when the selected model fails on every sign-in of its provider and its retries. The provider half is matched by id or display name without regard to case. Empty: the turn stops and says so. | `["anthropic:claude-sonnet-5"]` |
| `cluster.peers` | Cluster peers (`host` or `host:port`) contacted directly as well as over multicast, for a network that drops multicast. | `["10.0.0.2","10.0.0.3:4000"]` |
| `conversationGate.gatedSurfaces` | Channel surfaces whose inbound messages pass the conversation gate before a session sees them. | `["slack","telegram"]` |
| `contract.gates` | Quality gates a contract runs before it reports work done: objects `{ "name", "command", "enabled" }` with optional `required` and `verification`; a gate passes or fails on its command's exit code. A gate that cannot run is refused when saved. | `[{"name":"tests","command":"bun run test","enabled":true}]` |
| `worktree.setup.commands` | Commands run in a new worktree before an isolated agent starts in it. `[]` (auto, the default) runs the install command each lockfile names; `{"mode":"none"}` runs nothing. | `["bun install"]` |
| `worktree.setup.carryOverGlobs` | Untracked files copied from the main checkout into a new worktree. `[]` (auto) copies `.env` and `.env.*`; `{"mode":"none"}` copies nothing. | `[".env","config/*.local.json"]` |

These are settings only; "lists" in this section means these list-valued settings. GoodVibes has no shopping-list feature. Both apps have the same to-do list, the project's work plan, kept with `/todo` (`list`, `markdown`, `export`, `add <title>`, `edit <item> <title>`, `mark <item> <state>`, `next <item>`, `remove <item>`, `clear-done`; `/todo` alone opens these as a list to choose from). The Agent's model reads and changes it with the `agent_work_plan` tool, the terminal app's with the `work_plan` tool. Both are described in full in "The terminal app (`goodvibes`)" and "The Agent (`goodvibes-agent`)".

How to edit one, from each surface:

| Surface | How |
| --- | --- |
| Terminal app | `/settings set <key> <JSON list>`, for example `/settings set sandbox.egressAllowlist ["git","npm"]`; `[]` empties it. `/settings <key>` opens the settings workspace at the key. `-c <key>=<JSON list>` sets it for one launch. |
| Agent | `/settings <key>` opens the settings workspace at the key, where the list is edited. `/settings set` does not take a list. `-c <key>=<JSON list>` sets it for one launch. |
| Daemon command line | `goodvibes-daemon config get <key>`, `goodvibes-daemon config set <key> '<JSON list>'`, `goodvibes-daemon config unset <key>`, `goodvibes-daemon config list`. Quote the JSON for the shell. |
| Web UI | Settings: the key's field is a JSON editor that checks the list before it saves. |
| Operator API | `config.set` and the other `config.*` methods (described in "The daemon, the web UI and networking"). |

`notifications.webhookUrls` is set through `/notify add|remove|list|clear`, which keep each URL in the secret store. A value that fails the key's check is refused whole with the key's hint, for example `list of absolute paths`.

| `watchers.ciPollIntervalMs` | number | `60000` | integer in [1000, 86400000] | daemon file | Cadence (ms) for the daemon's recurring CI-watch poll; the poller enforces a 15s floor to respect the status source's rate limits. Read once when the daemon starts: a new value applies after the next restart. |
| `watchers.enabled` | boolean | `true` |  | daemon file | Enable managed watcher/listener services (checkpointing and recovery for long-running external sources). Default on: with no watchers configured the framework idles. |
| `watchers.heartbeatIntervalMs` | number | `15000` | integer in [1000, 3600000] | daemon file | Heartbeat interval for watcher services in milliseconds. |
| `watchers.pollIntervalMs` | number | `60000` | integer in [1000, 86400000] | daemon file | Default polling interval in milliseconds for new watchers registered through the API; existing watchers and other registration paths keep their own interval. |
| `watchers.recoveryWindowMinutes` | number | `10` | integer in [0, 1440] | daemon file | Recovery window for watcher restart and missed-event catch-up. |
| `watchers.triggers.backoffLadderMs` | string | `"30000,60000,300000,900000,3600000"` | comma-separated integers, each 1000..86400000 ms | daemon file | Comma-separated retry ladder in milliseconds, walked one rung per consecutive failure of a trigger check. The default climbs 30s, 60s, 5m, 15m, 60m so a briefly unreachable endpoint recovers fast while a genuinely broken one stops hammering. The last rung repeats until the breaker opens. Read once when the daemon starts; restart to apply a change. |
| `watchers.triggers.breakerStrikes` | number | `5` | integer in [1, 50] | daemon file | Consecutive check failures that open the trigger's breaker. An open breaker parks the trigger in a visible circuit-open state with the last error attached instead of retrying forever; the operator resets it explicitly. Raise it for a flaky-but-recoverable source, lower it to fail fast. Read once when the daemon starts; restart to apply a change. |
| `watchers.triggers.defaultCheckIntervalMs` | number | `60000` | integer in [1000, 86400000] | daemon file | Cadence used by a condition trigger that does not declare its own interval. This is the steady-state polling rate; the backoff ladder overrides it while a trigger is failing. |
| `watchers.triggers.enabled` | boolean | `false` |  | daemon file | Enable the trigger family: stream watchers over long-lived commands, model-free condition checks, and one-shot on-exit process triggers. Off by default because a trigger launches and supervises real processes on your machine without a person watching, turning it on is a deliberate choice, not a fallback. With it on and no triggers defined, the supervisor idles and consumes nothing. |
| `watchers.triggers.eventLogLimit` | number | `500` | integer in [10, 50000] | daemon file | Entries retained in the shared event log that cross-watcher correlation rules read. This log is the only channel through which one trigger can observe another, and it is bounded so correlation cannot grow without limit. Read once when the daemon starts; restart to apply a change. |
| `watchers.triggers.eventLogTtlHours` | number | `24` | integer in [1, 2160] | daemon file | Age ceiling in hours on the shared correlation event log. Correlation windows longer than this cannot see the older side of the pair, so raise it together with any long correlation window. Read once when the daemon starts; restart to apply a change. |
| `watchers.triggers.maxConcurrentChecks` | number | `4` | integer in [1, 64] | daemon file | How many condition checks may execute at the same moment. Checks beyond this wait their turn, so a large trigger set cannot saturate the machine or a rate-limited API. |
| `watchers.triggers.observationRingSize` | number | `200` | integer in [2, 10000] | daemon file | Observations kept per trigger in its persisted ring buffer. Every rule, change, transition, rate-of-change, windowed aggregation, is a pure function over this buffer, so this is the memory depth available to them. Larger windows need a larger ring. Read once when the daemon starts; restart to apply a change. |
| `watchers.triggers.onExitMaxDurationMs` | number | `21600000` | integer in [1000, 604800000] | daemon file | Hard ceiling on a supervised on-exit child. When it is reached the child is terminated and the trigger fires with an explicit timed-out termination state, so a process waiting on a prompt that will never come cannot hang forever. The six-hour default is sized for a long build. |
| `watchers.triggers.onExitStdin` | enum | `"none"` | `none`, `empty` | daemon file | Standard input handed to a supervised on-exit child. "none" closes stdin so a password-prompting process gets EOF and exits instead of blocking forever; "empty" attaches an immediately-closed empty pipe for programs that require a readable stdin handle. There is deliberately no interactive option, nobody is at the keyboard. |
| `watchers.triggers.outputTailBytes` | number | `8192` | integer in [0, 1048576] | daemon file | Bytes of trailing child output carried in an on-exit termination payload. Exit is not success, so the payload always includes this tail for the agent prompt to inspect alongside the exit code and signal. |
| `watchers.triggers.probeTimeoutMs` | number | `15000` | integer in [250, 600000] | daemon file | Ceiling on one probe execution (http request, file read, command run, or platform-tool call) before it is abandoned and counted as a failed check. Keeps a hung endpoint from stalling the whole check queue. |
| `watchers.triggers.runHistoryLimit` | number | `50` | integer in [1, 5000] | daemon file | Run records kept per trigger (when it ran, what it observed, whether it fired, what the action returned). Bounded on purpose: an append-only history is a disk leak with a nicer name. Read once when the daemon starts; restart to apply a change. |
| `watchers.triggers.runHistoryTtlHours` | number | `168` | integer in [1, 8760] | daemon file | Age ceiling in hours on retained run history. Records older than this are reaped by the recovery sweep even when the count limit has not been reached, and the sweep reports how many it removed. Read once when the daemon starts; restart to apply a change. |
| `watchers.triggers.streamBatchIntervalMs` | number | `1000` | integer in [50, 3600000] | daemon file | How long a partially filled stream batch waits before it is flushed anyway, so a slow trickle of matches still reaches an agent promptly instead of waiting for the batch to fill. |
| `watchers.triggers.streamBatchLines` | number | `25` | integer in [1, 10000] | daemon file | Matched lines gathered into one payload before an agent is invoked. Batching is what keeps a stream watcher from starting one agent turn per log line. |
| `watchers.triggers.streamQueueLimit` | number | `1000` | integer in [1, 1000000] | daemon file | Matched lines a stream watcher may hold before the oldest are dropped. The queue is bounded so a chatty log cannot exhaust memory; every drop is counted and reported on the trigger record rather than being silent. |
| `watchers.triggers.supervisionTickMs` | number | `1000` | integer in [250, 300000] | daemon file | How often the supervisor checks whether a supervised on-exit child has terminated and whether any condition check is due. This is the floor on how quickly an on-exit trigger notices its process ended; raise it to trade detection latency for less polling on a machine running long builds. Read once when the daemon starts; restart to apply a change. |
| `watchers.triggers.sweepIntervalMs` | number | `300000` | integer in [10000, 86400000] | daemon file | Cadence of the recurring housekeeping sweep: reap records whose owning process or session is gone, retire fired one-shot triggers, enforce the count and age bounds, and re-validate persisted state by content. A daemon that only sweeps at boot never sweeps. Read once when the daemon starts; restart to apply a change. |

| `surfaces.email.inbound.enabled` | boolean | `false` |  | daemon file | Turns on inbound notices: arriving mail is matched against open verification expectations, recorded and announced, and further accounts below are watched. Off by default. The daemon's own mailbox is read by one reader for the inbox as well whenever it is configured; this switch decides whether that mail is also announced. |
| `surfaces.email.inbound.expectationWindowMinutes` | number | `15` | integer in [1, 60] | daemon file | Default lifetime, in minutes, of a verification expectation opened for inbound-mail matching (for example an account signup awaiting its confirmation email). Raising it gives a slower-to-arrive confirmation more time to match; lowering it shrinks how long a stale expectation can be satisfied by a late message. Hard-capped at 60 to match MAX_VERIFICATION_WINDOW_MS. Applies after the daemon restarts. |
| `surfaces.email.inbound.gmailPollSecondsExpecting` | number | `5` | integer in [2, 60] | daemon file | How often the Gmail source asks Google what changed while something is actually being waited for, a signup mid-flight whose verification mail has not arrived yet. This is polling, not push: mail can sit unnoticed for up to this many seconds, and no setting makes Gmail faster than the interval. Five seconds is the floor worth having for a person watching a signup form; the underlying call costs 2 quota units against a daily budget in the billions, so a shorter interval buys latency rather than saving quota. Ignored entirely when the IMAP source is in use, which pushes instead. |
| `surfaces.email.inbound.gmailPollSecondsIdle` | number | `60` | integer in [10, 3600] | daemon file | How often the Gmail source asks Google what changed when nothing is being waited for. Again polling, not push: with nothing pending, mail is noticed up to this many seconds after it arrives. A minute keeps the daemon from asking Google every five seconds all week for mail nobody is waiting on; lowering it narrows that gap at the cost of a request every few seconds around the clock. Ignored entirely when the IMAP source is in use. |
| `surfaces.email.inbound.idleReissueMinutes` | number | `27` | integer in [5, 29] | daemon file | How often an open IDLE connection is torn down and re-issued. RFC 2177 advises re-issuing at least every 29 minutes, or the server may silently log the connection off; raising this toward 29 trims reconnect churn but leaves less margin against a slow round trip. |
| `surfaces.email.inbound.mailboxes` | string | `"{}"` | a JSON object mapping account names to {"host":"…","user":"…"}, with optional port, secure, mailbox and passwordRef | daemon file | JSON object giving each account after the first in surfaces.email.inbound.accounts its own IMAP mailbox, e.g. {"signups":{"host":"imap.example.com","user":"signups@example.com"}}. Fields: host and user (required), port (default 993, or 143 when secure is false), secure (default true; false only for a loopback host), mailbox (default INBOX) and passwordRef, a goodvibes://secrets/goodvibes/<KEY> reference whose key contains EMAIL, MAIL or IMAP as a word. Without passwordRef the password is read from the secret GOODVIBES_EMAIL_INBOUND_<ACCOUNT>_PASSWORD (the account name upper-cased, other characters as _). Each mailbox is watched with the same inbound settings as the first, and a change here takes effect without a restart. |
| `surfaces.email.inbound.maxRecords` | number | `5000` | integer in [100, 100000] | daemon file | Hard cap on the number of inbound mail records kept regardless of age. Whichever of this and retentionDays is reached first wins, so this bounds worst-case storage even under a burst of mail. Applies after the daemon restarts. |
| `surfaces.email.inbound.mode` | enum | `"auto"` | `idle`, `poll`, `auto` | daemon file | How the IMAP source receives new mail: "idle" holds a persistent IMAP IDLE connection, "poll" checks on a timer, "auto" uses IDLE when the server advertises it and falls back to polling when it does not. Leave at auto unless a specific provider needs to be forced one way. Applies only to the IMAP source; the Gmail source has no IDLE to hold and is always polled, on the two intervals above. |
| `surfaces.email.inbound.notice.mode` | enum | `"all"` | `all`, `expected-only`, `none` | daemon file | How much inbound mail generates an owner notice: "all" announces every message, "expected-only" announces only mail matching a registered expectation (quieter for a high-volume mailbox), "none" announces nothing. Choosing "none" means mail can arrive with no notice at all, a deliberate but silent choice. |
| `surfaces.email.inbound.notice.route` | string | `"default"` |  | daemon file | Where the owner is told about inbound mail: the literal "default" uses the owner's most recently used one-to-one conversation with the daemon (never a group or shared channel); a specific route binding id, shared or not, sends inbound-mail notices there instead. A second place to configure "where to reach me" is a second place to get it wrong, so most installations should leave this at default. |
| `surfaces.email.inbound.onInsufficientCapability` | enum | `"refuse-and-notify"` | `refuse-and-notify`, `notice-only` | daemon file | "refuse-and-notify" stops the watcher for that account and tells the owner once, naming what is missing and the exact step to fix it, the account is not watched again until the recheck above finds it fixed. "notice-only" is a deliberate downgrade: it keeps announcing that mail arrived using envelope fields alone (sender, subject, delivery evidence), stating plainly in every notice that bodies are unavailable, and it can never satisfy a verification expectation while degraded, an account signup or order confirmation will not work under it. "notice-only" applies to exactly one condition: a Google grant that authorizes message headers and excludes message bodies (the gmail.metadata scope), which is the only case where mail can be seen arriving without being readable. Every other insufficient condition, no stored password, a refused sign-in, a mailbox that will not open, a lost cursor, a refused or unreadable fetch, leaves no envelope fields to announce, so "notice-only" behaves as "refuse-and-notify" there and the notice says which one is in force. |
| `surfaces.email.inbound.pollIntervalSeconds` | number | `120` | integer in [30, 3600] | daemon file | How often the fallback poller checks the mailbox when IDLE is unavailable. Lower is more responsive but closer to a provider's rate limit; higher delays notice of new mail by up to this many seconds. Only applies when the connection is not using IDLE. |
| `surfaces.email.inbound.reconnect.maxBackoffSeconds` | number | `300` | integer in [10, 3600] | daemon file | Ceiling on the exponential reconnect backoff after a dropped connection or provider error. Raising it tolerates a longer provider outage without hammering it; lowering it shortens the worst-case silence after a disconnect at the cost of retrying a still-down server more often. |
| `surfaces.email.inbound.retentionDays` | number | `30` | integer in [1, 365] | daemon file | How many days an inbound mail record (sender, subject, delivery evidence, link verdicts, never the full body) is kept before it is reaped. Longer keeps a longer history to explain "why did I get that message"; shorter bounds how much of the owner's mail metadata the daemon retains. Applies after the daemon restarts. |
| `surfaces.email.inbound.source` | enum | `"auto"` | `auto`, `gmail`, `imap` | daemon file | Which mechanism reads the mailbox. "auto" uses Gmail when Google credentials have been adopted and the configured mail account is a Gmail account, and IMAP otherwise, so connecting Google is the whole of the setup and no IMAP host, username or app password has to be found. "gmail" and "imap" force one of them. The two are not equivalent and the difference is a real cost: IMAP holds an IDLE connection, which is true push and delivers in under a second, while Gmail has no push available to a daemon on a home machine and is POLLED on a timer, its worst-case delay is the whole poll interval below, never less. Forcing "gmail" without adopted Google credentials, or on an account that is not a Gmail account, is refused rather than quietly served over IMAP. |

| `voice.wake.activationSound` | enum | `"chime"` | `none`, `chime`, `custom` | each program | Sound played the moment a wake is confirmed. "custom" plays voice.wake.activationSoundPath; "none" is silent and leaves voice.wake.indicator as the only feedback. |

A browser tab cannot read a path on your machine, so it plays the built-in chime instead and reports that this row is not in force there, a wake stays audible either way. |

Applies to the utterance captured after a WAKE; push-to-talk always places its transcript in the composer, because a person who pressed a key is already looking at the screen. Off by default, matching the never-auto-send posture of the existing voice input: a misheard transcript must not become a submitted turn without a human seeing it first. |
| `voice.wake.browserBackend` | enum | `"wasm"` | `wasm`, `webgpu` | each program | Execution backend for the detector inside a browser tab. "wasm" is the default and the measured configuration: the per-frame cost already beats real time by a wide margin, and WebGPU cannot run the front end without splitting the graph across devices, which costs more in transfers than it saves. "webgpu" is available for hosts that measure otherwise. Read by the browser tab when it creates its inference sessions; a host surface always runs WASM and ignores this row. BOTH VALUES LOAD THE SAME ENGINE BINARY, the WebGPU-capable build carries the CPU engine too, so switching costs no extra download, and a tab set to "webgpu" on a browser without navigator.gpu falls back to the CPU provider inside the binary it already has. |
| `voice.wake.captureCommand` | enum | `"auto"` | `auto`, `pw-record`, `parecord`, `arecord`, `ffmpeg`, `sox` | each program | Which recorder feeds capture on a HOST surface, the terminal and the daemon child process. A browser tab ignores this row and uses getUserMedia. Feeds both consumers: wake detection and push-to-talk voice input. "auto" probes for pw-record, parecord, arecord, ffmpeg, then sox and uses the first present, mirroring how local audio playback discovers its player. Name one explicitly to pin the choice on a host where the probe picks a device-starved backend; a named recorder that is not installed reports that instead of quietly falling back, because pinning it was the point. |
| `voice.wake.captureMaxSeconds` | number | `10` | integer in [0, 120] | each program | Hard ceiling on how long capture runs before it stops on its own. Bounds memory and guarantees a stuck or silent stream cannot hold the microphone open indefinitely. Applies to post-wake capture AND to push-to-talk, where a key-release event that never arrives would otherwise leave the device open. 0 REMOVES THE CEILING: speech-to-text imposes no length limit of its own, so the ceiling is policy rather than a technical bound, and a long dictated thought is a real thing to want. It still defaults to 10 because the ceiling is the backstop for the OTHER stop condition failing. Post-wake capture normally ends about voice.wake.silenceStopMs after you stop talking, which depends on frames reading as silence, with the ceiling off, a stream that goes stuck or a room the silence floor cannot resolve holds the microphone open with nothing left to close it. Turn it off alongside a silence-stop you have seen work in your room; voice.wake.silenceFloorRms is the row that makes that reliable. |
| `voice.wake.cooldownMs` | number | `2000` | integer in [0, 60000] | each program | Milliseconds after a confirmed wake during which further detections are ignored, so one spoken phrase cannot fire twice as it passes through the detector's rolling window. Applied after patience confirms a hit. 0 disables the cooldown and lets every confirmed frame fire. |
| `voice.wake.crashWindowSeconds` | number | `60` | integer in [1, 3600] | each program | Rolling window in which repeated crashes count toward voice.wake.maxRestarts. Exceeding the ceiling inside this window latches the supervisor off so a detector that cannot stay up stops consuming the device; a clean run past the window resets the count. |
| `voice.wake.customModelDir` | string | `""` |  | each program | Directory searched for wake models whose ids are not the pinned default. Empty uses the managed wake model directory under the surface storage root. Set it to keep your own models outside the managed tree; files there are loaded as-is and are not checksum-pinned, unlike the managed download. |
| `voice.wake.enabled` | boolean | `false` |  | each program | Listens all the time for the wake phrase on the chosen microphone. Turning it on starts a supervised capture process and a persistent listening indicator; turning it off stops it and releases the device immediately. WHERE IT LISTENS depends on the voice.wake.surfaces.* rows: the terminal captures through a recorder subprocess and is on by default, the agent captures the same way and is opted in per surface, and a browser tab captures through getUserMedia and is opted in per origin. Off by default because an always-on microphone must be an explicit act, not something a user discovers after the fact. THE MODEL IS ALREADY THERE: installing goodvibes downloads and checksum-verifies the pinned classifier, and a daemon retries at boot if the install could not reach the network, so turning this on normally needs no setup step at all. Turning it on in the terminal app or Agent (settings, /settings, a model's settings call) runs the same setup as /voice wake-setup: it turns the wake rows on, fetches any missing wake-word model files and shows the plan; installing a speech-to-text engine is only proposed. |
| `voice.wake.indicator` | enum | `"statusline"` | `off`, `statusline`, `banner` | each program | How the surface shows that the microphone is live. "statusline" keeps a persistent listening marker for as long as the detector runs, not only at the moment of a wake, so an always-on microphone is never invisible: a footer row in the terminal, a status-strip chip in the web UI. "banner" is more prominent; "off" removes the marker entirely and is not the default for that reason. |
| `voice.wake.inputDevice` | string | `""` |  | each program | Capture device to listen on. Empty means the operating system default source. Shared by BOTH microphone consumers: wake detection and push-to-talk voice input open the same device through the same path, so this row moves both rather than only the always-on one. Device identifiers are host-specific, list real ones with `pactl list short sources` or `arecord -L`, or use a navigator.mediaDevices deviceId in a browser tab. Note pw-record takes a PipeWire node serial or node name here, not a PulseAudio device name, and sox cannot target a device at all (it reads AUDIODEV from the environment), which the surface reports rather than silently ignoring. |
| `voice.wake.maxRestarts` | number | `3` | integer in [0, 20] | each program | How many times the supervisor restarts a crashed detector process inside voice.wake.crashWindowSeconds before it stops trying and reports the failure. Matches the restart ceiling used for MCP clients. 0 disables restarts, so any crash is terminal and immediately visible. |
| `voice.wake.models` | string | `"hey_goodvibes"` | comma-separated ids made of letters, digits, dot, underscore and hyphen (no path separators) | each program | The wake-word models to listen with, by name, separated by commas. Default "hey_goodvibes" is the model the platform pins, hosts, and verifies by checksum. Additional ids resolve against voice.wake.customModelDir. Each model costs one classifier inference per 80 ms frame, the shared melspectrogram and speech-embedding front end is computed once regardless of how many models are listed, so a second model is far cheaper than a second detector. An empty list disables detection without stopping the service. Ids are letters, digits, dot, underscore and hyphen only, since each becomes a file name. |
| `voice.wake.noiseSuppression` | enum | `"none"` | `none`, `speex` | each program | Noise suppression applied to captured audio before anything reads it, the wake classifier scores filtered frames, and the utterance recorded after a wake (and push-to-talk voice input) is filtered audio too. "speex" is SpeexDSP's own denoiser, carried in the platform as a WebAssembly module and applied on every surface that has WebAssembly, which is both shipped ones: nothing to install, nothing to download, no per-host library. It attenuates the estimated noise floor by about 15 dB, measured at 13.2 dB against a synthetic tone-plus-white-noise set, for 0.24 ms of work per 80 ms frame beside the detector's own 3.46 ms. "none" ships as the default and is a true passthrough: the captured bytes reach the detector exactly as the device produced them. Choose "speex" on a noisy input (a fan, an air conditioner, street noise through an open window), and "none" on a quiet one, where a denoiser only has speech to work on. |
| `voice.wake.patienceFrames` | number | `2` | integer in [1, 10] | each program | Consecutive 80 ms frames that must all score above voice.wake.threshold before the wake fires. Two frames is about 160 ms of agreement, which removes most single-frame false accepts for one extra frame of latency. Set to 1 for the fastest possible trigger at the cost of more spurious wakes. |
| `voice.wake.preRollMs` | number | `500` | integer in [0, 2000] | each program | Milliseconds of audio kept from BEFORE the wake fired and prepended to the speech-to-text request, so a phrase run straight into the command ("hey goodvibes, what's—") is not clipped at the front. 500 ms covers the detector's own confirmation latency plus a fast speaker. 0 starts capture at the moment of detection. |
| `voice.wake.restartBackoffMs` | number | `2000` | integer in [0, 60000] | each program | Base delay before restarting a crashed detector, multiplied by the attempt number for linear backoff (2 s, 4 s, 6 s). Stops a process that fails instantly from becoming a restart storm. |
| `voice.wake.retainAudio` | enum | `"none"` | `none`, `session-temp` | each program | Whether captured audio is written to disk. "none" by default, nothing is stored, which is the only setting under which the microphone leaves no recording behind. "session-temp" keeps clips in a session-scoped directory that is deleted when the session ends and swept on recovery, and exists to debug a bad transcript, not as a recording feature. A browser tab has no filesystem to retain into: it reports that this row is not in force rather than appearing to store clips it is not storing. |
| `voice.wake.silenceFloorRms` | number | `0` | integer in [0, 8000] | each program | The audio level at or below which a frame counts as silence, on the int16 magnitude scale the capture path uses (full scale 32768, so 180 is about -45 dBFS). 0, the default, MEASURES IT PER UTTERANCE from the audio captured just before the wake fired, and places the floor 12 dB above the room's own noise. That measurement is what makes voice.wake.silenceStopMs work at all in a room that is not quiet: with a fixed floor, steady background noise above it means no frame is ever silent, silence never accumulates, and every capture runs to the voice.wake.captureMaxSeconds ceiling however long ago you stopped talking. The floor then FOLLOWS the room for the rest of the capture, tracking the quiet moments in the last second and a half, because a headset with automatic gain control raises the input once you stop talking and the room comes back louder than the number measured before it. It is never raised over a third of the speech being heard at the same time, so it cannot end up above your own voice. Set a number to pin the floor instead, which is worth doing if the measurement guesses wrong in your room: raise it if capture keeps running after you stop, lower it if capture cuts off while you are still speaking. A number you set here is used exactly as given AND frozen, it stays where you put it for the whole capture, with no following. The first measured value is never allowed below 180 or above 1440; the following that comes after it may reach 5760. |
| `voice.wake.silenceStopMs` | number | `1200` | integer in [100, 10000] | each program | Milliseconds of silence that end post-wake capture, so the request is sent when the user stops talking rather than at the voice.wake.captureMaxSeconds ceiling. Raise it if capture cuts off mid-sentence during natural pauses. Post-wake only: push-to-talk ends when the key is released, because someone holding it through a pause has not finished talking. |
| `voice.wake.speechRetriggerMs` | number | `150` | integer in [0, 2000] | each program | How long a run of sound above the silence floor has to last before it counts as you talking again. Shorter runs are counted as part of the silence they interrupted rather than starting the voice.wake.silenceStopMs wait over. This is what a close-worn or in-ear microphone needs: a breath, a lip tick or a chair creak is loud and lasts one or two frames, and treating each one as speech means the wait never completes and capture runs to the voice.wake.captureMaxSeconds ceiling every time however long ago you stopped. 150 ms sits under the shortest syllable anyone ends a sentence on and over the longest of those noises. Raise it if capture still will not end in a room full of short noises; lower it if the first word of a resumed sentence gets clipped. 0 turns it off, so every loud frame resets the wait, the behaviour before this row existed. |
| `voice.wake.surfaces.agent` | boolean | `false` |  | each program | Listen for the wake phrase on the agent surface, through a recorder subprocess on the host, the same capture path the terminal uses. Turning this on with voice.wake.enabled opens the microphone on the agent, and a confirmed wake sends the utterance that follows to speech-to-text and puts the transcript into the agent conversation input, or submits it when voice.wake.autoSubmit is on. Off by default because two surfaces on one machine both acting on a single spoken utterance is a confusing default, not because it does not work: turn it on when the agent is the surface you actually talk to, and consider turning voice.wake.surfaces.tui off when you do. |
| `voice.wake.surfaces.app` | boolean | `false` |  | each program | Listen for the wake phrase in the desktop companion app, which runs the detector inside its embedded webview on a WASM backend, the same runtime and download path the web UI uses. Off by default because webview capture is a separate stack with its own microphone permission prompt, it is opted into per install, not inherited from the host. While it is off the webview never calls getUserMedia at all, so no permission prompt appears. |
| `voice.wake.surfaces.tui` | boolean | `true` |  | each program | Listen for the wake phrase on the terminal, through a recorder subprocess on the host. On by default: once wake detection is enabled the terminal is the primary surface, and a wake that reaches no surface is a detector that appears broken. A confirmed wake plays the activation sound, shows the listening indicator, captures the utterance that follows and sends it to speech-to-text, then places the transcript in the composer, or submits it when voice.wake.autoSubmit is on. |
| `voice.wake.surfaces.webui` | boolean | `false` |  | each program | Listen for the wake phrase in the web UI, which runs the detector inside the browser tab on a WASM backend and downloads the pinned model through the daemon. This daemon's setting: once it is on, every browser that opens this daemon's web UI listens, each only after its own microphone permission prompt is accepted. Off by default because browser capture is a separate stack from the terminal's. While it is off a tab never calls getUserMedia at all, so no permission prompt appears. A plain-http origin cannot capture and says so instead of failing silently. |
| `voice.wake.threshold` | number | `0.9` | number in [0, 1] | each program | How sure, from 0 to 1, the listener must be before the wake phrase counts as heard. DELIBERATELY 0.9, NOT openWakeWord's upstream default of 0.5 and not the 0.5 originally accepted for this row: measurement on the shipped hey_goodvibes model showed 0.5 fires on 34.5% of never-trained minimal-pair phrases ("hey good vibe check", "hey goodbye vibes", ordinary English a user will actually say) at 99.2% recall, while 0.9 cuts that to 24.7% for 96.8% recall. Trading 2.4 points of recall to remove roughly a third of the wrong wakes is the better default for a microphone that is always on. Lower it toward 0.5 if the detector misses you; raise it above 0.9 if it fires when you did not speak to it. Recall figures here are synthetic-only, no human has recorded the phrase. |
| `voice.wake.vadThreshold` | number | `0` | number in [0, 1] | each program | Speech-probability floor, 0 to 1, from the speech gate run ahead of the wake classifier; frames below it are withheld from scoring instead of being classified. The gate is our own speech/non-speech head over the SAME embedding the wake classifier consumes, so it costs one extra inference of 0.025 ms per 80 ms frame, beside the detector's own 3.46 ms, and no extra front end. It provisions with the wake models. Measured on 106,390 held-out frames: at 0.3 it passes 96.0% of speech frames and withholds 95.7% of non-speech ones, which is the recommended value; lower passes more speech and screens less, higher screens more and starts costing wakes. 0 is the shipped default and turns the stage off entirely, it is the configuration that has been exercised longest, and a gate can only ever cost you a detection. A surface that has not loaded the gate REFUSES TO START with any value above 0, rather than running unscreened frames through a stage you have configured. |

| `payments.cvvHandling` | enum | `"stored"` | `stored`, `prompt` | daemon file | How the card verification value is handled at checkout. 'stored' (DEFAULT) keeps it in the daemon secret store beside the card number, encrypted at rest, so a purchase within budget completes while you are away, which is what autonomous action requires. Choosing 'prompt' stores nothing: when a purchase is approved and reaches payment, it stops and asks you to type the code in the terminal app (/payments pending) or the local web UI, waiting as long as an approval window, and nothing is bought if the code is not typed in time. So nothing completes while you are away. Never send the code in a chat; a likely code typed on a remote channel while one is awaited is refused there. Surfaces show CVV_PROMPT_TRADEOFF_WARNING at the moment you select it. Provisioning a virtual card with a hard issuer cap bounds what any leak of stored card material could cost; a real card number does not. |
| `payments.defaultCardId` | string | `""` |  | daemon file | A card id from payments.cards.list. A purchase that names no card is paid with this one; with this empty, every purchase must name its card. Deleting that card does not clear this setting, and a purchase that would use a deleted card is refused saying so. The card NUMBER, expiry and CVV live in the daemon secret store and never in config. |
| `payments.ebayMinSellerFeedbackCount` | number | `100` | integer in [0, 1000000] | daemon file | Minimum feedback ratings earned AS A SELLER before an eBay Buy It Now listing proceeds on silence. eBay's headline score combines buying and selling, so an account with a large number can have earned all of it buying, only the seller-side figure counts. Below this, or when the figure cannot be read from eBay's own seller widget, the purchase asks for your yes. The listing is read by code from the page the purchase runs on: its purchase controls and eBay's seller card, never the seller's text. Auctions and Best Offer listings are refused outright regardless, because there is no final price to show you before paying. |
| `payments.ebayMinSellerPositivePercent` | number | `98` | integer in [0, 100] | daemon file | Minimum positive feedback percentage AS A SELLER before an eBay Buy It Now listing proceeds on silence. Read from eBay's own feedback widget, never from the seller's listing text, if the figures cannot be attributed to eBay with confidence, the purchase asks for your yes rather than assuming. |
| `payments.enabled` | boolean | `false` |  | daemon file | Master switch for the payment capability. Default OFF. While false the daemon will not price, reserve, or charge anything, and the payments operator methods refuse. Turning it on does not by itself allow a purchase, the daily budgets below start at 0, so nothing goes through until you set an amount. |
| `payments.majorRetailersAdditional` | string | `""` | a comma-separated list of registrable domains | daemon file | Comma-separated REGISTRABLE domains (eTLD+1, e.g. 'microcenter.com', not 'www.microcenter.com') to add to the recognised-retailer list. A purchase at a recognised retailer gets the veto window, you are told and it goes ahead unless you object. Everything else asks for your yes. The test is recourse: is there a real path to remedy if it goes wrong. Additions are yours alone, nothing is learned onto this list, inferred from a page, or added by an agent, because a page that could argue itself onto it could buy from itself unattended. |
| `payments.majorRetailersExcluded` | string | `""` | a comma-separated list of registrable domains | daemon file | Comma-separated registrable domains to REMOVE from the shipped recognised-retailer list, so purchases there ask for your yes instead of proceeding on silence. A domain listed in both this and the additions is excluded (it asks for your yes), because on a spending path the stricter instruction wins. |
| `payments.notifyChannels` | string | `""` | a comma-separated list; only 'telegram' can deliver a notice today | daemon file | Comma-separated, ordered list of channels that ALSO receive approval and veto prompts and may answer them. Every purchase notice, window and confirmation is always posted to your owner inbox (/questions in both terminal apps, and the web UI), where it can be answered, whatever this says; these channels reach you away from them. Today only 'telegram' has a delivery path. EMAIL IS NOT AND WILL NEVER BE ACCEPTED HERE, an inbound email is content anyone can write and cannot authorize spending. An unrecognised name is rejected rather than ignored, because a channel you believe will reach you and does not is worse than none. Empty means the owner inbox only: an in-budget purchase is announced there and waits its veto window, and an above-budget one is asked there. |
| `payments.shipping.preferredTier` | enum | `"normal"` | `normal`, `fast`, `fastest` | daemon file | Preferred delivery tier, ordinal against WHAT THE CHECKOUT ACTUALLY OFFERS rather than delivery-day promises: its options are ranked cheapest-first and this indexes into that ranking. The chosen tier draws on the overage budget; when the budget cannot cover it, delivery steps down ONE tier at a time until it fits, stopping at the cheapest. A step-down needs no approval (it is within budget) but is recorded and shown to you, so you never learn about it from a late package. Default 'normal'. |
| `payments.shippingAddress.city` | string | `""` |  | daemon file | City or town. Where purchases are delivered. A purchase is REFUSED while the shipping address is incomplete, there is nowhere to send it, and guessing an address is not a thing this should do. When left empty, the matching address field of the owner profile is used once it has been verified. |
| `payments.shippingAddress.country` | string | `""` |  | daemon file | Country, as the checkout expects it (an ISO two-letter code is safest). Where purchases are delivered. A purchase is REFUSED while the shipping address is incomplete, there is nowhere to send it, and guessing an address is not a thing this should do. When left empty, the matching address field of the owner profile is used once it has been verified. |
| `payments.shippingAddress.line1` | string | `""` |  | daemon file | Street address, first line. Where purchases are delivered. A purchase is REFUSED while the shipping address is incomplete, there is nowhere to send it, and guessing an address is not a thing this should do. When left empty, the matching address field of the owner profile is used once it has been verified. |
| `payments.shippingAddress.line2` | string | `""` |  | daemon file | Second address line (apartment, suite); leave empty when unused. Where purchases are delivered. A purchase is REFUSED while the shipping address is incomplete, there is nowhere to send it, and guessing an address is not a thing this should do. When left empty, the matching address field of the owner profile is used once it has been verified. |
| `payments.shippingAddress.name` | string | `""` |  | daemon file | Recipient name. Where purchases are delivered. A purchase is REFUSED while the shipping address is incomplete, there is nowhere to send it, and guessing an address is not a thing this should do. When left empty, the matching address field of the owner profile is used once it has been verified. |
| `payments.shippingAddress.postalCode` | string | `""` |  | daemon file | Postal or ZIP code. Where purchases are delivered. A purchase is REFUSED while the shipping address is incomplete, there is nowhere to send it, and guessing an address is not a thing this should do. When left empty, the matching address field of the owner profile is used once it has been verified. |
| `payments.shippingAddress.region` | string | `""` |  | daemon file | State, province or region; leave empty where the country has none (it is required only for countries whose addresses use one, such as US, CA, AU, IN). Where purchases are delivered. A purchase is REFUSED while the shipping address is incomplete, there is nowhere to send it, and guessing an address is not a thing this should do. When left empty, the matching address field of the owner profile is used once it has been verified. |
| `payments.windows.approvalMinutes` | number | `60` | integer in [1, 10080] | daemon file | How long an ABOVE-BUDGET purchase waits for your explicit approval, in minutes. This is the opposite of the veto window: if you say nothing, the purchase is DENIED. Denial is the recoverable outcome, ask again and it goes through, so a short window costs friction while a long one leaves a cart holding a price that may drift. Default 60, which survives a meeting or a commute; raise it if you are away for long stretches. |
| `payments.windows.vetoMinutes` | number | `10` | integer in [1, 1440] | daemon file | How long you get to STOP an in-budget purchase, in minutes, starting once the final total is known and before payment. The notice is always in your owner inbox, and on the channels in payments.notifyChannels. This is a VETO, not an approval: if you say nothing, the purchase GOES AHEAD. One word (stop) cancels it. The window always runs its full length wherever you are, no presence, focus or activity signal shortens it, and an explicit acknowledgement buys immediately. |

Full entries (files, project rule, environment variable): "Settings" in the part "Reference", under "payments".

| Key | Type | Default | Allowed | Stored in | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `daemon.timezone` | string | `""` | empty (UTC) or an IANA timezone name like 'America/New_York' | daemon file | IANA timezone name the daemon reckons CALENDAR DAYS in, e.g. 'America/New_York', 'Europe/London'. Empty means UTC. This is the daemon's own location, not a display preference and not a per-schedule zone (schedules keep their own). Anything that resets daily reads it: the payment capability's daily budgets roll over at midnight in this zone. Changing it does not refill a spent budget: each spend keeps the day it was made on and counts until that day is over, and an agent cannot change it in a way that moves today; only the owner can. |

Full entries (files, project rule, environment variable): "Settings" in the part "Reference", under "daemon".

| Key | Type | Default | Allowed | Stored in | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `occasions.activeHours` | string | `"08:00-22:00"` |  | daemon file | The hours a nudge may arrive, HH:MM-HH:MM, reckoned in daemon.timezone. 08:00–22:00 because those hours are generally fine and anything outside them probably is not. Outside this window nothing is dropped, it waits. An empty or unreadable value means no restriction rather than permanent silence, so a typo cannot switch the feature off invisibly. |
| `occasions.awayAdjust` | boolean | `true` |  | daemon file | Let a plan that has you away from home move a nudge EARLIER, to the day before you leave. On because you cannot have something delivered to a house you are not in, so a reminder that arrives while you are abroad has already missed the window it existed to protect. When you have already left there is nothing earlier to move to and the nudge stands rather than waiting for your return. |
| `occasions.cadenceDays` | number | `3` | integer in [1, 60] | daemon file | How often an unresolved CONFLICT in your dates, two lines recorded for the same thing (two different dates, or one date written twice), is raised again, in days. It no longer governs birthday reminders: those speak twice, when the date enters its runway and on the day itself, and never repeat beyond that. A conflict is a fact about your file that stays wrong until you fix it, so it does keep coming back. |
| `occasions.calendarMirror` | boolean | `false` |  | daemon file | Write your occasions out to the connected calendar as well. Off by default because your profile is the record and the calendar is a copy, calendar entries are single occurrences that do not persist across years, which is exactly why these dates live in the profile instead. Nothing is ever read back the other way, and deleting a calendar entry never removes the occasion. |
| `occasions.enabled` | boolean | `true` |  | daemon file | Raise your important dates on their own, before they matter. On by default because a feature that ships off ships dark, and because being told about your wife's birthday in time is the whole point. Turning it off does NOT forget anything: the dates stay in your profile, stay readable, and are still answered when you ask, it only stops the system raising them unprompted. |
| `occasions.giftHistoryYears` | number | `10` | integer in [1, 50] | daemon file | How long the record of what you landed on is kept, in years. Ten, so year three is not steered by year one. This is the one part of the machine-owned state that deliberately outlives its occasion's answer, the answers expire with their date so next year asks fresh, the history does not. |
| `occasions.interviewQuestions` | number | `3` | integer in [1, 8] | daemon file | How many questions are asked after you say yes to sorting a gift. Three, because it is meant to guide you to an idea rather than fill in a form, and a long one is a form. The questions open from what your profile already knows about the person and from what you landed on last time; none of them recommends anything. |
| `occasions.leadDays` | number | `10` | integer in [0, 365] | daemon file | How many days ahead an occasion starts being raised. Ten because that is enough runway to order something and have it arrive. An individual entry overrides this by carrying "lead 21" on its line, so a date that needs longer does not force everything else earlier. |
| `occasions.nudgeChannel` | string | `"telegram"` |  | daemon file | Where a nudge is delivered: a comma-separated list of channel destinations, each a surface or surface:address, "telegram", "agent", "telegram,agent", "telegram:12345,agent". Telegram by default, because an occasion nudge that waits to be asked for has already missed the date it existed to protect, the owner ruled that these push out of the box, to Telegram and to the agent. Naming "agent" puts the reminder in the Agent's conversation: the host tells a connected Agent to read it at once (when no turn is running; otherwise when the turn ends), and an Agent that was not connected reads it at its next turn or idle check, because the reminder stays outstanding until you answer it. Naming both means both get it, and a broken credential on one cannot silence the other. Set it to empty to make the feature pull-only instead: nothing is pushed or announced, and a surface picks up what is outstanding at the end of a turn. The TUI is refused as a destination whatever is set here: it is a get-work-done interface, and life admin does not belong in it. |
| `occasions.suppressMirroredNudges` | boolean | `true` |  | daemon file | Stay quiet about an occasion that is already in a calendar, so the calendar's own reminder is the only ping. On by default because two pings for one birthday is how a useful reminder becomes one you mute. Turn it off if you would rather have both, an occasion marked "mirrored" on its own line is covered by this too. |
| `occasions.sweepIntervalMinutes` | number | `60` | integer in [5, 1440] | daemon file | How often the daemon looks for dates entering their lead window, in minutes. Hourly by default, which is frequent enough that a nudge lands within an hour of the window opening and cheap enough to be invisible, the pass reads memory and touches one small file. It cannot over-nudge whatever this is set to: each occasion carries its own next-due date, so a shorter interval makes the FIRST nudge land sooner and changes nothing about the rhythm after it. Housekeeping runs on every pass, including the ones that are inside quiet hours or that raise nothing. |

Full entries (files, project rule, environment variable): "Settings" in the part "Reference", under "occasions".

# The daemon, the web UI and networking
