| `rotate --now` | Stops accepting the old key at once and also replaces the group signing key and the join key. Use it when a key may have leaked. A machine asleep at the time takes the new key from the group when it wakes; a machine to be added needs the new join key. |

What they print:

```text
$ goodvibes-daemon cluster rotate
the group key is now generation 1
the previous key stays accepted for a few minutes so nothing is interrupted while
the other 2 machine(s) pick the new one up.

accepting generations 1 and 0

$ goodvibes-daemon cluster rotate --now --yes
the group key is now generation 2
the previous key stopped being accepted immediately, and the key the group signs with
was replaced too. A machine that is asleep right now takes the new key from the group when it wakes.

accepting generation 2
```

Key changes converge in any order and at any spacing (`rotate --now` then `forget` within a second, `forget` then `rotate --now`, several in a row, two members rotating at once). Each key generation is an entry of the group's record (who minted it, why, and a commitment to the key, never the key), and the key itself travels with it sealed to every current member, never to a removed one. The change is sent at once and again on each 30-second pass until every member's record covers it. A member that missed it, or several, notices on the group's next datagram (a generation it does not hold) or the next gossip of record heads, and asks a member for the record; the answer carries the newest generation, which it takes directly, however many it skipped. These requests and answers are signed with each machine's identity key, which never changes, so they work however far behind a member is. Which generations a machine accepts is worked out from the record, the same way on every machine, so a machine that joins later never reopens a key a removal closed. In testing every member, including one paused, one stopped and one restarted through the changes, showed the newest generation and the same record by the next status read after it was running again. A removal or `rotate --now` hands the new group signing key and join key to every remaining member the same way.

The join key is never rotated by the schedule; it changes only on `rotate --now` and on `forget`. Run `cluster key` afterwards to see the new one. A machine that was off through several rotations catches up by itself when it starts, as long as the group still lists it; its log says `took authority record changes from the group` and `adopted a replacement group key`.

### Renaming a group

```sh
goodvibes-daemon cluster rename "the workshop"
```

```text
the group is now called "the workshop"
this name is visible to anything on this network, and every machine in the
group will pick it up shortly.
```

The name is an entry of the group's record, so it is sent to every member at once (a member that missed it takes it with the next gossip of record heads), and it is advertised on the network.

### Confirmation

`leave`, `forget`, `rotate --now`, `publish` and `accept` cannot be undone. At an interactive terminal they ask `<what it does>. Type yes to continue:`. In a script, with `--json`, or from a slash command they must be given `--yes` (`-y`); otherwise they fail with code `not-confirmed`, exit `1` and change nothing:

```text
$ goodvibes-daemon cluster forget charlie
cluster: cluster forget was not run: this removes charlie from the group and replaces the group key immediately, and it was not confirmed
  nothing was changed. Run it again with --yes to confirm: cluster forget charlie --yes
```

### A complete run on one machine

These commands were run on three daemons on one machine, inside a network namespace with only a loopback interface, each daemon with its own `GOODVIBES_HOME`, working directory and control-plane port (39431, 39432, 39433), sharing UDP port 61860 over loopback multicast. Replace `--port` with your daemons' ports, or leave it out on separate machines. Each machine had `cluster.enabled` `true` and its own `cluster.nodeName` (alpha, bravo, charlie) before it started.

```sh
goodvibes-daemon cluster create --name home --json --port 39431                    # on alpha
goodvibes-daemon cluster key --port 39431                                          # on alpha
goodvibes-daemon cluster groups --port 39432                                       # on bravo: lists "home"
goodvibes-daemon cluster join --group <id> --key <join key> --port 39432           # on bravo: joined, 2 machines
goodvibes-daemon cluster join --group <id> --key <join key> --port 39433           # on charlie: joined, 3 machines
goodvibes-daemon cluster nodes --port 39431                                        # alpha, bravo, charlie
goodvibes-daemon cluster rename "the workshop" --port 39431
goodvibes-daemon cluster rotate --port 39431                                       # generation 1, old key still accepted
goodvibes-daemon cluster rotate --now --yes --port 39431                           # generation 2, new join key
goodvibes-daemon cluster status --port 39432                                       # repeat on every member until each shows "generation 2"
goodvibes-daemon cluster key --port 39431                                          # the new join key
goodvibes-daemon cluster forget charlie --yes --port 39431                         # removed; group key and join key replaced again
goodvibes-daemon cluster leave --yes --port 39432                                  # bravo leaves
goodvibes-daemon cluster join --group <id> --key <current join key> --port 39432   # bravo is admitted again
```

The outputs are the ones shown in the sections above. A wrong key (`gvj1-AAAA-...`) was refused at once with `a machine in that group answered and the join key did not match`.

### Election

Each surface has its own election. When several nodes can serve a surface, the winner is decided the same way on every node:

1. the newest daemon version wins;
2. then the node holding the fewest surfaces wins, which spreads surfaces across machines;
3. then a fixed hash of the node id and the surface id.

The holder sends a heartbeat every `cluster.heartbeatSeconds` (default 5). A node shut down normally hands its surfaces over at once. A node that crashes is noticed only by its silence: it is replaced after `cluster.masterTimeoutSeconds` (default 15, three missed heartbeats; never less than two heartbeats) plus a short election, about 20 seconds in all. A crashed node that is restarted takes its surfaces back after its boot probe. A starting node listens for `cluster.bootProbeSeconds` (default 3) before claiming a surface. A cluster holds at most 64 members.

### Clustering without a group

With `cluster.enabled` `true` and no group, a machine listens (so `cluster join` can list groups) but sends nothing and gates nothing. `cluster.secret` is for machines that coordinate without a group: when it is set, their messages are signed with it and unsigned messages are ignored. When it names a stored secret that cannot be read (deleted, or the secret store cannot be opened), the machine sends and takes no coordination messages at all rather than run unsigned; its `/status` cluster section reports `electionAuthentication: "unavailable"`, `cluster status --json` the same, and the daemon log says `cluster.secret names a stored secret that could not be read`. Store the phrase again (`secrets set`) or clear `cluster.secret`, then restart. Inside a group it is not used.

### Diagnosing a node that is behind or unreachable

The product has no single "behind" or "unreachable" state for a node. These are the signs it does report, what each means, and where to read it:

| Sign | Meaning | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `could not reach <where>` (code `unreachable`) | The node's control plane did not answer the command: the daemon is stopped, or its HTTP port is not reachable from where you ran the command. This says nothing about the cluster. | Any `goodvibes-daemon` command with `--host`. |
| `LAST SEEN` growing on the other members, or `not heard since this daemon started (...)` | The other members hear no cluster traffic from this node: it is stopped, it lost the network, UDP 61860 or multicast is blocked between them, or it no longer holds a key they accept. | `cluster nodes` on a healthy member. |
| `group key: generation N` lower on this node than on the others | Behind on keys: it missed a rotation. Its datagrams are dropped by the others as "on an old key". | `cluster status` on each node. |
| `... on an old key` climbing in the `traffic:` line | This node is receiving datagrams signed with keys it does not accept (if it is the one behind), or is receiving them from a node that is behind. | `cluster status`. |
| `0 received` or a `received` count that does not move | Nothing arrives: multicast is dropped or UDP 61860 is blocked. | `cluster status`. |
| `shared settings: ... at revision N` lower than elsewhere, or `differs from another machine or is still catching up; settings are being exchanged`, `... change(s) from the group not applied here yet`, `... credential(s) known to the group have not arrived here yet` | Behind on shared settings. It catches up by itself (retried every 30 seconds, credentials every minute) as long as it can hear the group. | `cluster status`. |
| `version:` older than the other nodes | Behind on the program version. It still works; the newest version wins each election. | `cluster status`, `goodvibes-daemon status`. |
| `membership: unreadable-key-material` (`--json`) with advice `group membership storage could not be confirmed ...` | The node cannot read its group keys from the encrypted secret store (for example `secrets.key` missing or changed). It retries every 30 seconds; a restart retries at once. | `cluster status`. |

A procedure, run in this order:

1. On the suspect node: `goodvibes-daemon status`. Exit `1` with `could not reach the daemon on this machine` means the daemon is down: `goodvibes-daemon service-status`, then `start-service`.
2. On a healthy member: `goodvibes-daemon cluster nodes`. Note the suspect's `LAST SEEN`.
3. On every node: `goodvibes-daemon cluster status`. Compare `group key: generation`, `version`, the `shared settings` revision, and the `traffic:` line.
4. If the suspect's `received` count does not grow: check that UDP 61860 is allowed in and out on both machines, that every node has the same `cluster.port` and `cluster.multicastGroup`, and that multicast crosses the network; if it does not, set `cluster.peers` on every node (`goodvibes-daemon config set cluster.peers '["10.0.0.2","10.0.0.3"]'`) and restart them.
5. If the suspect's key generation is lower than the others' while its `received` count grows, it catches up by itself within about a minute of hearing the group. If it stays lower, its `cluster status` will say whether the group removed it; to put it back, `cluster join --group <id> --key <current join key>` on it (no `leave` needed).
6. Read its log for `cluster:` lines: `grep "cluster:" <working dir>/.goodvibes/logs/activity.md | tail -30`. `took authority record changes from the group` followed by `adopted a replacement group key` is a member catching up; `this machine was removed from its group by another member` means it was removed; `dropped a reply to this machine's return that it could not authenticate` means a machine whose own record no longer lists it could not be re-keyed.

### Which node holds a channel

`cluster status` lists only the surfaces this machine holds (`surfaces held by this machine:` with lines such as `cecb9f3b947e049ad6e5b13dd53118f9: elected for ntfy (ntfy:cecb9f3b)`). The full picture, from any node, is in its status document:

```sh
goodvibes-daemon status --json | python3 -c "import json,sys;c=json.load(sys.stdin)['data']['identity']['cluster'];print(json.dumps(c['surfaces'],indent=1));print(json.dumps([{k:p[k] for k in ('nodeId','version','holds')} for p in c['peers']],indent=1))"
```

Each entry of `surfaces` is one inbound surface this node can serve: `label` (`ntfy:cecb9f3b`, a digest, never the topic or bot name), `kind`, this node's `role` for it (`master` when it holds it, `standby`, `probing`, `electing`, `awaiting-handoff`, `resigning`, `fenced`, `stopped`), `holderNodeId` (the node this one believes holds it), and `consuming`. `peers` lists the other nodes with their `version` and the surface digests each `holds`. Match `holderNodeId` against `cluster nodes` to get the machine's name.

A surface cannot be moved by command. To move one, stop its holder (`goodvibes-daemon stop-service` on that machine): a clean stop hands it over at once; a crash is noticed after `cluster.masterTimeoutSeconds`. A `fenced` role means the consumer did not stop when told to; only a restart of that daemon clears it. Such a surface carries `drainFailure`, the reason its consumer did not stop, and stays listed as `fenced` (never `stopped`) after the cluster is stopped, whose stop then fails naming it.

### Cluster failure codes

With `--json`, every failure is `{ "ok": false, "code": "<code>", "error": "...", "fix": "..." }` and exit code `1`. The codes: `usage`, `not-confirmed`, `not-interactive`, `no-group-found`, `invalid-port`, `invalid-host`, `token-missing`, `unreachable`, `auth-refused`, `route-missing`, `unreadable-reply`, `refused` (the daemon's own refusal; its `error` and `fix` are passed through). Over HTTP the routes are `GET /api/cluster/status|key|nodes|groups` and `POST /api/cluster/create|join|forget|rotate|leave|rename|publish|accept`, all admin; a refusal is HTTP `409` with `{ "ok": false, "error", "fix" }`.

### Cluster settings

Changes to `cluster.enabled`, `cluster.peers` and `cluster.secret` need a daemon restart; the daemon's own refusal messages say so. The settings marked "Applies after the daemon restarts" in their description also need one.

| Key | Type | Default | Allowed | Stored in | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `cluster.beaconSeconds` | number | `15` | integer in [5, 3600] | daemon file | How often this machine advertises its group on the local network, in seconds. The advertisement carries the group's id, its name, how many machines are in it and this build's version, and nothing else. It is what lets a new machine running `cluster join` see the group and pick it from a list. Lower means a new machine finds the group faster; higher means slightly less traffic. Applies after the daemon restarts. |
| `cluster.bootProbeSeconds` | number | `3` | integer in [1, 300] | daemon file | How long a starting node listens for an existing responsible node before claiming the role itself, in seconds. Applies after the daemon restarts. |
| `cluster.enabled` | boolean | `false` |  | daemon file | Let this machine share inbound channel work with your OTHER goodvibes machines on this network, so exactly one of them reads each inbox (Telegram polling, ntfy subscriptions, inbox pollers) instead of all of them answering the same message. For a homelab where you run goodvibes on several machines that are all yours and configured with the same surfaces: switch it on everywhere and they sort it out between themselves, including taking over at once when one is shut down normally, and within about 20 seconds when one crashes (cluster.masterTimeoutSeconds, 15 by default, plus a short election). Off by default because switching it on asserts that every goodvibes node on this network belongs to you, on a shared network (an office, a shared house) a stranger's node would join the same coordination and one of you would stop receiving messages with nothing to indicate why. Outbound sends, sessions and the control plane are unaffected either way. |
| `cluster.heartbeatSeconds` | number | `5` | integer in [1, 3600] | daemon file | How often the responsible node tells the others it is still alive, in seconds. Lower means slightly faster notice that a node is alive and more network chatter; it does not by itself shorten a crash takeover, which waits for cluster.masterTimeoutSeconds. Applies after the daemon restarts. |
| `cluster.keyRotationGraceMinutes` | number | `5` | integer in [1, 120] | daemon file | How long both the new and the previous internal group key are accepted around a rotation, in minutes. This exists so that machines which have not yet picked up the new key are still heard while they catch up, without it, a rotation would look like every other machine going silent at once, and the group would needlessly hand work around. Raise it if your machines are often asleep or on a flaky link. It does NOT apply when you remove a machine: that rotation takes effect at once, which is the point of it. Applies after the daemon restarts. |
| `cluster.keyRotationHours` | number | `24` | integer in [1, 8760] | daemon file | How often the group replaces the internal key it signs coordination messages with, in hours. This is NOT the join key you type when adding a machine, that one is stable and changes only when you change it. This key rotates by itself, is never shown to you, and rotating it limits how long a copy taken off an old disk or a backup would be accepted. Lower means a shorter window and a little more network traffic once per rotation; the changeover never interrupts anything, because both the new key and the previous one are accepted for a few minutes either side of it. Applies after the daemon restarts. |
| `cluster.masterTimeoutSeconds` | number | `15` | integer in [2, 86400] | daemon file | How long a standby node waits without a heartbeat before it decides the responsible node has crashed and holds an election, in seconds. This is the CRASH path only: a node shut down normally hands over immediately, so ordinary restarts never wait this out. Used as at least two heartbeats: a value below that is raised to two heartbeats at runtime. Applies after the daemon restarts. |
| `cluster.multicastGroup` | string | `"239.255.71.86"` |  | daemon file | IPv4 multicast group the nodes coordinate over. The default sits in the administratively-scoped range (239.0.0.0/8), which routers do not forward off the local network. Every node that should coordinate must share this value. Applies after the daemon restarts. |
| `cluster.nodeName` | string | `""` | up to 48 characters | daemon file | A name for THIS machine in the group's member list (`cluster nodes` and the web UI), such as "desktop" or "laptop", so you can tell the machines apart when removing one or reading which machine holds a surface. Up to 48 characters. Empty, the default, shows "machine" and the first 8 characters of its node id; the hostname is never used, because the member list replicates and the group is advertised on the network. Kept on this machine only. Other machines record the name this machine had when it created or joined the group. Applies after the daemon restarts. |
| `cluster.peers` | array | `[]` | list of host or host:port strings, for example ["10.0.0.2", "10.0.0.3:4000"] | daemon file | Static list of cluster peers (host or host:port) contacted directly as well as over multicast. Set it on a network that drops multicast, so the nodes still find each other. |
| `cluster.port` | number | `61860` | integer port in [1, 65535] | daemon file | UDP port used for node-to-node coordination on the local network. Every node that should coordinate must share this port. Change it only to avoid a collision with something else on your network. Applies after the daemon restarts. |
| `cluster.revocationRetentionMinutes` | number | `43200` | integer in [1, 525600] | daemon file | How long a removed or revoked entry (a deleted schedule, a revoked device token, user, grant or peer) is kept on the group's record before it is dropped, in minutes; 43200 (30 days) by default. A machine that has not heard the group for longer than this, or has never synced with the group it is in, takes the group's record as the truth when it returns: what the group no longer holds is dropped on that machine, not brought back, unless that machine made it after it last synced, and `cluster status` lists what was dropped. It must span four gossip rounds: at least 4 x cluster.rosterGossipSeconds (counted as 30 when lower), in minutes rounded up, so 4 with the default gossip; a lower value is refused naming the minimum, and one in a hand-edited file is raised to it. Set the same value on every machine. |
| `cluster.rosterGossipSeconds` | number | `60` | integer in [10, 3600] | daemon file | How often this machine tells the others which revision of the group's shared settings and of its record (members, removals, key generations, devices, users) it holds, in seconds. A change is sent to every machine when it is made; this is how a machine that missed one (a lost message, or switched off at the time) notices and takes it. Checked on a 30 second timer, so any value below 30 behaves as 30. Higher means a missed change settles more slowly. Applies after the daemon restarts. |
| `cluster.secret` | string | `""` |  | daemon file | Optional shared phrase for coordinating machines that are not in a group (no `cluster create` or `cluster join`). When set, their coordination messages are signed with it and any message that does not verify is ignored, so only nodes that know the phrase can take the responsible role; every such node must use the same value. When it names a stored secret that cannot be read, this machine sends and takes no coordination messages at all until it can (rather than run unsigned), and `cluster status` says election traffic is unavailable. Inside a group it is not used: the group key signs every coordination message. |

Full entries (files, project rule, environment variable): "Settings" in the part "Reference", under "cluster".

## Hosted sessions

A hosted session is a full conversation loop (the same orchestrator, tools and permission gate a terminal runs) composed inside the daemon for one workspace folder. It keeps working when the client that started it closes, and any client can attach to it later.

Ways to create one:

- the web UI (Work, new session);
- Agent with `hostedSessions.routeConversationTurns` `true` (its turns run in the daemon);
- inbound channel conversations with `hostedSessions.promoteInboundConversations` `true`;
- the API method `sessions.hosted.create` (see "Starting a hosted session and sending a turn" in the next part).

The workspace must be the daemon's working directory or a registered workspace, or a folder inside one (`sessions.hosted.workspaces` lists them; `workspaces.registrations.add` adds one). The home directory and the filesystem root cannot be registered.

What happens when clients leave is the detach policy:

| Policy | When the last client detaches |
| --- | --- |
| `kill` (default) | The session ends with reason `detached`. |
| `survive` | The session stays alive and idle, and can be attached again from any client. |

`hostedSessions.detachPolicy` sets the default; `detachPolicy` on `sessions.hosted.create` overrides it for one session. An attachment is a lease of `hostedSessions.attachmentTtlMs` (default 10 minutes); a client whose control-plane connection is open renews it automatically, and attaching again renews it. A crashed client's lease lapses, and the session then counts as detached.

At most `hostedSessions.maxSessions` (default 8) sessions are live at once; another create is refused with the count and the setting named. Ended sessions are kept, listable with their reason and with their transcript readable through `sessions.hosted.history` (by the credential that created them, one an owner shared them with through `sessions.hosted.share`, or an admin one), for `hostedSessions.terminatedRetentionMs` (default 24 hours), also across a daemon restart. Each session's newest `hostedSessions.maxMessagesPerSession` messages (default 500) are saved to disk; after a daemon restart, attaching rebuilds the loop and adds a line to the transcript saying the turn that was running did not survive.

End a session with `goodvibes-daemon sessions kill <id>` or `sessions.hosted.kill`.

| Key | Type | Default | Allowed | Stored in | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `hostedSessions.attachmentTtlMs` | number | `600000` | integer in [30000, 86400000] | daemon file | How long a client stays attached to a daemon-hosted session without renewing, in milliseconds. Attaching again renews it, and a client whose control-plane connection is still open renews automatically. A client that crashed or closed its tab never detaches, so without this its attachment stands forever and a kill-policy session waits for a departure that never comes. When the last attachment lapses the session is treated as detached, and hostedSessions.detachPolicy decides what happens next. Between 30 seconds and a day. |
| `hostedSessions.detachPolicy` | enum | `"kill"` | `kill`, `survive` | daemon file | What happens to a daemon-hosted session when its last client detaches. kill (default): the session ends, which is what closing a client has always done. survive: the session stays alive and reattachable, so work continues while nothing is watching and you can pick it up again from any surface. A single session can override this when it is created. |
| `hostedSessions.maxMessagesPerSession` | number | `500` | integer in [1, 100000] | daemon file | How many of a hosted session's most recent messages are written to disk. The transcript in memory is unaffected; this bounds what a restart can restore, so one long conversation cannot grow its file without limit. |
| `hostedSessions.maxSessions` | number | `8` | integer in [1, 1000] | daemon file | How many daemon-hosted sessions may be live at once. Creating one past this is refused with the count and this setting named, rather than accepted and starved. Terminated sessions do not count. |
| `hostedSessions.promoteInboundConversations` | boolean | `false` |  | daemon file | Hand inbound channel conversations to the daemon to host, instead of answering them inside the surface process that received them. Off (default): a message from Telegram, Slack, email or any other channel is answered by that process, and it stops when the process stops. On: the first message of a conversation creates a daemon-hosted session and every later message is steered into it, so the conversation keeps its context and keeps running while no surface is open. What happens when the last client leaves is still hostedSessions.detachPolicy. |
| `hostedSessions.routeConversationTurns` | boolean | `false` |  | daemon file | Only goodvibes-agent reads this; the terminal product (goodvibes) always runs turns in its own process. Off (the default): the agent's conversation turns run in the agent process, with the agent's own prompt, persona, skills, memory and tools; work that must outlive the terminal goes to the daemon through /work, channels and schedules. On: with a connected daemon reachable, the first message of a conversation creates a daemon-hosted session rooted at this surface's working directory and every later message is steered into it, so the turn survives this process closing; that hosted turn is still an Agent turn, with the agent's operator policy, persona, skills, routines, memory and its profile, occasions, artifact, document, research-run, research-source, review-packet, media, notify and work-plan tools, while the agent tools that run only in this process are named to the model and refused there. With no connected daemon reachable the turn runs locally regardless, and the transcript says so in one line naming the reason. |
| `hostedSessions.terminatedRetentionMs` | number | `86400000` | integer in [0, 31536000000] | daemon file | How long a terminated hosted session's record and transcript are kept before they are retired, in milliseconds. Until then the session is still listable with its termination reason, and its transcript (its reply included) stays readable with sessions.hosted.history by the client that created it, also after a daemon restart. |

Full entries (files, project rule, environment variable): "Settings" in the part "Reference", under "hostedSessions".

## Fleet

The fleet is every agent and process the daemon is responsible for: spawned agents, Agent Client Protocol agents it hosts, contract units, workflows, triggers, schedules, watchers and background processes. `fleet.maxSize` (default 8) is the ceiling on agents this daemon runs at once; agents launched outside GoodVibes and only observed do not count.

The web UI shows the fleet in Work, grouped by the work board (the reading in `@goodvibes/engine/contracts` `readWorkBoard`, the same one the terminal's "Your agents" panel reads): Waiting for you (every open ask: approvals and the owner inbox's questions, purchase windows, claims, held actions and reports, each in the words of its presentation), Running now (only nodes that serve you in a working state, running tasks and hosted turns; an agent's row is what it is doing in the tool's words, `Reading 2 files`, or its task when no call is in flight, never a tool's name), Scheduled (idle or paused schedules, triggers, watchers and CI watches) and Finished (the ten newest). "Open sessions between turns" lists the newest 50 sessions; "Show older sessions" reads further back with `sessions.search` until every one is listed. A waiting row's second line says who asked and from which chat, when, and the presentation's consequence as a clause (`this weakens a safety setting` for a settings change the gate holds because it loosens a protection, known without a decision model); a purchase window posted by the payments host reads `Buy <item> from <shop> for <amount>?` with `From "<chat>" · inside your daily budget · goes ahead in 9 min unless you say no` (the chat whose turn began the checkout: the agent's `payments.checkout.begin` sends its turn's session as `askedInSession`, and the window's inbox item carries it; a purchase a schedule began reads `From your schedule "<name>"`, one under a standing authorisation otherwise `From your standing authorisation`), the countdown counted to the window's own deadline (`purchaseDeadline` on the inbox item; the item itself expires a minute later). A node's `serves` field decides whether it is yours or the platform's own: a `system` node (heartbeats, pollers, the code index) is counted in the line "Background services: N healthy" and listed only while stalled or failed. A platform watcher that a process only restored from a `watchers.json` it shares with the daemon, waiting for the component that registered it, is not listed by that process: the daemon's own reading of it is. A watcher whose beat is only due (past one interval, inside two) is between checks; it reads as stopped answering once its heartbeat is two intervals old or it reports an error. The header chip, the sidebar badge and the account menu read the board's counts. An approval for a chat also shows inline in that chat, with its choices. The API methods (all through the invoke route; see the next part) are:

| Method | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `fleet.snapshot` | Every live and finished process as a flat list linked by `parentId`, at most 2000 nodes. Each node carries `serves`: `system` for the platform's own upkeep (the runtime and daemon heartbeats, the CI watch poller, the code index), `you` for everything else; an agent node carries `progress` (`filesRead`, `filesChanged`, counted from its settled read, write and edit calls) and, while a call runs, its activity in the tool's words (`Writing docs/usage.md`); a schedule, trigger or watcher node carries `schedule` (its `cadence`, `lastRunAt`, `lastOutcome`; for a trigger `firedCount`, `lastFiredAt`, `since`). An agent's label is its archetype's display name (`Helper agent` for `general`). |
| `fleet.list` | The same, filtered by kind and state, with cursor pagination. |
| `fleet.stop` (admin) | Hard-stop one node; `cascade: true` stops its descendants first. |
| `fleet.interrupt` (admin) | End an agent's current turn, or pause a trigger or schedule. |
| `fleet.resume` (admin) | Re-arm a paused trigger or schedule. |
| `fleet.archive`, `fleet.archiveFinished`, `fleet.unarchive`, `fleet.archived.list` | Move finished trees out of the live view and back. |
| `fleet.attempts.list`, `fleet.attempts.judge`, `fleet.attempts.pick` | Best-of-N attempt groups: list, ask a judge model, pick a winner (`confirm: true` to apply). |
| `fleet.conflicts.list`, `fleet.conflicts.resolve`, `fleet.conflicts.retry` | Work items whose merge conflicted. |
| `fleet.graph.get` | `GET /api/fleet/workstreams/{workstreamId}/graph`, one workstream's dependency graph. |
| `fleet.observed.steer` | Type text into an observed outside coding-agent session; the owner is asked first. |

| Key | Type | Default | Allowed | Stored in | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `fleet.maxSize` | number | `8` | number in [1, 20] | each program | Maximum fleet size, the one ceiling on agents this daemon is responsible for: native spawned agents, ACP-hosted agents, and elastic fix-task agents all count against it. Externally-launched agents merely observed on the host never count. Renamed from orchestration.maxActiveAgents. |

Full entries (files, project rule, environment variable): "Settings" in the part "Reference", under "fleet".

## Encryption, retention and redaction of stored data

There is no switch that turns on encryption at rest, and none is needed for the one thing GoodVibes encrypts itself:

- **Encrypted, always:** the secret stores (`secrets.enc`, one per tier): provider API keys, channel bot tokens, OAuth credentials, the cluster group keys and every other credential put in the secret store. They are encrypted with AES-256-GCM using the 32-byte key in `~/.goodvibes/secrets.key` (mode `0600`). The key is created once and never rotated by the programs. If the key file is empty or malformed, the programs refuse to write to the stores rather than overwrite them, and the message says to restore the key from a backup. The stores and their read order are described in "Secrets" in "Permissions, decisions and safety".
- **Not encrypted:** everything else is plain files and plain SQLite databases: settings, `operator-tokens.json` (the operator token itself, protected only by mode `0600`), sign-in users (password hashes), device tokens (hashes), sessions and transcripts, hosted sessions, memory, knowledge stores, the owner inbox, the activity log and crash logs.
- **The user's own step:** to protect those at rest, use the operating system's whole-disk or home-directory encryption (LUKS on Linux, FileVault on macOS, BitLocker on Windows). GoodVibes neither sets it up nor checks for it. `secrets.key` sits beside the stores it encrypts, so the secret stores are only as safe as the disk once someone can read the user's files.

What the programs do instead for the plain files:

| Setting | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `atRest.redactionEnabled` | `true` | Credential patterns (API keys, bearer tokens, GitHub, GitLab, Slack and AWS credentials) are replaced with `[REDACTED_*]` markers when the per-agent transcript journal is written. Crash reports are always redacted. Home paths are not redacted. |
| `atRest.retentionMaxAgeDays` | `30` | Transcript journals, the execution ledger, the activity log, crash logs and crash-recovery snapshots older than this are deleted at start and every six hours. Saved conversations are never deleted by it. |
| `atRest.retentionMaxTotalMb` | `512` | Each of those file sets is kept under this many megabytes, oldest first. |

These `atRest.*` settings are shared settings in a cluster.

| Key | Type | Default | Allowed | Stored in | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `atRest.redactionEnabled` | boolean | `true` |  | daemon file | When true (default), credential patterns (API keys, bearer tokens, GitHub/GitLab/Slack/AWS credentials) are redacted at WRITE time from the on-disk transcript journal (per-agent <agentId>.jsonl), reusing the same pattern set as the telemetry egress. Home paths are NOT redacted. The local execution ledger gets the same treatment only when the application embedding the platform wires the policy in. Crash reports are always redacted, whatever this setting says. A redacted value shows a [REDACTED_*] marker, a record never pretends the content was absent. Set false ONLY for local debugging where plaintext secrets in the transcript journal are acceptable. |
| `atRest.retentionMaxAgeDays` | number | `30` | integer in [1, 365] | daemon file | Age cap (days) for the append-only files: per-agent transcript journals, the execution ledger, the activity log, crash logs and crash-recovery snapshots. Files older than this are pruned at start and every six hours (the journal also prunes on each new agent session; the ledger on each export). Saved conversations are never pruned by it. Generous by default; bounded so the files cannot grow without limit. |
| `atRest.retentionMaxTotalMb` | number | `512` | integer in [1, 1048576] | daemon file | Total-size cap (MB) for each of the append-only file sets named under atRest.retentionMaxAgeDays (transcript journals, execution ledger, activity log, crash logs, crash-recovery snapshots). When exceeded, the oldest are deleted first (rotated backups before freshly-written active files) until under budget. Saved conversations are never deleted by it. |

Full entries (files, project rule, environment variable): "Settings" in the part "Reference", under "atRest".

## Backups

There is no backup command. To back up a GoodVibes installation, stop the daemon (`goodvibes-daemon stop-service`) and copy:

| Path | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `~/.goodvibes/` | Every setting, credential store, token, session, memory and knowledge store, and the cluster group key material inside the secret store. |
| `~/.goodvibes/secrets.key` | Without it every `secrets.enc` is unreadable. Keep it with the backup of the stores it encrypts, and protect the backup accordingly. |
| A checkout installation (`scripts/install-from-checkout.sh`): its data directory, `~/.local/share/goodvibes-data/` unless `--data-dir` named another | Instead of `~/.goodvibes/`: that installation's commands run with `GOODVIBES_HOME` set to the data directory, so its whole tree is `<data dir>/.goodvibes/` (daemon home `<data dir>/.goodvibes/daemon/`, `secrets.key` included), plus the installer's `environment` file and ownership record in the data directory itself. Its service's working directory is the `--workspace` given to the installer (the checkout itself by default), so the per-working-directory state below is under `<workspace>/.goodvibes/`. Stop it with `goodvibes-daemon stop-service` as for a release installation. |
| `<project>/.goodvibes/` in each project | Project settings, checkpoints, the code index, the activity log. |
| `<daemon working directory>/.goodvibes/` | The daemon's per-working-directory state under `tui/`: the cluster node id (`tui/cluster/cluster-node-id`), device grants (`tui/devices/`), channel routes (`tui/operator/channel-routes.sqlite`), remote-node state (`tui/remote/`), watchers (`tui/watchers.json`) and decision records, plus its activity log (`logs/activity.md`). The service runs in the working directory written into its definition: the release installer runs `install-service` from the home directory, so for that service this is `~/.goodvibes/` and already covered; `install-service` run by hand records the directory it was run in (or `-C <dir>`). A daemon started with `-C <dir>` (or a saved working directory, see `daemon-settings.json`) keeps it under `<dir>/.goodvibes/`. The service's working directory is the `WorkingDirectory=` line of `~/.config/systemd/user/goodvibes.service` on Linux. Without it a restored daemon starts with a new cluster node id and without its device grants and channel routes. |

Then start the daemon again. To restore, stop the daemon, put the files back at the same paths with the same owner and modes (`operator-tokens.json`, `secrets.key` and the secret stores are `0600`), and start it. On a new machine, install GoodVibes first, then restore while the daemon is stopped. Restore `secrets.key` together with the `secrets.enc` files it encrypted: a store encrypted under another key cannot be read, and the programs refuse to write to a store they cannot read. Settings that hold absolute paths (`controlPlane.webui.bundleDir`, `controlPlane.tls.certFile`, registered workspaces, project paths) must name paths that exist on the new machine; with a different home path or user name, correct them with `goodvibes-daemon config set` (and `goodvibes-daemon webui enable --bundle-dir <dir>`). The service definition, the installed programs and the web UI bundle are not part of the backup; the installer puts them back. A restored cluster member rejoins its group by itself when it starts, as long as it was not removed. Do not run the old machine and its restored copy at the same time: they would share one node id. The API also exports and imports some data on its own: `memory.records.export` and `memory.records.import`, `calendar.ics.export` and `calendar.ics.import`, and the home graph (`homeassistant.homeGraph.export` and `.import`). `goodvibes support-bundle export` (terminal app) collects settings, diagnostics and posture for a support report; it is not a backup.

## Logs and diagnostics

There is no log level to set: no setting, flag or environment variable changes what the daemon logs. Everything is always recorded:

- **The activity log**, `<working dir>/.goodvibes/logs/activity.md`, gets every entry the daemon writes, at every level, `DEBUG` included, as lines `[<ISO time>] [DEBUG|INFO|WARN|ERROR] <message>`, some followed by a JSON block. Credentials and card numbers are masked before they are written. It rotates to `activity.md.1` at 10 MB, and the retention settings `atRest.retentionMaxAgeDays` and `atRest.retentionMaxTotalMb` prune it. For a service, the working directory is the unit's `WorkingDirectory=` (`systemctl --user cat goodvibes.service`) or the plist's `WorkingDirectory`. Cluster messages (`cluster: ...`), relay messages (`relay: ...`) and update messages are all here.
- **Standard output and error** carry only the start-up lines (`starting`, `bound`, `host started`), the pairing block on an interactive terminal, and a few `[goodvibes-daemon] ...` warnings. Under systemd they go to the journal; under launchd (macOS) the plist names no output file, so they are discarded.

| Where | What |
| --- | --- |
| `<working dir>/.goodvibes/logs/activity.md` | Everything, as above. Read it with `tail -f`. |
| `journalctl --user -u goodvibes.service` | Start-up lines and fatal start-up errors when the daemon runs as a systemd user service (Linux). |
| `~/.goodvibes/daemon/service/<platform>.log` (or `service.logPath`) | Output of a daemon started by the service commands when `service.platform` is `manual`. `service-status --json` names it as `logPath`. |
| `~/.goodvibes/tui/crashes.jsonl` | Crash records, always redacted. |
| `goodvibes-daemon status` | Health, channels, cluster, sessions, last update. |
| `ops.doctor` (API) | Give it a symptom in plain words ("stuck turn", "approval never answered") and it runs the matching checks against the live daemon. |
| `GET /api/health`, `GET /api/ops/memory` | Health snapshot; memory pressure and budgets. |
| `goodvibes control-plane status` (terminal app) | Bind posture, reachability, local sign-in, bootstrap file and tokens. |

### Giving the service environment variables (for example OTLP export)

The service definition GoodVibes writes sets only `GOODVIBES_DAEMON_TOKEN`, `GOODVIBES_HTTP_TOKEN` (each only when it was set in the environment of the command that installed the service) and `NODE_ENV`. Other variables, such as `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT`, have to be added outside that file, because `refresh-service` (which every upgrade runs) rewrites it.

On Linux (systemd), use a drop-in, which `refresh-service` does not touch:

```sh
mkdir -p ~/.config/systemd/user/goodvibes.service.d
cat > ~/.config/systemd/user/goodvibes.service.d/otel.conf <<'CONF'
[Service]
Environment=OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT=https://collector.example:4318/v1/traces
Environment=OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_HEADERS=authorization=Bearer%%20<your-collector-token>
CONF
systemctl --user daemon-reload
goodvibes-daemon config set telemetry.otelMode remote-export
goodvibes-daemon restart-service
systemctl --user show goodvibes.service -p Environment
```

(`%%` is how a unit file writes a literal `%`.) If `service.serviceName` is set, use that name instead of `goodvibes`.

On macOS (launchd), the plist GoodVibes writes is rewritten on upgrade, so edits to its `EnvironmentVariables` do not last. Set the variables in the user's launchd domain and restart the service:

```sh
launchctl setenv OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT https://collector.example:4318/v1/traces
goodvibes-daemon config set telemetry.otelMode remote-export
goodvibes-daemon restart-service
```

`launchctl setenv` values are lost when the user logs out or the machine restarts; repeat them then (for example from a login item). This macOS recipe follows launchd's documented behaviour and was not run on a Mac for this guide.

## Telemetry

By default no telemetry leaves the machine. The programs contain exactly two telemetry exporters, both off by default, and neither has a built-in destination: each sends only to an address the owner supplies.

| Setting | What leaves the machine |
| --- | --- |
| `telemetry.otelMode` `off` (default) or `in-process` | Nothing. Spans (`in-process`) are kept in the daemon's memory and served only through its own API (`/api/v1/telemetry/...`). |
| `telemetry.otelMode` `remote-export` with `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT` set (or `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT`, to which `/v1/traces` is added) | Trace spans, as OTLP/HTTP JSON, `POST`ed in batches of up to 512 to that endpoint, with the headers in `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_HEADERS` (or `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS`) as `key=value,key=value`. The spans are the telemetry API's safe view, the same projection a read client gets without asking for the raw view: content attributes are withheld (`[REDACTED_TEXT]`), among them tool arguments and output (`tool.args`), agent and task descriptions (`agent.task`, `task.description`), prompts, questions and answers, and credential-shaped text in what remains is masked. They carry, among other attributes: model provider and model, token counts, stop reasons and errors (`llm.*`); the turn id, outcome, token counts and the prompt's length in characters (`turn.*`); the tool name; MCP server ids, plugin ids and paths, transport endpoints, session ids and message counts. With `remote-export` and neither variable set, nothing is sent and the daemon logs `telemetry.otelMode is remote-export with no OTLP endpoint, spans are recorded in-process only`. |
| `telemetry.decisionOtlpEnabled` `true` with `telemetry.decisionOtlpEndpoint` set | One record per permission-gate decision, as an OTLP span (`<endpoint>/v1/traces`), log (`<endpoint>/v1/logs`) or both, per `telemetry.decisionOtlpSignal` (`span`, `log`, `both`; default `span`). Attributes: `decision.id` (a rising number), `tool.name`, `command.class`, `permission.mode`, `decision.layer`, `decision.reason`, `decision.allowed`, `policy.bundle.id` when set, and the resource attribute `service.name`. Tool arguments are not included. The trace id is derived from the session id. |
| `telemetry.includeRawPrompts` | Nothing; it only allows raw (unredacted) reads through the daemon's own API, which also need `read:telemetry` and admin or `read:telemetry-sensitive`. |

Outbound traffic that is not telemetry also happens by default, and is listed here so nothing is a surprise: the daemon checks for updates at `update.releasesUrl` (GitHub) every `update.intervalMinutes` when `update.auto` is `true` (default); at start it fetches the public model lists of providers whose list needs no key (in testing a fresh daemon with no credentials fetched those of openrouter, aihubmix, groq, mistral, huggingface, nvidia, llm7 and opencode-zen, cached under `~/.goodvibes/tui/provider-models/` for 24 hours); and each conversation turn calls the chosen model provider.

Reading telemetry through the API (all need `read:telemetry`):

| Route | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/v1/telemetry` | Snapshot: aggregates, runtime state, recent records. |
| `GET /api/v1/telemetry/events` | Event feed with cursor resume. |
| `GET /api/v1/telemetry/errors` | Records with error metadata. |
| `GET /api/v1/telemetry/traces` | Readable spans. |
| `GET /api/v1/telemetry/metrics` | Aggregates and runtime metrics. |
| `GET /api/v1/telemetry/stream` | Server-Sent Events stream of telemetry. |
| `GET /api/v1/telemetry/otlp/v1/traces`, `.../otlp/v1/logs`, `.../otlp/v1/metrics` | The same data as OTLP JSON documents. |

| Key | Type | Default | Allowed | Stored in | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `telemetry.decisionOtlpEnabled` | boolean | `false` |  | each program | Export permission/policy decision-log records to an OTLP endpoint (export-only, no ingestion). Requires telemetry.decisionOtlpEndpoint. |
| `telemetry.decisionOtlpEndpoint` | string | `""` |  | each program | OTLP/HTTP JSON endpoint base for decision-log export (empty = disabled). Spans POST to <base>/v1/traces, logs to <base>/v1/logs. |
| `telemetry.decisionOtlpSignal` | enum | `"span"` | `span`, `log`, `both` | each program | Which OTLP record shape each decision is emitted as: span, log, or both. |
| `telemetry.includeRawPrompts` | boolean | `false` |  | each program | Allow raw telemetry reads from this daemon while enabled. Default false rejects raw reads; safe views always redact content. HTTP raw reads also require read:telemetry and an admin session or read:telemetry-sensitive scope. Active raw streams stop after this opt-in is revoked. Raw prompts may contain private data. Enabling the setting at startup emits a WARN log. |
| `telemetry.otelMode` | enum | `"off"` | `off`, `in-process`, `remote-export` | each program | OpenTelemetry instrumentation: off (default, no OTel SDK initialization; a daemon left at the default records spans in-process so its telemetry traces list answers, and setting off explicitly turns that off too), in-process (spans for LLM calls, turns, tool calls, agents, tasks, plugins, MCP servers, transport, permission checks, sessions, compaction and health cascades, recorded and exported in-process only; a turn span records the prompt length, not its text), or remote-export (additionally export spans as OTLP/HTTP JSON to the collector named by OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT, or OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT with /v1/traces appended). Switching away from off requires a restart; in-process <-> remote-export applies live. |

Full entries (files, project rule, environment variable): "Settings" in the part "Reference", under "telemetry".

# The operator HTTP API

Every GoodVibes client (the terminal app, Agent, the web UI, `goodvibes-daemon` itself, scripts and other programs) drives the daemon through one API: the operator API on the daemon's control plane. This part explains how an automated client authenticates, which scopes exist, how to call any method, how to run a conversation and a task, how to answer approvals, how to stream events and reconnect, how errors and retries work, and which SDK entry points wrap all of it. The list of every method with its route and scopes is in "Operator API methods" in the reference, and the list of every event in "Events".

## Terms used in this part

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| method | One operation of the operator API, named by an id such as `sessions.create`. There are 648 in 3.3.3. |
| REST route | The HTTP method and path a method is bound to, such as `POST /api/sessions`. |
| invoke-only method | A method with no REST route. It is called through `POST /api/control-plane/methods/<id>/invoke` or a WebSocket `call` frame. |
| access | Each method is `public` (no credential), `authenticated` (any valid credential holding its scopes) or `admin` (an admin credential). |
| shared session | A conversation record in the daemon's session broker: messages, inputs, participants. Every conversation has one, whichever process runs its model loop. |
| hosted session | A shared session whose model loop runs inside the daemon. Its id starts with `hosted-`. |
| turn | One model response to one user input, with the tool calls it makes. |
| input | A queued user message for a session (a steer or a follow-up), with a state: `queued`, `delivered`, `completed`, `failed`, `cancelled`. |
| approval | A pending permission ask raised by the permission gate for one tool call. |

## Base address and how to call it

The base address is the daemon's control plane: `http://127.0.0.1:3421` by default. When the daemon was started on another port, use that port. When it is reached through a proxy, Tailscale or TLS, use that address (see "Network exposure" in "The daemon, the web UI and networking").

There are four ways to call a method:

| Way | When to use it |
| --- | --- |
| The method's REST route | The method has one (`GET /api/sessions`, `POST /api/sessions/{sessionId}/follow-up`). |
| `POST /api/control-plane/methods/<id>/invoke` | The method has no REST route (all `sessions.hosted.*`, `pairing.*`, `fleet.*`, `inbox.*`, `relay.*`, `tailscale.*`, and others), or you want one route for everything. |
| A `call` frame on the WebSocket `/api/control-plane/ws` | You already hold a WebSocket open for events. |
| The SDK (`@goodvibes/engine`) | You write TypeScript or JavaScript. See "SDK entry points". |

The daemon describes itself:

| Route | Returns | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /api/control-plane/methods` | Every method with its id, title, description, access, scopes, REST route, input JSON Schema and output JSON Schema. | `read:control-plane` |
| `GET /api/control-plane/methods/{methodId}` | One method. | `read:control-plane` |
| `GET /api/control-plane/events/catalog` | Every event, its scopes, domains and payload schema. | `read:control-plane`, `read:events` |
| `GET /api/control-plane/contract` | The whole contract document. | `read:control-plane` |
| `GET /status` | Version, build and cluster status. | `read:control-plane` |

Example: what does `sessions.hosted.create` take?

```sh
curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $GV_TOKEN" \
  http://127.0.0.1:3421/api/control-plane/methods/sessions.hosted.create
```

### Three rules clients trip on

1. **The invoke route takes an envelope.** `POST /api/control-plane/methods/<id>/invoke` reads the method's input from a field called `body`, with an optional `query` beside it. Send `{"body":{"workspaceRoot":"/home/alex/projects/app"}}`, not `{"workspaceRoot":"/home/alex/projects/app"}`. The bare form is refused with `400` `{"error":"Missing required field: body. Expected envelope shape: { query?, body }","status":400}`. REST routes take the input directly as the JSON body; only the invoke route uses the envelope.
2. **A non-admin watches only its own sessions live, with `read:own-sessions`.** `GET /api/sessions/{sessionId}/events` answers a non-admin `403` `{"error":"Admin role required","code":"ADMIN_REQUIRED",...}`, and the event domains that carry a turn (`session`, `turn`, `tools`, `gate`) are admin-only for every other session. A credential holding `read:own-sessions` opens `GET /api/control-plane/events?domains=turn,tools,gate,session` and receives those frames, and the `approval-update` and `hosted-session-update` events, of the sessions its own principal created or an owner shared with it (`sessions.hosted.share`), and nothing of any other session (see "The least-privilege client").
3. **To make a hosted session run a turn, use `sessions.followUp` (or `sessions.steer`), not `sessions.messages.create`.** `POST /api/sessions/{sessionId}/messages` with no `kind` (which means `kind: "message"`) answers `202` with `"routedTo":"conversation"` and records the message in the transcript, but the hosted session's loop does not run a turn for it. Send `POST /api/sessions/{sessionId}/follow-up` with `{"body":"<text>","messageId":"<id>"}`.

Every response from the daemon carries the header `x-goodvibes-decision-policy` (for example `{"policy":"Hybrid","operation":"decision","reason":null,"revision":0}`), which says which decision model policy is in force.

## Authentication

Every method except three needs a credential. The three public methods are `control.auth.current` (`GET /api/control-plane/auth`), `control.auth.login` (`POST /login`) and `control.auth.logout` (`POST /logout`). The web UI bundle served at `/` is also public.

A credential is sent in one of two ways:

- `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, for any token;
- the cookie `goodvibes_session=<token>`, which `POST /login` and the web UI's `POST /api/browser-session` set (`HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Strict`, `Secure` over HTTPS), with the readable marker `goodvibes_identity` beside it (a generation and who is signed in, no credential). A request on the cookie is held to the page's origin: a state-changing one must carry the daemon's own `Origin` (or one in `controlPlane.cors.allowedOrigins`), and a read, the event stream included, is refused `403` `ORIGIN_NOT_ALLOWED` when it names another origin.

When both are present, the bearer header is used.

### Which credential an automated client should use

| Situation | Credential |
| --- | --- |
| A script on the daemon's own machine, run by the owner | The operator token from `~/.goodvibes/daemon/operator-tokens.json` (field `token`). It has full authority. |
| A script or service anywhere that should be able to do only some things | A device token minted with a scope list (below). It can be revoked on its own. |
| A program that must keep working after the shared token is revoked | A device token of its own. |
| A person signing in from a browser | A sign-in (`POST /login`), 12 hours. |

Reading the operator token in a shell:

```sh
GV_TOKEN=$(python3 -c "import json,os;print(json.load(open(os.path.expanduser('~/.goodvibes/daemon/operator-tokens.json')))['token'])")
```

### Checking a credential

`GET /api/control-plane/auth` is public and reports what the request authenticated as.

```sh
curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $GV_TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:3421/api/control-plane/auth
```

```json
{
  "authenticated": true,
  "authMode": "shared-token",
  "tokenPresent": true,
  "authorizationHeaderPresent": true,
  "sessionCookiePresent": false,
  "principalId": "shared-token",
  "principalKind": "token",
  "credential": "local",
  "admin": true,
  "scopes": ["read:accounts", "read:approvals", "...", "write:worktrees"],
  "roles": ["admin"],
  "expiresAt": null
}
```

`authMode` is `anonymous` (no credential sent), `invalid` (a credential that does not authenticate), `shared-token` (the operator token) or `session` (any other valid credential: a device token as well as a sign-in; use `credential` to tell them apart). `credential` is `local` (the operator token sent straight from the daemon's machine), `shared-token` (the operator token from anywhere else, or through a proxy), `device-token`, `agent` (the Agent's own pairing) or `user-session`. `principalId` is `shared-token`, `pairing:<token id>` for a device token, or the sign-in user. `expiresAt` is set for a sign-in.

### Minting a scoped token for a script

A device token with a scope list holds only those scopes and is never admin. `pairing.tokens.create` is not an admin method: any credential holding `write:control-plane` may call it, except the Agent's own credential (the method is owner-only). An admin caller may name any scopes; a narrowed caller may name only scopes it holds itself. Example with the operator token:

```sh
curl -sS -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $GV_TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  http://127.0.0.1:3421/api/control-plane/methods/pairing.tokens.create/invoke \
  -d '{"body":{"name":"nightly report","scopes":["read:sessions","read:transcripts","read:events","read:tasks"],"attemptId":"nightly-report-1"}}'
```

```json
{"token":{"id":"pair-d58c1c36-428d-4bd7-811d-dc96988d9afa","name":"nightly report","token":"<the secret, shown once>","createdAt":1795022092889}}
```

Rules:

- The secret is returned once and starts with `gvp_`. Only its hash is stored.
- The token is an offer until its first use. If nothing uses it within 15 minutes it stops working (`PAIRING_OFFER_EXPIRED`). Use it once right away.
- `attemptId` must be 8 to 128 letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `:` or `-` (otherwise `400` `INVALID_ARGUMENT` `attemptId must be 8 to 128 letters, digits or . _ : -`). Sending the same `attemptId` again while the token is still unused returns the same token id with a new secret; the earlier secret of that offer stops working, so use the newest one. A lost reply therefore never creates a second token.
- Subset rule: a narrowed caller (not admin) can grant only scopes it holds. Naming one it does not hold is `403` `MISSING_SCOPE` (`A paired device cannot be given scopes this credential does not hold: read:events. Name only scopes you hold, or ask an admin.`). A narrowed caller that leaves `scopes` out gives the new token exactly its own list.
- An admin caller that leaves `scopes` out mints a token with full authority (admin).
- `scopes` must be a nonempty list of scope names. `"*"`, an empty list or an empty name is refused with `400` `INVALID_ARGUMENT` (`scopes must be a nonempty list of operator scopes (such as read:sessions); leave it out for full operator authority.`).
- `client` is `"agent"` or absent (anything else is `400`). `client: "agent"` mints the Agent's own credential; do not use it for scripts.
- Revoke with `pairing.tokens.delete` (`{"body":{"id":"pair-..."}}`). It answers `{"id":"pair-...","revoked":true,"alsoRevoked":["pair-...",...]}`: every token that the revoked token minted is revoked with it, and so on down. A script that mints child tokens with its own device token loses all of them when its own token is revoked. The next request with any of them gets `401`, and their open streams receive a `closed` frame. An unknown id is `404` `PAIRING_TOKEN_NOT_FOUND`. Who may revoke: `pairing.tokens.delete` is not an admin method and needs only `write:control-plane`, so any credential holding that scope can revoke any device token (in testing, a device token holding only `write:control-plane` and `read:pairing` reached the lookup and got `404` for an unknown id, not `403`), with one exception: the Agent's own credential is refused, because the method is owner-only (`403` `{"error":"pairing.tokens.delete is the owner's own act; a call the Agent makes for him is refused. The owner does it from his own app.","code":"OWNER_ONLY","category":"authorization","status":403}`). So do not give `write:control-plane` to a token that should not be able to cut other devices off.

The new token, checked:

```json
{"authMode":"session","principalId":"pairing:pair-d58c1c36-428d-4bd7-811d-dc96988d9afa","principalKind":"token","credential":"device-token","admin":false,"scopes":["read:events","read:sessions","read:tasks","read:transcripts"],"roles":[]}
```

### Signing in with a username and password

```sh
curl -sS -i -X POST -H 'content-type: application/json' http://127.0.0.1:3421/login \
  -d '{"username":"admin","password":"<password>"}'
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
set-cookie: goodvibes_session=<token>; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Expires=Thu, 19 Nov 2026 05:14:45 GMT; Max-Age=43199
set-cookie: goodvibes_identity=<generation>.<username, base64url>; Path=/; SameSite=Strict; Expires=Thu, 19 Nov 2026 05:14:45 GMT; Max-Age=43199
```

```json
{"authenticated":true,"token":"<token>","username":"admin","expiresAt":1795065285233}
```

The `token` works as a bearer token or as the cookie until `expiresAt` (12 hours). A wrong password answers `401` `{"error":"Invalid credentials"}`. Five attempts per minute per address are allowed; the sixth answers `429` with code `RATE_LIMITED` and the header `Retry-After: 60`. A body sent without `content-type: application/json` answers `415` `SIGN_IN_NOT_JSON` and does not count as an attempt. `POST /logout` with the same credential ends that sign-in and answers `{"revoked":true}`; a credential that is not a sign-in answers `401` `SESSION_UNKNOWN`. Creating users and the bootstrap password are in "Sign-in users" in "The daemon, the web UI and networking".

### Credentials over the WebSocket

The upgrade request to `/api/control-plane/ws` must itself be authenticated: send `Authorization: Bearer <token>` on the upgrade, or, from a browser on the same origin, the sign-in cookie. An unauthenticated upgrade answers `401`. An upgrade with an `Origin` header must come from the daemon's own origin or one listed in `controlPlane.cors.allowedOrigins`.

## Scopes

### What a credential holds

| Credential | Scopes held |
| --- | --- |
| Operator token, device token minted without a list, sign-in user with role `admin` and no list | Every scope (admin). |
| Sign-in user without the `admin` role and no list | Every `read:` scope except the owner-private ones below and `read:telemetry-sensitive`. No `write:` scope and no `ingest:` scope. Not admin. |
| Device token with a scope list | Exactly that list. Not admin. A device token's list can never contain `*` (minting refuses it). |
| Sign-in user with a stored scope list | That list, never more than the role's default. Not admin. A stored list containing `*` counts as no list (the role's default set, admin for an `admin` user). |

A method requires every scope it lists, and an `admin` method also requires an admin credential. Some admin methods are additionally owner-only: the Agent's own credential is refused (for example `approvals.approve`, `approvals.deny`, `inbox.answer`, `sessions.permissionMode.set`). Answering what was put to the owner (`approvals.approve`, `approvals.deny`, `inbox.answer`, the purchase answers `payments.purchase.approve`, `payments.purchase.deny`, `payments.checkout.approve`, `payments.purchase.reconcile` and the standing authorizations `payments.standing.create` and `payments.standing.delete`) and entering a card (`payments.cards.create`, `payments.purchase.securityCode`) need the owner's own credential, not only an admin one: any other admin gets `403` `OWNER_ONLY`. Entering a card is also refused, `403` `CARD_ENTRY_TRANSPORT`, unless the request reached the daemon from its own machine, over TLS or over the tailnet. The owner is the operator token, an app on the daemon's own machine, the first sign-in user the daemon holds (the user created at first start), and a device the owner paired himself (`origin: owner-pairing`); an admin sign-in of anyone else and a full token minted for automation are admins, not the owner. A write that loosens a security, permission, judgment or payment setting is put to the owner when an admin who is not the owner makes it (see "A change only the owner makes").

`read:own-sessions` is the scope for a client without the admin role that follows its own work live: it receives the turns, tool calls, approvals and lifecycle notices of the sessions its principal created or was shared, and nothing of any other session (see "The least-privilege client"). A non-admin sign-in holds it by default.

The owner-private read scopes, which a non-admin sign-in does not get by default: `read:email`, `read:profile`, `read:profile-document`, `read:payments`, `read:occasions`, `read:memory`, `read:transcripts`, `read:pairing`, `read:remote`, `read:checkpoints`, `read:calendar`, `read:approvals`, `read:principals`, `read:browser-content`, `read:knowledge-content`, `read:channel-content`, `read:automation-content`, `read:fleet-content`, `read:skill-content`.

### Every scope

Each family has a `read:` scope for looking and a `write:` scope for changing; some families also have a `-content` read scope for the bodies (messages, pages, records) as opposed to their metadata. The complete list of scopes, with how many methods and event streams need each one and whether a read-only grant includes it, is "Operator scopes" in the reference; which scopes each method needs is in "Operator API methods" there.

Scopes that no method lists, because an HTTP route checks them directly:

| Scope | Checked by | Who has it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `read:telemetry` | `GET /api/v1/telemetry/*` and the telemetry stream. | Every credential without its own scope list, including a non-admin sign-in; a scoped token only when its list names it. |
| `read:telemetry-sensitive` | The raw (unredacted) telemetry view, `?view=raw`. It also needs the setting `telemetry.includeRawPrompts` on; without it the answer is `403` `TELEMETRY_RAW_DISABLED`. | Admin credentials, and a token minted with it. Never part of a non-admin sign-in's default set, although it is not one of the owner-private scopes. |
| `ingest:telemetry`, `write:telemetry` | `POST /api/v1/telemetry/otlp/v1/traces`, `/logs` and `/metrics` (OTLP over HTTP into the daemon). Either one is enough. | Admin credentials, and a token minted with one of them. |

## Access: what each route family and event needs

Every method has one of three access levels, and an event has one of two:

- **public**: no credential.
- **scope** (the contract calls it `authenticated`): any valid credential that holds every scope the method lists. A narrowed device token or a non-admin sign-in can call it when it holds those scopes.
- **admin**: an admin credential (the operator token, a device token minted without a scope list, or a sign-in user with the `admin` role and no narrowing list), and the method's scopes. A non-admin is refused with `403` `ADMIN_REQUIRED` (`Gateway method requires admin access: <method>`, or `Admin role required` on some routes) whatever scopes it holds. A few admin methods need the owner himself (see "Scopes"); another admin is refused `403` `OWNER_ONLY`.

What a method may do is decided from the effects it declares (`effects` on its descriptor, for example `["approval.answer"]` or `["sessions.write", "record.destroy"]`); its access, scopes and owner-only mark are computed from them, so the contract says what the daemon enforces. A refusal body names the effect that refused (`effect`) and what is missing (`missing`: a scope such as `read:transcripts`, or `admin`, `owner`, `peer`).

Each method's access is in the Access column of "Operator API methods" in the reference (`authenticated` there is "scope" here). A client can also ask the daemon: `GET /api/control-plane/methods/{methodId}` answers `{"method":{...}}`, the method's descriptor wrapped in `method`, with the fields `id`, `title`, `description`, `category`, `access`, `scopes`, `effects` (the effects it causes, from which access and scopes are computed), `effect` (`read`, `write` or `outward`), `http` (its REST route, when it has one), `invokable`, `transport`, `source`, `inputSchema`, `outputSchema`, `repeat` (`safe`, `keyed` or `unsafe`: what sending it twice does, see "Idempotency and safe retries"), and, when the method declares them, `replay` (its retry key) and `errorCodes` (`[{code, status, meaning}]`). `GET /api/control-plane/methods` lists them all. By family (the method id's first part, as the contract groups them), the access of the methods that only read and of those that change something:

### Access of every event

Every event needs `read:events`; some need more. Each event a client can subscribe to, with its catalog name, its SSE name (the `event:` line of a frame), its domain, its access and its scopes, is in "Event streams a client subscribes to" in the reference. A runtime domain's catalog name is `runtime.<domain>` and its SSE name is the domain name; the other events have their own SSE names (`control.approval_update` is `approval-update`). The rules that matter to a client:

- Admin only: the domains that carry a conversation or the daemon's inner state, among them `session`, `turn`, `tools`, `tasks`, `agents`, `gate` (approvals and the owner inbox), `config` and `fleet`, and the `approval-update`, `owner-inbox-update`, `hosted-session-update` and `session-update` events. One exception: a credential holding `read:own-sessions` receives the `turn`, `tools`, `gate` and `session` frames and the `approval-update` and `hosted-session-update` events of the sessions its principal created or an owner shared with it (`sessions.hosted.create`, `sessions.hosted.share`), frame by frame, and of no other session; a frame that names no session is withheld. It must name those domains (`?domains=turn,tools,gate,session`). Ownership is saved with the session and holds across a daemon restart.
- Any credential with the scopes: the rest, among them `providers`, `automation`, `surfaces`, `transport`, `ops` and the `ready` and `heartbeat` frames. `surface-message` also needs `read:transcripts`, and the `remote-*` events `read:remote`.
- An event a plugin adds is admin-only.
- Two frames are not in the catalog: `gap` (events were dropped, see "Reconnecting") and `closed` (the daemon ended the stream, see "Server-Sent Events"). Any stream can receive them.

### The least-privilege client

What a non-admin credential can and cannot do with conversations, for a device token holding `read:sessions`, `write:sessions`, `read:transcripts` and `read:own-sessions`:

| Action | Non-admin? | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| List workspaces, create a hosted session, give it its first turn | Yes | `sessions.hosted.workspaces`, `sessions.hosted.create` with `initialPrompt` (not with `originSurface` `agent`). |
| Send a further turn (`sessions.followUp`, `sessions.steer`, `sessions.messages.create`) | No | Admin methods. |
| Stream the turn (text deltas, tool calls), its approvals and its lifecycle | Yes, its own sessions | `read:own-sessions`: `GET /api/control-plane/events?domains=turn,tools,gate,session` delivers the frames of the sessions this principal created or attached to, and the `approval-update` and `hosted-session-update` events for them. Every other session's frames are withheld. |
| Know the turn has ended | Yes | Live: `TURN_COMPLETED` on `turn`, or `hosted-session-update` with `hosted-session-turn-ended`. By polling: `sessions.hosted.list` (`read:transcripts`), where the session's `status` goes `running` then `idle`, and `turnCount` and `lastTurnAt` move. |
| Read the reply | Yes, also after the session ended | `sessions.hosted.history` (`read:transcripts`) returns `session` and `history` with the `user`, `assistant`, `system` and `tool` messages, for a live or an ended session, also after a daemon restart, for `hostedSessions.terminatedRetentionMs` (24 hours) after it ended. `sessions.hosted.attach` (`write:sessions` and `read:transcripts`) returns the same `history` while the session is live. `GET /api/sessions/{id}/messages` does not have the reply (see "7. Read the transcript"). |
| Cancel a running turn | Yes | `sessions.turns.cancel` (`write:sessions`). |
| Detach, kill | Yes | `sessions.hosted.detach`, `sessions.hosted.kill`. |
| Approve or deny a tool call the turn asks for | No | Admin and owner-only. In `ask-me` mode a non-admin's turn waits for the owner; with `read:own-sessions` the client sees the ask (`approval-update`) and its answer. |
| Run a task | No | `tasks.create` is admin. |

So the least-privilege client that works end to end is:

- **One turn per session, followed live:** a device token with `read:sessions`, `write:sessions`, `read:transcripts` and `read:own-sessions`. Open `GET /api/control-plane/events?domains=turn,tools,gate,session`, create the session with `initialPrompt`, follow its frames by its id until the turn ends, then call `sessions.hosted.history` and read the last `assistant` message in `history` (a failed turn leaves a `system` message instead, for example `No model 'openrouter:openrouter/free' for provider 'openrouter' in registry.`). Without `read:own-sessions`, poll `sessions.hosted.list` about once a second until the session's `status` is `idle` and its `turnCount` has grown. Kill or detach the session when done.

**The reply stays readable after the session ends.** A session whose detach policy is `kill` (the default, `hostedSessions.detachPolicy`) ends by itself when its last attached client detaches or its attachment lease lapses (an attach renews it; the lease is `leaseMs` on attach, 30 seconds to 24 hours, default `hostedSessions.attachmentTtlMs`, 10 minutes), when no client was ever attached and it has sat idle for one lease after its last turn, and when the daemon restarts. A `survive` session ends only when it is killed. Once ended, `sessions.hosted.attach` answers `409` `HOSTED_SESSION_TERMINATED` (the reason in brackets says why it ended), but `sessions.hosted.history` still returns the record and the whole transcript, the reply included, to the credential that created the session or one an owner shared it with (any admin credential reads any session), for `hostedSessions.terminatedRetentionMs` (24 hours) after it ended, and across a daemon restart. After that the id answers `404` `SESSION_NOT_FOUND`. Another non-admin credential is refused `403` `HOSTED_SESSION_NOT_OWNED`.

- **Several turns, approvals or tasks:** an admin credential. Use a device token minted without a scope list, so it can be revoked on its own.

## Calling a method

### REST routes

Path parameters are in the path; for `GET`, other inputs are query parameters; for `POST`, inputs are the JSON body. Example:

```sh
curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $GV_TOKEN" 'http://127.0.0.1:3421/api/tasks?limit=5'
```

```json
{"queued":0,"running":0,"blocked":0,"totals":{"created":0,"completed":0,"failed":0,"cancelled":0},"tasks":[]}
```

### The invoke route

`POST /api/control-plane/methods/<methodId>/invoke` calls any invokable method by id. The request body is an envelope: the method's input goes under `body`, and `query` is optional.

```json
{ "body": { "<input field>": "<value>" }, "query": { } }
```

Sending the input without the envelope is refused:

```json
{"error":"Missing required field: body. Expected envelope shape: { query?, body }","status":400}
```

An unknown method id answers `404` `{"error":"Unknown gateway method","code":"METHOD_NOT_FOUND","status":404}`. A method that is in the catalog but cannot be dispatched by id (for example the streams, `/login`, `/logout`) answers `400` with code `NOT_INVOKABLE`. The response body is the method's output.

### The WebSocket

Open `ws://<daemon>/api/control-plane/ws?domains=<comma list>` (or `wss://`) with `Authorization: Bearer <token>` on the upgrade. Optional query parameter `clientKind`: `tui`, `web`, `slack`, `discord`, `ntfy`, `daemon` or `webhook` (default `web`). The daemon must serve the WebSocket (`controlPlane.streamMode` `websocket` or `both`; see "Live update streams" in the previous part); otherwise the upgrade answers `409` `STREAM_MODE_NOT_SERVED`.

Frames are JSON text. The client sends:

| Frame | Effect | Reply |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `{"type":"auth","token":"<optional>","domains":["session"],"label":"<optional>"}` | Confirms the principal and optionally subscribes. | `{"type":"auth","ok":true,"clientId":"cp-...","principalId":"shared-token"}`, or `ok:false` and the socket closes. |
| `{"type":"subscribe","domains":["turn","tools"]}` | Add event domains. | `{"type":"subscribed","clientId":"...","domains":[...]}` |
| `{"type":"unsubscribe","domains":["tools"]}` | Remove domains (all when `domains` is omitted). | `{"type":"unsubscribed",...}` |
| `{"type":"ping"}` | Keep-alive. | `{"type":"pong","ts":1795022871821}` |
